Punch your holes in one clean stroke with the awl held true, since a hole driven at a slant tips the rivet, and the collar then bites crooked. Slide the shank home, cap it with its washer, and work the head with short taps rather than heavy blows. One hard strike flattens the metal sideways and spoils the seat it ought to sit in. Check at every stage that the lining inside has not rucked up, because a fold will let the whole assembly sink under use and the stitching will give way in the middle. Last of all, take your time smoothing the rim of the head, so that no tool marks remain: a sharp edge will cut through any thread that brushes it.

units: glass-blowing workshops share the same burden over energy
their furnaces have to be kept hot without a break
a mass of glass that has cooled cracks when the heat comes back
the workshops keep firing even when orders fall away
that obligation weighs heavily on what they spend
several workshops are trying out a shared furnace kept alight at all times
the blowers come to draw their material at slots spread through the day
the system calls for containers that can be moved and better insulation
the first readings show less fuel burnt for each object made
the arrangement does not suit workshops too far from the shared furnace
text: In a valley where glass has been blown for generations, the workshops all live with the same burden: their furnaces can never be allowed to cool down, since a chilled mass of glass cracks the moment the heat comes back into it. So the makers keep the fire up even when orders thin out, and the bill for that weighs heavily on what they spend. A group of workshops has just tried out a shared answer. One furnace, held at heat around the clock, serves the blowers of the neighbourhood in turn, each of them coming to draw glass at an agreed slot. It calls for pots that can be shifted, insulation of a better sort, and a firm hold on the timetable. The first readings show less fuel burnt for each object made. Those running it accept that the arrangement suits nobody sited too far from the shared furnace.

units: two hammers lying together look identical at first glance
the metal-beater's hammer has a rounded polished head
that head leaves no mark on the surface it strikes
its handle is short and thick, for a quick movement
the decorator's tool has a light, almost flat head
its handle thins down and turns supple towards the grip
the first tool shifts the material in bulk
the second works only on the surface
the traces of wear differ sharply from one tool to the other
neither can stand in for the other
text: Two hammers lie next to each other on the workbench, and a careless glance would readily take them for one and the same tool. The first belongs to the metal-beater: its head is domed and polished, so that it slides over the sheet without printing any mark on it, and the handle is short and thick, cut for a quick stroke. The second is the chaser's. Its head is light, almost flat, and the shaft narrows steadily towards the grip until it flexes under the fingers. The one drives the metal into shape, the other barely grazes it. Wear tells the same story: the beater's cheeks are scuffed all over, while the edges of the chaser's head stay crisp. Set together, they speak of two opposite dealings with matter, the one after volume, the other after the mark. Neither could ever stand in for the other.

units: teaching often ranks the manual trades as a fallback
that ranking misses the mental demand of skilled movement
fine adjustment calls for constant judgement of the material
no written work replaces that direct reading
repeating a movement is not the same as acting mechanically
the craftsman alters his settings at every attempt
a technique that stops being practised is lost within one generation
such techniques rarely leave any written trace
goods that can be mended cost less in use than goods that are thrown away
the writer asks for fair recognition and not for idealisation
text: Too many schools still present the manual trades as a second choice, the place you land when you have failed elsewhere. That ranking deserves taking apart point by point. It ignores, first, how much thinking a skilled movement demands: fitting a part to within a fraction means reading the material without let-up, and no book stands in for that. It confuses repetition with mindless routine, when in truth the maker alters every setting each time he begins the movement again. It overlooks how easily the knowledge dies, for a technique that stops being practised is gone within one generation, leaving nothing written behind. And it rests on a false idea of worth, since goods that can be mended cost less over their life than goods thrown away. Restoring these trades is not about dressing them up, but about granting them what an honest reckoning would allow.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: the goldsmith avoids setting stones at the end of the day because her hands tremble
her mother practised the same craft in front of her during her childhood
watching her mother settled her choice of trade
the lack of fine tools in the family workshop forced her to improvise
she smoothed her pieces with a hide stretched over a wooden block
that early constraint gave her great patience
her work is known for holding fast and staying free of scratches
her refusal of short deadlines lengthens the queue of her customers
she maintains that haste always leaves a mark in the material
text: By evening her hands shake, just a little, and that is why she settled long ago on a rule she has never broken: no stone goes into its setting once the light has gone. As a child she watched her mother tilt a blade against warm metal, and the sight settled the question of what she would do with her life. The family workshop held no tool fine enough for the job, so she learnt to smooth her pieces on a hide stretched over a block of wood, and the slowness of it left her with a patience out of the ordinary. That is what lies behind the name she carries now: her settings hold, and her surfaces come away unscratched. Because she turns down anything hurried, the queue of people waiting on her grows longer every season. Rush the material, she says, and it keeps the mark of it.

units: the product is criticised because it sets too early
a dry mark appears across wide surfaces and can no longer be removed
the thinner lifts too quickly in heated rooms
the maker advises adding an additive that slows the drying
this additive does not weaken the final coat
he also advises laying it on in thin overlapping bands
tests on hardwood confirm the improvement
the scraping tool must be honed before each application
the assessment is mixed and depends on the willingness to change one's practice
text: The complaint that follows this varnish everywhere is that it grabs too soon. Brushed across a wide panel, it begins to set before the brush has finished its run, and the dry edge left behind can never be worked out again. Examination points to the thinner, which lifts far too fast in a heated room. The maker offers an answer in two parts. A retarder, poured in small amount, stretches the working time without weakening the cured coat. The second part is about the hand: lay the varnish on in narrow bands that overlap, never in broad sweeps. Trials on hardwood panels bear the gain out, provided the scraper is honed before each coat. The judgement therefore stays mixed. It is a demanding product, dependable for anyone willing to rework their habits, disappointing for anyone who wants a result straight away.

units: the writer is writing from a workshop recommended by his correspondent
the rods are sorted before the weaving in this place
the objects made keep their shape once dry
in the earlier workshop the pace was faster
the pieces from the earlier workshop lost their shape quickly
the former teacher merely showed a movement to copy
the present teacher breaks down each movement and allows mistakes
the writer advances more slowly but remembers more
the difficult stages are carried out in silence in this new workshop
text: I am writing from the basket workshop you recommended to me, and I should like to set out what separates it from the last. Here the rods are sorted before any weaving begins, and the difference tells: the baskets keep their curve once they have dried. Where I was before, the pace was quicker, but the pieces lost their shape within days. The teaching differs as well. My former master would show a movement and wait for me to copy it, whereas the one here breaks every movement down and lets me get it wrong without stepping in. I come on more slowly, and I remember far more. The room itself is unlike the other, too: the delicate stages are done in silence, where the old workshop hummed with talk. I thank you for pointing me towards this place, and I send you my respectful regards.

units: three qualities are named as conditions for entering this trade
the folding tool must be held without stiffening the wrist
a tightened wrist sends the fold off course
the shades of the covering materials must agree whatever the light in the room
the sequence of operations for the rounded spine cannot be altered
the workshops say the training has no set length
a beginner's progress is described as uneven
those who practise the trade name the freedom of the hand among its rewards
mending a damaged object brings a satisfaction the practitioners mention
text: What is asked of anyone who wants a place in a bookbinding workshop? Three aptitudes come up again and again in the masters' answers. The first belongs to the hand: the folder is held without stiffening the wrist, or the fold runs off at an angle. The second belongs to the eye, since leather and cloth must agree with one another under a dim light as surely as under a bright one. The third is a matter of remembering movements, because a rounded spine comes out of a sequence whose order will bear no swapping. And the training, how long does it run? The workshops answer that it has no set end, and that a careful beginner comes on in uneven steps. What is there to gain from so exacting a path? Those who practise it name the freedom of the hand, the variety of the work, and the pleasure of seeing a ruined volume put back into use.

units: the beginner turned up before the appointed hour
he asked for permission to handle the cutting tools
the craftsman refused and gave him a cleaning task
the request was made again seven days later
the craftsman then supplied a metal plate and asked for a straight line
the line that came out ran off course
the craftsman corrected the position of the tool and of the finger without any remark
the next day's line was distinctly better
the craftsman played the success down by mentioning how many lines would be needed
he quietly admitted having done worse at the same age
text: The apprentice turned up ahead of time and asked the engraver outright whether he was allowed to touch the burins. Not yet, said the master, who handed him a broom instead and laughed about it. A week on, the lad came back and asked the same thing again. This time the engraver put a copper plate down on the bench and told him to try cutting one straight line, nothing more. The line wandered off to one side. The master made no criticism of it; he only showed him how to angle the tool and where the thumb belongs. The next day the apprentice cut a line that was almost clean, and he made rather a lot of it. One line is not a trade, the engraver told him, and it would take thousands of them before he had any right to talk like that. Then he added, more quietly, that his own had been less straight at the same age.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: the widening of the trade routes brought more orders than the workshops could handle
the craftsmen changed the way they bent the boards
round hearths replaced heating each piece on its own
several boards were softened at the same time
the vessels that came out had identical measurements
the merchants could work out the size of their loads in advance
disagreements over the quantities carried grew fewer
the rise in demand called for more young people in training
the trade bodies made entry to the craft harder
the fear of seeing the craft weakened led to a setting of the movements into rules
text: As the trading routes widened, the cooperages found themselves with more orders than they could ever fill. The pressure pushed the craftsmen to rethink the way they bent their staves: instead of heating each piece on its own, they built round hearths where a dozen boards softened together. The change carried a consequence nobody had looked for. Since the casks now came out to the same measurements, merchants could work their loads out in advance, and quarrels about the quantities delivered fell away. Standard sizes fed the demand, and the demand called for more apprentices. The trade bodies then tightened their rules of entry, afraid of watching the craft thin out. Out of that fear grew the long setting of the movements into rules that the workshops kept up long afterwards.

units: an uneven surface takes up the colour unevenly
dark patches appear instead of a smooth gradation
wood cut across its fibres drinks more of the product
the correction rests on a graded run of abrasives
one starts with a harsh abrasive that removes the ridges left by the tool
no intermediate grade may be skipped
each abrasive removes only the marks of the one before it
the final smoothing follows the direction of the fibres
wetting the wood before the last pass raises the fibres so that they can be laid down for good
text: A rough surface drinks the stain unevenly, and the craftsman who overlooks so small a thing finds dark patches spreading where he had hoped for a soft gradation. The fault lies in the grain itself: cut across, it opens and swallows three or four drops where flat grain will take only one. The remedy is a patient climb. Begin with a biting abrasive, which levels off the ridges the blade has left behind. Move on to a medium grit, then to a fine one, and never skip a stage, since each paper takes out nothing but the scratches of the one before it. Polish last of all along the run of the grain, and wet the wood before the final pass, so that the fibres it raises may be laid down for good. The surface then comes smooth under the palm, and the stain settles across it in one even tone.

units: two cutting edges were shown to a doubting beginner
the first edge was ground to a close angle
it took long shavings in a soft wood
it buckled on meeting a hard patch in the wood
the second edge had a more open angle
it damaged the soft fibre and left an uneven bottom
it went through the hard patches without harm
the conclusion drawn is that a tool can be judged only against its use
the close angle is kept for finishing passes
the open angle suits the quick removal of material
text: Two blades laid side by side on the bench served as the lesson for a trainee who doubted that angles mattered. The first, a plane iron ground to a close angle, bit into soft wood in unbroken shavings, yet it crumpled the moment it entered a knotty log. The second, ground blunter, tore the soft fibre and left a ragged bottom, and still it crossed the knot without flinching. The workshop drew its conclusion: a tool is worth nothing apart from the job it is meant for. So the keen edge is kept for finishing, where what comes away is counted in the thinnest of slivers, and the stout edge for roughing out, when shifting bulk matters more than the surface left behind. The trainee held on to the rule and put it in his own words: you choose an angle against the material, not against the man beside you.

units: four supplies must be gathered on the working surface
the suppleness of the rods is checked by bending them
rods that are too stiff must soak for about sixty minutes
the assembly starts with eight rods crossed in the shape of a star
the centre is held down with the finger during the weaving
each pass must be drawn tight against the one before without any sideways pull
the upright rods are then raised to form the sides
evenness is checked by holding the object at eye level
the top edge is folded inwards and then held with a stitched seam
the drying is done flat and away from any source of heat
text: Before you begin, set out on the bench the following: a bundle of softened fibres, a curved needle, waxed thread and a pair of straight-bladed scissors. Check that the rods will bend without cracking; should they resist, soak them and leave them there for an hour. Turn next to the setting-up. Cross eight rods in a star, hold the centre down under your thumb, then weave, drawing each pass tight against the one before it and never pulling to one side. Raising the walls comes next. Bring the uprights up one by one and carry the weave round in a spiral, checking the evenness at eye level. Finish the piece. Cut the ends on the slant, turn the top edge inwards over the uprights, and stitch right round with waxed thread. Leave the work to dry flat, well away from any source of heat.

units: a demonstration open to the public is taking place in a forge in an old district
the craftswoman lit her fire and told the public what she would be doing
the metal brought to a high heat was curved with the hammer
those watching saw the colours of the piece change
the piece was cooled in a trough
a file served to even out the surface
the craftswoman pointed out that strength does not rule out a fine finish
children were invited to hold the gripping tool
an opening one evening a week was announced
the neighbours will be able to follow the making of a grille
text: Onlookers are pressing round the forge in the old quarter of the town, where a public demonstration has just opened. Early in the afternoon the smith lit her hearth and told the crowd gathered there what she meant to make. An hour later the bar came out of the coals glowing and took its curve under measured blows of the hammer. Those watching saw the piece pass from white to brown, then darken in the quenching trough. The smith next took up a file and brought the surface smooth, remarking that strength is no excuse for rough work. Towards the close of the afternoon she invited the youngest of them to hold the tongs while she struck. The session ended on an announcement: the workshop will open one evening a week, so that the neighbourhood may follow the making of a balcony grille.

units: the clay delivered to the workshop loses its moisture too quickly
a body that is too dry breaks and the walls give way before the kiln
the craftsman wraps every block in a soaked cloth
the blocks are kept away from heat and from draughts
this treatment makes the body supple again and easy to throw
the dust that settles on damp pieces spoils the glaze
a sheet has been stretched above the shelves
the floor is damped before every throwing session
the vessels leave the kiln with a smooth, soft surface
the potter puts the success down to the care given to what surrounds the hand
text: The clay reaches the pottery workshop in dark blocks, and it gives up its moisture far too quickly. Worked too dry, the body crumbles beneath the fingers; the walls slump long before the kiln. The potter has answered with patience. He now wraps every block in a soaked cloth and sets it down in the shade, well out of the draught. The body softens again, yields to the palm, turns willingly on the wheel. One trouble still remains. Dust drifts onto the damp pieces and dulls the glaze. To keep it off, he has stretched a fine sheet above the shelves and damps the floor before each throwing session. The bowls then leave the kiln with a smooth, satin skin, warm to look at. Success, he says, rarely lies in the hand alone; it lies in the care given to everything that surrounds the hand.

units: the writer sets two ways of joining the timbers of a roof against each other
the traditional joint spreads the loads through the thickness of the wood
this joint grows tighter as it ages
fixing with bolts gathers the stresses around the holes
repeated shaking weakens the metal part
the argument from speed leaves out what later repairs cost
strength is measured by the ability to shift without snapping
experienced hands set a timber according to the way the tree grew
that judgement cannot be handed over to a machine
the writer judges a method by how long it serves
text: Set a roof frame cut with tenons and mortices beside one held together by bolts, and a badly framed argument comes clear. The jointed frame passes its loads through the whole thickness of the timber, takes up movement and grows tighter as it ages. The bolted frame gathers its stresses around the drilled holes, where steel turns brittle under repeated shaking. Speed of erection is the usual boast, and it leaves out what the later repairs cost. A strong joint is not the one that holds best through its first winter; it is the one that shifts without snapping. Carpenters trained the old way read the grain, keep clear of the knots, and set each timber the way the tree grew. No machine makes that call. Defending them is not nostalgia. It is admitting that a method is judged by how long it serves, not by how fast it goes up.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: the woman described works at bookbinding and is held by her fellows to be experienced
she learnt the trade beside a master who did not speak
that master corrected her way of working by moving her hands
her equipment includes bone tools, a sewing frame and presses of old timber
she uses skins, undyed cloth and papers marbled in a trough
she takes on two pupils every season
she picks them for their staying power rather than their skill
she holds that failure teaches more than success
she keeps her own early failures at home
her bindings are found in study collections and carry no name
text: The binder in question has worked at her bench for enough winters to be held by her fellows as a thoroughly seasoned hand. Her account falls into parts. Training first: years beside a master who never spoke, and who set her hands right by moving them. Then the equipment, bone folders, a sewing frame, presses whose knotted timbers groan at every turn of the screw. Then the materials: soft skins, undyed cloth, papers marbled in the trough. Teaching last, for she takes on two apprentices a season and picks them for their staying power rather than their neatness of hand. A failed binding, she holds, teaches far more than one that comes right, and she keeps her own early failures in a drawer at home. Her volumes pass through study libraries, and not one of them carries her name.

units: the visit follows the order its makers intended
the opening room shows unsharpened blades straight from the forge
the critic finds this first part plain and spare
the second section gathers tools that have been used
one cutting tool bears a nick left by a hard place in the wood
another tool shows an edge blunted by repeated use
the labels stay easy to follow without losing precision
the third room jumbles the trades together and confuses the visitor
the end of the visit shows silent images of hands at work
the verdict is favourable in spite of a weakening in the middle
text: An exhibition given over to cutting tools unfolds exactly in the order its makers intended. The opening room holds raw blades, straight from the forge and still black with scale; the argument is plain there, the staging spare. Next come the tools that have worked for a living, and the interest rises: a chisel nicked by a hard knot, a plane whose blunted iron speaks of thousands of passes. The labels keep clear of jargon without thinning the description. The third room disappoints. Cases are piled up, trades are jumbled together, and the thread so carefully laid out slips from the visitor's hand. The closing sequence partly recovers it, projecting hands at work in silence, with no music at all. One leaves persuaded by the whole demonstration, in spite of a marked hollow at the centre of the route.

units: the writer answers a question about how well his workshop is running
the seat he made would not stand level
the cause lies in a joint driven home into timber that was not dry enough
the shrinking of the wood as it dried loosened the joint
the writer took the whole piece apart
a craftsman nearby had warned him
he let the wood dry for a whole season before making it again
the joints hold now and the surface comes up smooth easily
he blames his own hurry rather than any lack of skill
he asks to borrow a hollow tool because his own is finished
text: You ask whether the workshop is running properly at last, so I had better be straight with you. The stool I put together over the winter wobbled, and it wobbled because I drove the tenons home into timber that was still damp. As the leg dried it shrank, the joint worked loose, and the thing ended up limping. So I pulled it all apart. The old joiner in the shed next door had warned me, and this time I let the boards breathe for a whole season before starting again. The joints hold now, and the surface I left rough after the first sanding comes up smooth with hardly any effort. It was my hurry that beat me, far more than my skill. If you come this way, bring your curved gouge. Mine has given up and I daren't hollow a seat without one. Write soon, and tell me whether your kiln is drawing.

units: a guild of weavers sees its plantations failing
the shoots they cut have grown shorter and snap during shaping
worn-out ground is held to blame
cutting that comes round too often tires the stools of the plant
the plots are now worked at longer intervals
organic matter is worked into the ground
older and suppler varieties have been put back into cultivation
output dropped by a third in the first season and then climbed again
the spokesman of the group grants a rise in the price of the objects sold
the collective hands on to beginners a way of cutting that was almost abandoned
text: What becomes of a trade when its raw material runs short? Put to a guild of basket weavers whose beds of willow are failing, the question drew an answer in three movements. The finding first: the rods they cut come up shorter now, and they snap under the weave. Then the diagnosis, worn-out ground and cutting that comes round too often for the stools to recover. Then the correction, two seasons old: longer rotation between the plots, compost worked in, older and suppler varieties put back into the ground. Output dropped by a third in the first season and has since climbed again, their spokesman explains. Asked about the price of a basket, he grants the rise and stands by it, since lasting work costs what it costs. The group now teaches beginners how to cut, a skill almost no workshop was still handing on.

units: a stoneworker teaches his pupil that every block calls for its own hand
the first stone is coarse in texture and full of hard grains
that stone rings brightly when it is struck
the second stone is softer and comes off with a smooth finish
the pupil wants to know which of the two is the better
the master refuses to weigh one material directly against the other
he holds that only the intended use can settle it
the coarse stone suits a step because it does not slip
the smooth stone suits a sill because water runs off it
the master foretells that the pupil will one evening stop asking
text: The stonemason was explaining patiently to his apprentice that no two blocks laid side by side ever call for the same hand. The first, he said, is coarse, full of hard grains that catch the punch and ring bright under the mallet. The second is softer, gives itself up to the drag and comes off satin, almost kind to the palm. The apprentice then asked which was the better stone of the two. There is no sense in the question, the mason answered: you do not weigh one material against another, you weigh what is wanted of them. A stair tread wants the coarse block, which will not slip under a boot; a window sill takes the other, which water washes and leaves. Then he added, wiping the white dust from his forearms, that the lad would choose for himself on the evening he stopped asking.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: the changes in the metal casting shops are set out strand by strand
charred wood was given up for a denser fuel
that change raised the heat reached in the vessels
the air devices were at first worked by arm
they were later driven by the force of water
this mechanisation made the heating steady
rammed sand took the place of clay for forming the impressions
this material stands changes of heat better and draws away without cracking
a measured addition of tin gave a metal that took knocks better
a post for watching the furnace appeared and cut into the founder's authority
text: To follow the history of the metal casting shops properly, one has to take the strands apart. The fuel to begin with: charred wood gave way to denser coals, and the heat in the vessels climbed with it. Then the bellows, at first pumped by arm alone, later swung by wheels that running water turned, which made the heating steady. The moulds too: rammed sand took the place of raw clay, since it stands the sudden changes of heat better and draws away without cracking. And the alloys, where a measured dose of tin yielded a metal less brittle, able to ring without flying apart. Every one of these gains rearranged the division of the work itself. The founder gave up part of his authority to the man who watched and set the furnace, a post that had existed in none of these shops before.

units: the worker lifts a quantity of molten glass on the end of his iron
that mass is almost runny at the moment it is taken up
it is rolled along a metal surface to bring it true and firm the outside
blowing air opens a cavity inside the mass
brief reheats alternate with spells of shaping
glass that has gone too cold splits at the smallest knock
the opening at the top is widened with a pair of jaws
the piece is then handed to an assistant
a last stay in an oven brings the heat down by stages through the night
without that gradual cooling the object would break of itself
text: The glassblower begins by dipping his iron into the molten bath and lifting out a thick orange gather, so nearly liquid that it hangs by its own weight alone. He rolls it along a steel plate to bring it true and firm the outside. Then the first breath: a bubble opens in the heart of the mass and widens as the air presses. From here he works in turns, brief reheats against spells of shaping, for glass that has lost its heat grows brittle and splits at the smallest knock. Once the belly is right, he flares the neck with a pair of jaws, frees the piece and hands it to an assistant. The last stage belongs to the annealing oven, where the heat comes down by stages through the night. Without that measured descent, the strains inside would burst the object as it stood quietly on a shelf.

units: a damaged drain let water through above a gilding workshop
the store room was reached by the leak
the fine metal leaves kept there are extremely light
the paper sheets between them buckled under the damp
the leaves welded together and became unusable
the shortage of supplies halted the repair of an old frame
the woman who placed the order saw her date pushed back
the accident had consequences for three other trades
the store was moved down low and shut into a cupboard
a notebook now records the state of each batch every time it is opened
text: A split length of gutter above the gilding workshop was enough to upset a whole season. Water crept into the store, where beaten leaves of gold lay sleeping, so thin that a breath will carry them off. The damp buckled the tissue papers that kept the sheets apart, and the sheets welded together, good for nothing at all. With no stock to hand, the gilder had to break off the repair of an old frame, which pushed back her client's order, and the client in her turn was working to a date. Step by step the accident reached a joiner, a varnisher and a carrier. Out of it the gilder drew a rule she keeps to now: the store has come down to floor level, into a shut cupboard, and a notebook records the state of each batch every time it is opened. The roof still leaks, but the gold sleeps dry.

units: a mountain route is split into stretches classed by the ground underfoot
the woodland stretch runs in wide bends over soft earth
the slope there stays gentle and even
the scree comes from the rock face broken up by frost
these stones shift underfoot and force quick footwork
the ridge stretch is swept by the wind and narrows in places
the descent leads to a damp gully where water-polished rock is slippery
each stretch calls for its own kit
mapmakers mark these kinds of ground with a graphic symbol
this information lets the walker weigh the effort before setting off
text: Mapmakers break a mountain route into stretches, each one named after the ground you cross. The first is the woodland path, which swings through wide bends over soft earth, and the slope there stays gentle and even. Then comes the scree, where stones prised off the rock face by frost shift under the boot and force you to step quickly and lightly. The third stretch runs along a ridge open to the wind, narrowing in places to little more than the width of a table. The fourth drops towards a damp gully, where the water has polished the rock until it is slippery. Every stretch calls for its own kit: a soft shoe under the trees, a stiff sole on the stones, a light rope near the drop. Hatching on the map marks these surfaces, so that a walker can weigh the effort before setting off.

units: the party left the shelter very early
a veil of mist still lay over the lower valley at the start
the guide had warned that the ford might be cut off if the snow melted quickly
the descent to the river was made without a pause
the river was fuller than the day before
the crossing was arranged in order of increasing weight
a rope was strung between two boulders to make the passage safe
the packs were carried over separately from the heaviest walkers
the party then dried off in an open clearing in the wood
the guide saw the manoeuvre as an ordinary precaution
text: The party left the stone shelter at first light, with mist still lying thick in the bottom of the valley. The guide had warned them the evening before: if the thaw quickened, the ford would be impassable by midday. So they went down to the river without stopping, reaching it as the fog began to tear apart. The water stood higher than the day before, rolling pebbles along with a dull, heavy sound. The crossing was made in order of weight, the lightest first, with a rope strung between two boulders to make the passage safe; the packs went over on their own, apart from the heaviest walkers. It took less time than anyone had feared. On the far bank a clearing gave dry ground, and there each of them wrung out their clothes. The walkers spoke of it afterwards with restrained pride; to the guide it was no more than an ordinary precaution.

units: the angle of the slope must be judged before committing to a mountain flank
the gradient governs the danger
a gentle slope holds its snow in place
a steep slope lets go as soon as it is walked on
a pole serves to test how the layers of snow are stacked
a surface layer shifting over a hardened one means turning back
it is better to move along a rib than in a groove of the ground
a groove gathers moving snow and magnifies it
walkers must go over one at a time so as not to be swept away together
the sound of water under the snow reveals a hollow underfoot
text: Before you commit to a steep flank, judge the angle of the slope, because the angle is what governs the danger. A gentle incline holds its snow in place; a steep one lets go at the first footfall, and the slide carries the walker down with it. Probe the layers with a pole, and if the top layer shifts over a hardened crust, turn back, since that structure is on the point of breaking. Look for a line that follows a rib rather than a groove in the ground, because a groove gathers the moving snow and multiplies its force. Send the party over one at a time, so that a single fall cannot sweep everyone away. Listen, too, for water running beneath the snow: that sound means a hollow underfoot, and a hollow gives way under load. If doubt remains, go back down; turning back costs no more than an extra stretch of walking.

units: the coast path has been losing ground for two seasons
salt spray and swell are hollowing out the rock face from below
walkers use the stretch all the same
the warning sign is regularly hidden by the plants
the person in charge of the paths admits that the ban has failed
a fresh line has been set out further from the sea in the low scrub
this line has steps and a wooden handrail
walkers choose it for its comfort and not out of obedience
the old stretch is closing over on its own under the scrub
the warden reckons a better offer beats a telling-off
text: For two seasons now the coast path has been losing ground, eaten away by spray and by the swell that hollows out the cliff from underneath. Walkers use it all the same. The view is good, the going is easy, and the warning sign keeps vanishing under the undergrowth. The warden in charge of the paths admits it without hedging: banning people did not work, they have tried that. So they tried something else. A fresh line has been pegged out further back, in the low scrub, with steps cut into the ground and a wooden handrail. People take it because it is more comfortable, not because they have been told to. Meanwhile the threatened stretch is quietly closing over under the thorn bushes. You gain nothing by telling walkers off, she says with a shrug; you gain by offering them something better.

units: two valleys on either side of the same range have very little in common
the eastern valley is wide and flat
its river loops slowly through it and carries silt
grassland comes down to the water's edge there
the western valley forms a narrow cut
a fast stream drops from pool to pool there and throws up foam
the sides carry scattered trees clinging to the rock
the difference comes from the steepness of the ground
ground that is almost level lets the river wander
the first valley is walked without effort while the second is climbed
text: Two valleys lie on either side of the same mountain range, and they have almost nothing in common with each other. The eastern one opens out flat and wide, and its river loops slowly through it, silent, brown with silt, while grassland runs right down to the water's edge. The western one is a narrow cut in the rock: a fast stream drops from pool to pool, white with foam, and thin trees cling to the sides wherever they can find a hold. The difference comes down to the steepness of the ground. Where the ground barely falls, the river takes its time and spreads into bends; where it plunges, the water runs straight and digs. Walkers feel it in their legs. The first valley is strolled through, the second is climbed like a staircase. Two neighbouring landscapes, two ways of wearing down the rock.

units: the author speaks of what is felt before a line of peaks veiled in mist
he blames packaged travel for working like a tick-list
he offers three ways of giving up a fixed programme
the first is to move very slowly
stopping when the shade takes over belongs to this first way
the second is to walk the same path again at another time of year
this return shows that the colours the sounds and the smells have changed
the third is to ignore the names of the peaks on purpose
the author refuses to treat a landscape as something to be hoarded
he sets the one who agrees to dawdle against the one who comes to take stock
text: Who has never stood before a ridge drowned in mist and felt that the eye was after something more than a picture? Travel, as it is sold to us, comes in lists: a viewpoint, a lake, a photogenic clearing, and one ticks them off. I want to argue for three ways of losing your route. The first is slowness: walking at the pace of a grazing herd, stopping wherever the shade settles. The second is return: coming back to the same path in the opposite season and finding that its colours, its sounds and its smells have all changed. The third is chosen ignorance: not learning the names of the peaks beforehand, letting them stand as pure shapes. A landscape is not a thing to be collected. It gives itself to anyone willing to lose an afternoon in it, and shuts against anyone who comes to take stock.

units: the path maintenance worker started out carrying stone for his elder
his first jobs were physical ones
he had to clear away rockfall that had come down on the track
he laid wooden drainage devices across the slope
he was then given the setting of the waymarks
a badly placed marker can send a walker over a drop
he was trained in fitting stone without mortar
he built a first retaining wall under someone else's supervision
he now lays out the routes himself working out the acceptable gradient and the run-off
he teaches his learners that a path the water leaves cleanly looks after itself
text: The man who keeps the paths in repair learned the trade by carrying stone for the man before him. His first jobs were the heavy ones: clearing away rockfall that had spilled onto the track, laying wooden drains across the slope, scouring out the channels. Waymarking came later, and it asked more of him, since a badly placed marker sends a walker over a drop. He was trained in fitting stone without mortar, then built his first retaining wall under another man's eye. These days he lays out the routes himself, working out what gradient the ground will take, turning the path so that the water leaves it instead of following it, choosing where the footing goes. Now he trains learners of his own in turn, and the first lesson he passes on fits in a single line: a well-drained path mends itself.

units: the book deals with high mountain paths and carries conviction
its quality follows from a method the author owns up to
he walked in person every route he presents
he covered them at different times of year
the times given can therefore be trusted
first-hand experience brings out dangers that are absent from maps
the book points in particular to seeping rock a ford swollen by rain and a scree slope loosened by the thaw
the reader comes away better equipped and more careful
the photographs are faulted for showing nothing but clear skies
this visual choice makes the route look too reassuring
text: The book on high mountain paths carries conviction, and its success rests first of all on a method the author owns up to. He walked every route he sets out, and walked them at every time of year; the times he gives can therefore be trusted, and first-hand experience brings out dangers that no survey map would ever show. So the descriptions point to the place where the rock seeps, to the ford that swells after rain, to the band of scree that loosens in a thaw. The reader comes away better equipped and, in consequence, more careful. The photographs are another matter: taken under clear skies, they leave out the mist that governs half of these outings. The choice weakens the argument, because it makes the route look kinder than it is. The book instructs; it reassures rather too quickly.

units: the writer doubts that his previous message was sent on

he announces a departure two stages earlier than planned
text: I hope my last card reached you in the end, though the village postbox looked as if nobody had come to empty it in an age. I am writing from an inn down in the valley, where I have stayed on rather longer than I meant to. Two things went wrong: my boots gave out on the third pass, and the coach that was meant to bring me back does not run outside the busy season. At first I thought I would have to give up and make my own way home. The innkeeper had another idea. His brother-in-law drives down every week with crates for the next town along, and he is glad to take me. In the meantime a cobbler has fitted fresh soles to my boots for very little. So I set off the day after tomorrow, two stages shorter and one story richer. Write to the return address; I shall pick up the post when I arrive.

units: visitor numbers vary a great deal from one time of year to another
the gap is not where you would imagine it

they gather on a very small number of waymarked routes
they move about little and take an enormous number of pictures

it is these scattered visitors who do the most damage
ground trampled by a group recovers
a walker crossing a clearing in the wood upsets the breeding of the birds
the warden favours opening further routes and putting up explanatory signs over penalties
text: Does the number of visitors change from one season to the next? Hugely, says the warden, but not in the way you would expect. In the warm months they arrive in crowds and stay bunched on three or four waymarked paths; they walk very little and photograph endlessly. In the cold months there are hardly any of them, but they go everywhere, off the paths included. And which group causes the trouble? The second, no question. A herd of walkers on a path packs the soil down, and soil recovers. One person cutting across a clearing disturbs the nesting birds, and that does not recover. So what is done about it? The warden would rather widen the choice: further routes opened in the quiet months, and signs that tell the story of a nest instead of forbidding things. And does it work? Better than fines, she says, laughing.

units: the walk leader talks the group through the route before setting off

text: Before departure the leader of the outing talked his group through the entire route in some detail. Fill your bottles at the spring behind the mountain hut, he said, because the next water anywhere along the way lies beyond the summit. The opening stretch follows a deeply rutted track where it is easy enough to injure yourself. One of the walkers questioned the point of carrying a compass on a path that was already waymarked. Mist obliterates the painted marks, he responded, and a marker post knocked over misleads quite as readily as it guides. He asked everyone to tighten their rucksack straps for the climb and slacken them again on the descent. The group moved off with dew still lying across the grass, having agreed the rocky headland at the far end as their meeting place.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: the line of the old trading routes depended on the lie of the land more than on distance

text: Old trading routes were shaped far more by the lie of the land than by sheer distance. A pass that rose too steeply meant harnessing additional draught animals, and that expense alone was enough to divert the wagon trains along a neighbouring corridor, considerably longer but easier going. Entire settlements grew out of that detour. A staging post appeared wherever the animals needed resting; a blacksmith established himself alongside; eventually a market gathered in front of the smithy. Then engineers drove a tunnel beneath the ridge, and the movement reversed. The wagon trains recovered the direct line, the staging posts emptied, and the town that owed its prosperity to the obstacle declined alongside it. Travellers today cross such valleys without suspecting why they are so quiet.

units: a heavily used path grows wider and wider
walkers step round the puddles and destroy the plants along the edges

waterlogged ground turns to a quagmire underfoot
one answer is to put in a timber boardwalk

another answer is to spread compacted stone over a sheet of filter fabric
that layer lets water drain through without being washed away
plants grow back along the sides from the following season
text: A well used path grows wider with every passing year. Walkers step round the puddles, crush the plants along the edges, and before long the route has become a bare strip with water running freely down it. On soft ground the process speeds up: soil that is already soaked cannot take the traffic and turns to a quagmire underfoot. Those who look after wild places have two answers to this. The first is a timber boardwalk, which lifts the walking surface clear of the wet peat and holds everyone to a single fixed width. The second is a bed of crushed stone rolled flat over a sheet of filter fabric, so that rain drains straight through instead of carrying the surface away with it. Either way, plants creep back along the margins by the following season, and the path stops spreading.

units: the narrator remembered a gently shaped shore with a broad sweep of sand
he comes back to that coast after a long absence
the sea has eaten into the foot of the cliff
the wooden steps down to the beach hang in mid air
a fisherman from the village puts the change down to two seasons of storms
the place where the narrator played as a child is now taken by the sea
the narrator feels more surprise than sadness
no human action accounts for the transformation
he leaves by the path that runs along the fields above
text: I had preserved a picture of a soft, rounded coastline with a great sweep of pale sand beneath it. Returning to that coast after years away, I found something else altogether. The sea had eaten into the foot of the cliff, and the wooden steps that once descended to the beach hung in mid air with nothing whatever underneath. A fisherman from the village blamed two winters of storms for the entire transformation. Where I used to run about as a child, water was breaking against bare rock. Oddly, it surprised me rather more than it saddened me. Nobody had excavated anything, nobody had built anything, and yet the bay had been dismantled. I walked back by way of the upper path that borders the cultivated fields, thinking that the shore of my memory existed nowhere any longer.

units: the text sets out the precautions to take before a sea crossing to a nearby island
the wind sweeps the quayside unhindered and empties a bag left half open
it advises strapping down the outer pockets and keeping papers inside
sailings follow the tide and the time posted the day before often changes
it recommends turning up at the landing stage well ahead
the swell builds as soon as the boat clears the sheltered bay
it advises standing in the middle of the deck with your eyes on the shore
nothing necessarily waits for foot passengers at the other end
text: Three things are worth sorting out before you take the ferry across to a neighbouring island. Luggage first: nothing whatever breaks the wind on the quayside, and a bag left half open will empty itself in seconds, so strap down the outer pockets and keep your papers in an inside pocket. Waiting second: the sailings follow the tide, the time posted the evening before is often altered, and anyone with sense turns up at the landing stage well ahead. Seasickness third: the swell builds as soon as the boat clears the sheltered bay, and you will fare better standing in the middle of the deck with your eyes on the shore than shut in a cabin. And at the other end, nothing is bound to be waiting for foot passengers, so expect to walk to the nearest village with your load on your back.

units: workmen have cleared the last slide of mud blocking the road over the pass

an engineer checked the firmness of the new stone on foot

the first vehicles edged round the rocky headland at walking pace
text: At first light the workmen finally cleared the last slide of mud from the road over the pass. The job had begun at the thaw, after a slab of the bank had given way above the hairpin bend. Around midday a digger ground its way up the slope to reinforce the embankment, while two teams pinned steel mesh across the fractured rock face. The wind carried the dust out over the open moor, where half wild horses watched the machine without troubling themselves to move. Late in the afternoon an engineer walked the length of the carriageway, testing the firmness of the fresh stone with his heel. The barrier rose before darkness fell. The first cars edged round the headland at walking pace, and their lights drew a trembling line along the ridge, like a vein of fire opened in the rock.

units: a coastal dune builds up in stages that can be followed without instruments
the wind off the sea rolls dry sand across the foreshore
the sand comes to rest behind an obstacle such as a tuft of grass or a piece of debris
the mound formed in this way slows the wind and increases the deposit
the roots of creeping grasses hold the new layer in place
the hump grows taller instead of blowing apart
a second dune appears seaward of the first once the crest is out of reach of the waves
a damp hollow between the two dunes shelters particular plants because fresh water rises there
a gap cut through the crest lets the wind back in and undoes the whole structure
text: A coastal dune builds itself in stages that anyone can follow without instruments. Dry sand rolls in off the foreshore ahead of the sea wind until something stops it: a tuft of grass, a piece of driftwood, a stranded plank. Grains accumulate in the shelter behind, a small mound forms, and the mound itself slows the wind, so further sand settles. Creeping grasses drive their roots through the fresh layer and anchor it, which is why the hump gains height rather than blowing apart. Once the crest stands above the reach of the waves, a second dune begins seaward of the first, with a damp hollow between them. Fresh water rises close to the surface there, and the plants thriving in it grow nowhere else. Cut a single gap through the crest, by boot or by wheel, and the returning wind undoes the entire structure.

units: the author questions the organised drawing of crowds to places that crowds wear out

the car parks and the paths were never built for such numbers
the author rules out closing the places, which he judges unfair
he proposes a free booking system to spread arrivals across the week
he proposes shared transport to take queues of vehicles off the narrow lanes
he proposes honest signposting that sends people towards quiet valleys next door
text: Should we keep drawing crowds to wild places that crowds wear out? Local councillors are uneasy with the question, since their income depends on the visitors, while the people who live there put up with the congestion and gain nothing from it. The pattern is familiar. A view that is passed around on screens can see its traffic double within a single season, though neither the car parks nor the paths were built for anything of the kind. Closing such places would be unfair, and it is not the answer; spreading the load is. A free booking system moves arrivals across the week. A shared bus takes the queues of cars off the narrow lanes. Honest signposting sends people towards quiet valleys next door that are every bit as fine. What must stop is the selling of silence as though the supply were endless.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
