she says the most dependable equipment fails during heavy swells at night
as a child she went with her mother on the supply runs to the islands
the man before her held every reef in his memory whereas she finds them by their coordinates
text: The woman who keeps the lighthouse describes her post as an occupation of patience, unlike anything her predecessor knew. He lived out on the rock for weeks together, wound up the wick, greased the mechanism and recorded the visibility by hand in a paper log. She monitors an automatic lantern from an office ashore, where a bank of screens flags the slightest malfunction. None of this saddens her in the least. The sea, she reckons, demands precisely the attention it always demanded, and the most dependable equipment imaginable will choose to fail on the night the swell rises. As a child she accompanied her mother on the runs carrying supplies out to the islands. Her predecessor held every reef in his memory; she locates each of them by its coordinates, and never trusts those alone.

units: the author recommends a coastal route opened recently, faults and all
the line of it follows the water almost the whole way
it alternates high stretches with drops into tiny coves
it keeps clear of long tarmac sections
the waymarking is judged clear and evenly spaced without a forest of signs
finding the way becomes uncertain on the approach to the villages
there is nowhere to sit and only one water point a third of the way along
the dry toilets promised in the literature have never been put in
what the author keeps above all is the feel of the route, with the surf, the birds skimming the waves and no other walkers
text: Honestly, this newly opened coastal route is worth the journey, faults and all. The line of the route first: it clings to the water almost the entire way, swinging up onto the cliff tops and dropping again into coves barely wide enough to sit in, and it spares you the long tarmac sections that ruin so many walks. The waymarking next: clear, evenly spaced, no forest of signposts, though you hesitate a moment on the approach to each village. The facilities last, and here I do grumble: nowhere whatever to sit down, a solitary tap roughly a third of the way along, and dry toilets promised by the leaflet that exist nowhere but in the leaflet. What carries it, though, is the atmosphere: surf beneath your boots, birds skimming the waves, nobody whatever ahead of you for an entire hour.

units: the sender is staying in an upstairs room of a place that takes travellers in
the message sets out why the party is behind schedule
the planned route follows a line of high ground open to the wind
the unbroken wind costs the walkers more effort
the party slowed its pace
rain the day before had made the stones slippery
the party went round the narrow gorge by another way
the way round lengthens the walk but keeps the danger off
a long rest was taken beside a spring
the exact hour of arrival will be given later
text: I am writing from the upstairs room of the guesthouse, with the route book lying open in front of me. You asked why we are behind, so here is the whole of it. The track we meant to take runs along an open ridge, and the wind up there never drops. It chills the skin and it eats into your strength, so we shortened our stride and walked more slowly than any of us had reckoned on. Then there was the rain of the day before. It had soaked the loose stone all down the slope, and every step slid a little, which is why we went round the narrow gorge rather than push through it. The way round adds a fair stretch to the walk, but it takes the danger out of the day. We also rested a long while beside a spring, longer than any of us had meant to. I shall give you the exact hour of our arrival tomorrow evening.

units: a correspondent asks about the crowding of wild places
the trouble comes of visitors gathering in one spot at one time of year
the most walked path breaks down under repeated tread
one answer is to open further loops reaching the same high ground
those further loops take other flanks of the mountain
booking ahead staggers the arrivals
it keeps the high shelters from being overwhelmed
another line is to make coming outside the busy season a pleasure
that calls for shelters that stay open and transport that can be relied on
explaining how thin the plant cover is cuts down treading off the path
text: A reader asks us what can be done about the crowds wearing out the finest wild places, and the question deserves a proper answer. The trouble is that nearly everyone turns up in the same spot within the same few weeks, so the one favoured path breaks down under the tread. What can be offered instead? Begin by spreading walkers out: waymark further loops that reach the same high ground from other flanks of the mountain. Booking ahead helps as well, since it staggers arrivals and keeps the high shelters from filling past what they can hold. A third answer is to make the quiet months worth choosing, which means huts that stay open and transport that runs when it says it will. The last is simply telling people how thin the plant cover is up there; walkers who know it keep to the path.

units: a walking guide reckons the southern side is the easier one
a woman who works with maps disputes this without heat
the southern path crosses grazing land and rises at an even gradient
that path asks no particular skill of anybody
the northern flank has stony breaks in the slope
the northern flank gives shade all the way and water in quantity
the guide notes that the evening air cools the southern side
she holds that this air comes and goes while trees shelter without a break
the lodging is comfortable on one side and bare on the other
the two of them conclude that the routes come out level
text: The guide kept saying the southern valley walked better than the northern one, and the mapmaker kept disagreeing, quietly. His path, he said, wound through soft grazing land, rose at an even gradient and asked no skill of anybody. She granted him that, then turned him to the far side: broken and stony, yes, but shaded the whole way, with water at every turn. He came back at her with the evening air, which takes the heat out of the southern slope by late afternoon. She answered that such air comes and goes as it pleases, while a wood shelters you without a break. They went on to the beds: a warm inn on one side, a bare hut on the other. He ended by saying it came down to the walker and to what his legs would take. She allowed that the two routes came out level, for opposite reasons.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: before dependable surveys, people travelled on the strength of spoken accounts
old accounts of travel turn on three unchanging worries
routes bent towards water even when that lengthened them
a stage with nothing to drink cost travellers dearly
the lie of the land pushed people to work round walls of rock
a high pass was climbed only when it cut the journey short by a good deal
travellers wrote down the places where one slept out of the rain
a lodging thought safe pulled a whole flow of traffic into some valley
the dread of fog and of shifting slopes weighed on the routes as well
such routes look senseless on a survey but answered a need to stay safe
text: Picture the old roads, long before anyone had a dependable survey: you set out on hearsay and little else. The accounts of travel that survive circle round three worries, and they hardly shift from one to the next. Water first. Routes bent towards springs however far it took them, because a stage with nothing to drink was paid for dearly. Then the ground itself. A wall of rock was worked round rather than climbed, unless the pass overhead cut whole days off the way. And lodging: men wrote down carefully where a roof would keep the rain off, and one house with a good name could pull the whole traffic into a valley that had nothing else to recommend it. Add the dread of fog and of shifting scree, and you get lines that look senseless drawn on a map yet answer, all of them, to staying safe.

units: a heap of sand starts up around some very slight obstacle
air carrying grains loses its speed behind that obstacle
the sand it was carrying settles there
the mound rises with every gust
the shape that results has an easy slope on the windward side and an abrupt one opposite
the grains climb the exposed face and drop down the other side
that handover shifts the whole shape little by little
plants taking root pin the sand down
the shape then stops travelling and becomes a fixed rise
text: Where does a dune begin? With almost nothing: a tuft of grass, a pebble, a scrap of driftwood lying on flat sand. Wind loaded with grains slows as soon as it passes behind that small thing, and what it slows it lets go of. A swelling forms, and every fresh gust adds a little more to it. Season upon season the heap grows into a shape of its own, with one long easy slope facing the wind and a short abrupt one in its lee. The grains ride up the exposed face, tip over the crest and slide down the far side. That one steady handover is what carries the whole mass forward, a few paces at a time. Then, once plants take hold, their roots pin the sand down where it lies and the travelling comes to an end. What had been moving becomes a settled hill, one the breeze can no longer redraw at will.

units: the boat started letting water in just after leaving the cove
the current made it impossible to get back to the shore they had left
the two aboard drifted to a shore no survey mentioned
their soaked food had to be left where it lay
that loss sent them up the cliff face towards somewhere inhabited
they came out on a flat top covered with low shrubs
from up there they made out a house standing on its own
the man who worked the farm put them up for two nights
one of them said he owed the finest view of his life to the mishap
text: The boat began to let water in as soon as they had cleared the cove, and that was where the trip turned into something else. There was no rowing back against the current, so the two of them let it carry them to a shingle beach that no survey had bothered with. Their food had swollen with the wet and was fit for nothing, and they left it where it lay. That loss is what sent them up the cliff face to look for people. The climb was long and thirsty, and it opened onto a flat top of heather with the wind running clean across it. From up there they made out a roof of pale tiles, and the wreck turned into a piece of luck. The man who worked the farm put them up for two nights and dried their clothes. One of them said, leaving, that a split hull had bought him the widest view of his life.

units: the piece speaks to anyone whose shoulders ache from the first climb onwards
the first move is to tip the whole contents out on flat ground
the belongings are sorted into three heaps according to how far they are needed
the useless heap goes, with no argument
what is kept should weigh no more than a fifth of what the walker weighs
heavy things go against the back and high up
a load carried too low pulls the walker backwards
the hip belt is pulled tight before the shoulder straps
the setting is checked on a short descent
a strap that hurts should be let out a notch before another try
text: Do your shoulders start complaining on the first climb of the day? Then work through this. Tip the pack out on flat ground, the whole of it, and sort what comes out into three heaps: what you cannot do without, what earns its place, and what does not. Get rid of the third heap and do not argue with yourself about it. Weigh what is left; it should come to no more than a fifth of what you weigh. Pack the heavy things against your back and high up, level with the shoulder blades, since weight riding low pulls you backwards and unsteadies you on loose stone. Pull the hip belt tight before you touch the shoulder straps, because the hips must carry the bulk of it. Then go and test the setting on a short descent that you can run down. If a strap bites, let it out a notch and try again.

units: two valleys side by side settled on opposite ways of taking visitors in
one put its money into road works and structures for crossing water
the number of visitors there has doubled
trade has set itself up there
the people living there complain of a noise that never stops in the busy season
the other valley closed the drivable track above the last inhabited place
visitors get in on foot or by shared transport
earnings there rise more gently
the wearing away of the riverbanks has eased and the quiet draws people
neither valley is thinking of turning back
text: Two valleys side by side took opposite roads on the question of visitors, and the difference now shows on the ground. The first spent its money on getting people in: a widened road, a car park cut into terraces, metal footbridges thrown across the torrents. Numbers there have doubled, shops have opened, and those who live in the valley speak of a hum that never stops through the busy months. The second closed the drivable track above the last hamlet, so that anyone going higher walks or rides the shuttle. Earnings climb more gently there, but the riverbanks have stopped wearing away and the quiet has become the thing that draws people. The councillors of both valleys call on one another often. Each of them sees in the other what he most dreads. Neither talks yet of turning back.

units: the high ground described comes in successive levels of differing character
grazing land holds the foot of it, quartered by hedges
a path of pale sand threads between the enclosures
higher up the ground dries out and the plants keep low
grey rock breaks through there in patches
a wall of stone laid without mortar runs along the crest for a great distance
that wall once served to steer the herds
the top is open to the wind and carries a smell of stone
two shallow stretches of water there bring down birds on passage
the far side drops into a wooded hollow with a resting place
text: The plateau gives itself away in steps, and each step has a look of its own. At the foot lies grazing land, quartered by low hedges, with a path of pale sand threading between the enclosures and the drinking troughs. Higher up the heath takes over: the ground dries out, the plants keep close to it, and grey rock breaks through in patches. A wall of stone laid without mortar runs along the crest for a great distance; it was raised long ago to steer the herds to the summer grazing. At the top the wind has nothing to push against, and the air carries a smell of stone. Two shallow pools hold the rainwater and bring down birds on passage. On the far side, last of all, a wooded slope drops into a closed hollow, where a resting place offers a bench, a timber shelter and a spring caught under a slab.

units: the writer holds that the way we travel has slipped by degrees
at the start you went out walking along a river with no fixed plan
you came home tired with very few pictures
then came the lists of places one absolutely had to see
the device worked its way in between the traveller and the country
a mountain pass is now looked at through a lens
walkers come down a glorious path with their eyes on nothing
they hurry towards a viewpoint picked out beforehand
the writer does not want some golden age brought back
he asks only for a halt with no purpose, for the pleasure of breathing
text: We have let travelling go to seed, and it happened by degrees. At first you went out to walk. You followed a river, slept wherever the day ran out, came home with hard calves and two blurred pictures. Then came the lists: the places you absolutely had to see, ranked, scored, ticked off one by one. After that a screen slid in between us and the country, and we took to looking at a pass through a lens before looking at it at all. Now you meet people coming down a glorious path with their eyes on nothing, in a hurry to reach the viewpoint they picked out the night before. I am not asking for some golden age to be brought back; those old rambles were badly prepared as often as not. I ask only that we let ourselves halt for no purpose, in the middle of nowhere, for the pleasure of breathing.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: a specialist in mapping footpaths inspects the routes before the walking season
waymarks hold badly on steep rock faces
walkers lose the route when mist comes down
she measures the slope of the ground with a dedicated instrument
she sets a rod sealed with resin into hard rock
she chooses a weighted post in crumbling rock
each mark must be visible from the one before it
this method cuts down the number of rescue call-outs
she records the positions in a register read by the maintenance teams
text: Before the walking season opens, the woman who maps a footpath network goes out to inspect every route in turn. She knows the trouble well: waymarks hold badly on steep rock faces, and walkers stray off the line as soon as the mist comes down. So she measures the slope with a clinometer, notes what the rock is made of, and picks an anchor to match it. In hard, compact stone she sets a rod sealed with resin; in flaky, crumbling rock she prefers a weighted post that no frost will lift. Then she marks the way in short runs, placing each sign where the one before it can still be seen. The method cuts down the number of rescue call-outs and stops walkers turning back for no reason. Every position goes into a register, which the maintenance teams read through before they set off on their rounds.

units: two viewing platforms look out over the same valley
the upper platform is built on a rocky spur above the gorge
the upper platform is reached by very steep steps
the second platform lies lower down on a grassy shelf
the view from the lower platform is partly hidden by the rock wall
the lower approach suits groups with children better
a strong wind makes the upper platform unpleasant
the writer finally judges the lower platform more satisfying
the quality of a built facility depends on the fit between a place and its public
text: Two viewing platforms look out over the same valley, and they deserve very different verdicts. The higher one stands on a spur of rock above the gorge, and it makes you work for it: the steps are steep, the handrail narrow, and you arrive out of breath in front of a panorama that repays the climb. The lower one sits on a grassy shelf and costs almost nothing to reach, though what the view loses in sweep it gains in gentleness, since the rock wall hides part of it. You might favour the first for its harshness, the second for its kindness towards groups with children. Once the wind gets up, though, the comparison settles in favour of the lower one: the high platform turns unpleasant, while the sheltered ledge keeps its charm. What makes such a place work is less its height than the fit between the site and the people who come to it.

units: the writer is writing from lodgings set on a slope
the wind beats against the shutters of the house
the room is bare and the bed uncomfortable
the window looks out onto a dry expanse
meals include warm flatbreads and a very salty cheese
the drink served has a bitter taste
the walking starts at sunrise on tracks that wind about
the travellers meet more farm animals than vehicles
a man minding beasts gave them water
the writer announces a return worn out and changed
text: I am writing from an inn that clings to the side of a hill, where the wind beats at the shutters half the night. Let me set the trip down in pieces, the way it comes back to me. The room first: bare walls, a hard bed, a huge window that opens onto a dry, empty plateau. The food next: warm flatbreads, a goat's cheese so salty it stings the tongue, and a bitter brew the landlady pours into chipped bowls. Then the walking: we set off at sunrise along tracks that wind and double back, and we meet far more flocks than vehicles. One last heading, the people we came across: a man minding his beasts gave us water, and a village teacher told us the story of her hamlet. Nothing here looks like what I pictured before leaving. I shall come home browned by the sun, worn out, and probably a little altered.

units: the walker set off alone to empty his mind
he missed his first public transport
he waited under a metal shelter
he finished his journey by getting into passing vehicles
he slept behind an embankment to keep out of the wind
he strung a sheet of canvas between two posts as a shelter
the night was freezing but the clear sky kept him from sleeping
a storm turned the track to mud on the way back
he had to turn round and go back to the village
he would do it again with better equipment
text: So what possessed you to head off alone across that plateau? One sentence covers it: I wanted to walk until my head had emptied itself. And the start, did that go smoothly? Not at all. I missed the first bus, sat waiting under a tin shelter, and ended up crossing the plain in whatever passing vans would take me on board. Where did you sleep, then? Behind an embankment, out of reach of the gusts, with a sheet of canvas strung between two posts. Was the night rough? Freezing, yes, but the sky was so clear that I gave up on sleeping altogether. And coming back? That was where it went wrong: a storm turned the track to running mud, and I had to double back as far as the village. Would you do it again? Without a second thought, but with a proper tent and boots that grip on loose stone.

units: the warden of a mountain refuge describes the collapse of a path
the rain fell without a break and the stream swelled
a slope stripped of its trees no longer soaked up the water
the bank broke away after a sound of tearing
a small group of walkers stayed trapped above the break
the rescuers reached them by way of the ridge line
the walkers were led along a narrow, steep passage
no casualty was reported
the footbridge is destroyed for good
the local authorities are considering a new line higher up
text: The warden of a refuge high in the mountains tells of the night the path gave way. “The rain came down without a break, and the stream doubled in size,” he says. The cause is easy enough to pin down: a slope stripped of its trees held nothing back, and the water ran off in one unbroken sheet towards the track. “We heard something tear away, and then the bank went,” he goes on. The result was immediate. A handful of walkers found themselves trapped above the break, with no way down to the valley floor. A rescue team reached them along the ridge and led them out over a narrow, steep ledge. “Nobody was hurt, but the footbridge is lost for good,” he concludes. The valley council are already looking at a replacement line, higher up and well clear of the channel the water has carved.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: crossing a mountain range was once a risky undertaking
trains of pack animals went through snowbound gorges
even experienced guides lost their bearings
the difficulty came from the lack of visible landmarks
mist wiped out the shapes of the land
piles of stone were knocked over by the wind
wooden poles driven into the ground rotted in the damp
in the end notches were cut into the rock face and whitened
these notches stayed visible in spite of fresh snow
present-day waymarking systems descend from that invention
text: Crossing a mountain range was once a gamble with poor odds. Trains of pack animals pushed into gorges where snow wiped out the trail, and even seasoned guides lost their bearings between two slopes that looked alike. The difficulty lay not in the distance but in having nothing fixed to steer by once the mist swallowed the shapes of the land. Piles of stone were tried first, raised at intervals, and the wind knocked them over. Wooden poles came next, and the damp rotted them through. The answer arrived as a modest idea: cut a notch into the rock face at head height, then whiten it with lime, so that it showed even under fresh snow. The mule drivers could work their way from one notch to the next, with no need to read a sky that told them nothing. The waymarking systems in use now all descend from that invention.

units: a valley shaped by ice differs from a valley shaped by a river
the glacial valley has a broad, level floor
the walls of a glacial valley are almost vertical
the mass of ice wears away the base as much as the sides
the river valley forms a narrow, deep cut
water eats away mainly along the line it follows
the stones carried by the current grind the rock like an abrasive tool
the side valleys of a former glacier arrive high up
the side valleys of a river meet the main channel at the same level
text: A valley carved out by ice and a valley carved out by running water can be told apart at a glance. The glacial one has a broad, level floor between walls that rise almost straight up, because a thick, heavy mass of ice scrapes away at the base and the sides alike. The river valley cuts a narrow, deep groove instead, since water bites mainly along the line it follows and leaves the slopes to fall in under their own weight. The stones the current drags with it grind at the rock like a file. The side valleys give the difference away as well. Those of an old glacial valley arrive high up, left hanging, and spill down as waterfalls. Those of a river valley meet the main channel at the same level. That one detail is often enough to settle the question in front of a landscape you do not know.

units: the narrator reports a crossing he remembers precisely
the landscape was stony and had no tall plants
the swells of the ground fooled the eye about distance
the journey counted seven stages begun before sunrise
a halt took place in the shade during the greatest heat
the water came from built cisterns that the guides could find
the food was limited to hard flatbreads and a store of salt
a strap snapped and one of the party hurt a foot
a train of traders was coming the other way and reported a blocked well
the narrator concludes that bare ground holds many readable signs
text: One crossing has stayed sharp in my memory, and it is worth setting out its parts one by one. The setting: a desert of stone, no tall plant anywhere, rippled by swells of ground that fooled the eye about distance. The marching: seven stages, each begun before sunrise and closed at dusk, with a halt in the shade of a boulder through the worst of the heat. The supplies: water drawn from built cisterns that our guides found without hesitating, hard flatbreads, and a store of salt. The mishaps: a strap snapped, a foot cut open, a night when the wind flattened our shelter. The encounters, last of all: a train of traders working the same track the other way, who warned us of a well filled in with rubble. What I take from it is that bare ground is not empty, and reads like a crowded page.

units: the pack must be got ready the evening before departure
everything must first be laid out flat to spot what is missing
heavy items go against the back, halfway up
the rain gear is stowed at the top of the pack
the water bottles are filled before leaving the hamlet
the route must be checked on the map before setting off
the springs and the steep sections must be located
regular stops serve to air and dry the feet
the pitch for the night is chosen dry and well away from streams
on waking, the marks of the fire must be rubbed out
text: Pack your rucksack the evening before you leave, never at the last minute. Start by laying everything out flat on the floor: you will see at once what is missing and what is nothing but dead weight. Load the heavy items against your back, halfway up, so that the pull does not drag your shoulders backwards. Slip your rain jacket right at the top, where you can grab hold of it. Next morning, before you walk out of the hamlet, fill your bottles and check the line on the map, marking the springs and the steep sections. On the way, stop at regular intervals, take your boots off and let your feet dry properly. Choose your pitch for the night while it is still light, on a dry shelf of ground, well away from stream beds. When you wake, rub out every mark of your fire before you shoulder the pack again.

units: the number of walkers on a plateau path rose after it spread online
the village car park is full very early
meadows are being used as parking space
fences give way and the livestock escapes
the widening of the passage has destroyed the plant cover
rain now cuts grooves down the slope
the council is putting a shared shuttle in place
the number of spaces available is now limited
the path closes at the start of the week to let the grass recover
the shopkeepers protest while the stock farmers approve
text: It was meant to be a quiet season, and it has turned into a headache for the valley. Since the plateau path started doing the rounds online, walker numbers have shot up and the car park fills before the sun is properly over the ridge. Meadows are serving as parking space, fences give way, and the stock farmers watch their animals wander off. Naming the cause is easy; living with what follows is not. As boots have widened the passage, the plants that bound the soil have gone, and rain now cuts grooves down the slope. So the council has acted. A shuttle takes the place of cars, the number of spaces has been capped, and the path closes at the start of the week to let the grass recover. The shopkeepers grumble, the stock farmers breathe again, and the valley waits for the next season.

units: two different routes lead to the same high crossing point
one of them climbs a steep face whose ground is covered with stones
on that steep route the walkers move upward in tight zigzags
the other route loops round a soft rolling landform
the gentle route is half as long again as the steep one
its steady gradient makes it possible to hold an even pace
workers record the height, the width and the type of ground every season
on the steep way timber steps are set and held by driven pegs
on the gentle way channels are cut to run the water off
a heavily loaded walker will take the less steep way
text: Two separate paths reach the same high saddle, and the two could hardly be less alike. One takes on a steep face where the ground lies loose with stones, so walkers work upward in tight zigzags, planting each boot flat on the tilted slabs. The other swings round a soft rolling shoulder of hillside. It runs half as long again, yet the gradient never changes, and that lets a walker hold a single steady pace from bottom to top. The crews who look after both routes measure the rise, the usable width and the make-up of the ground before every season. On the steep line they set timber steps and hold them with driven pegs. On the gentle line they cut side channels so the water runs off. Anyone carrying a heavy load will pick the easier gradient; anyone racing the mist to the ridge will not.

units: the writer looks into the reasons that push people to go far away
he lists three motives shared by most travellers
the first is the change of setting, which sharpens the attention
the second is the exchange with those who live in the place
the writer holds conversation to be worth more than looking alone
the third motive consists in piling up places visited
this piling up is criticised because it turns a site into a catch
the writer advises going more slowly and staying put
he proposes giving up bringing back any trace of the journey
text: It is worth asking what we are really after when we cross into distant country. Three motives turn up in most travellers. The first is the shift of setting: you leave a familiar backdrop for a horizon whose rules you do not know, and your attention sharpens at once. The second is exchange. An hour of talk with a herder, a fisherman or a weaver is worth more than gazing at one grand view after another. The third is harder to own up to, and it amounts to collecting: places are stacked up the way others stack picture cards. That last motive deserves hard scrutiny, since it turns a clear valley into a trophy and the traveller into a book-keeper of his own feats. A decent way of moving through the world would mean slowing down, staying put, and carrying home no proof at all.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: the woman described leads walkers in the mountains

she can judge a party's exhaustion from the way it walks
she now trains future guides
she says the only thing she misses of her father's work is the smell of fodder
text: The woman who leads walkers into the high country grew up as a stock-breeder's daughter, in a cluster of houses where the road gave out at the last meadow. She was still small when she began driving the animals along tracks that ran with water, and she learnt to read the sky before the other children did. As a girl she left for a training school, where maps became a language to her and where she was taught to bring an injured body off broken ground. She came home with her certificate and offered herself to the walkers passing through. Ten seasons of that taught her to gauge a party's exhaustion from its gait alone. Now she trains guides herself: how slopes read, where to halt, how to announce that a summit must be given up. Of her father's trade she misses only the smell of cut fodder.

units: the speaker was let down by a walk along the sea
the leaflet announced a shore left in its wild state
the path has in fact been widened to let machines through
a barrier runs the whole length of the route
that barrier hides the drop and removes the sense of danger
the walker ends up watching the ground instead of the landscape
the gravel surface turns dangerous under fine rain
the final part of the route becomes narrow and wild again
the speaker finds there the interest he had expected from the outing
text: Honestly, that walk along the coast let me down, and it took me a good while to work out why. The leaflet had promised a shoreline left wild. What you actually get is a track widened for maintenance machinery, with a railing running the whole way along it. Because the railing blocks the drop, the sense of exposure goes, and exposure is the whole point of walking a cliff edge. So you push on quickly, you watch your feet, and there is nothing left to fear or to admire. Add to that the gravel they have laid down: it turns slippery the moment a light drizzle sets in, so you brake the whole way without getting anything back for it. Only the very last stretch rescues the outing. There the path narrows down again, a heavy sea batters the rocks, and you get at last what brought you out.

units: the writer of the message is staying at a mountain inn
the local economy depends on walkers coming
rainfall has brought down a long stretch of the usual path
bookings were cancelled and the lodging emptied
a solution was found after three evenings of argument
the women of the place suggested a replacement route on the other flank
a woodworker is building a log crossing over a boggy hollow
the postal worker drew the new route on a public map
the walkers came back the following week
text: I am writing to you from an inn up the valley, and I will set out what has happened here as a reporter would. The hamlet lives off passing walkers, and after the rains a long stretch of the main path slid away. Visitors called off their bookings, the rooms emptied, and the innkeeper began talking about a lost season. A way out took shape over three evenings of argument. It was the women of the place who put forward a replacement route along the shaded flank, longer but sound underfoot. A carpenter is building a log crossing over the boggy hollow. The postman, who knows every short cut in the district, has marked the altered route on a map pinned up at the entrance to the village. The walkers were back within the week. I leave tomorrow by that path and will tell you how it holds up.

units: the question asked sets the sea edges against the summits
an old walker answers by asking what one wants from walking
he links flat expanses with the loss of oneself
he explains that flat ground strips away the landmarks
he links the summits with physical hardship
effort high up hands the walker back the feel of his skeleton
he is asked which setting leaves the most lasting trace
he chooses the emptiest setting, since it offers little to memorise
he sets that emptiness against a rich valley that scatters into small details
he holds that one never finds the place as one left it
text: Shore or summit, which is the better ground for walking? An old walker used to meet the question with one of his own: what is it you want from walking? If it is the loss of yourself, he said, take the flats, since a level expanse strips away every landmark and lets the mind drift under a low sky. If it is the ordeal you want, the ridge wins. Every step up there is paid for, and the effort hands the walker back the feel of his own bones. He was asked next which of the two settings prints itself deeper on the memory. He chose the barer one without pausing: a naked expanse, no tree, no roof, stays with you because it gives you so little to hold, whereas a fertile valley crumbles into small particulars. The last question was about going back. You never return, he smiled, to the place you left.

units: a rock specialist teaches how to examine a slope before climbing it
a rock that splits into thin leaves lets water work its way in
that kind of ground becomes dangerous after rain
a slope held by shrubs stands up better than a slope without plants
the roots pin down the loose part of the ground
a flank kept from the sun holds its water for longer
flat shelves on a slope show where earth has slipped in the past
a member of the party asks the specialist about gullies that look dry
the answer is that a stony bed fills with water in a downpour
the closing advice is to avoid any steep slope whose exit cannot be seen
text: The rock specialist showed the party how to read a slope before committing to it. He began with the stone itself. Where it splits into thin leaves, he said, water works its way in, and the ground turns treacherous once rain has fallen. He moved on to what grows there: a slope held by shrubs stands up better than a bare bank, because the roots pin down the loose layer. He noted in passing that a flank kept out of the sun holds its wet long after the rest has dried. Last came the shape of the ground, and he dwelt on the flat shelves, which mark where earth has already slipped. Someone asked whether a gully can be trusted when it looks dry. Not at all, he answered: a stony bed fills in one downpour. His closing advice was to go round any steep passage whose exit you cannot see.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: high crossings first served practical needs
carriers of goods opened the first ways over
those ways took up the lines worn by the herds
builders then put up works spanning the watercourses
those works cut several weeks off the journeys
travel remained the business of merchants and of those who carried letters
scholars later climbed the summits out of pure curiosity
their published accounts created a taste for steep country
the earlier generation found that country ugly
the boring of tunnels did away with the hardship of the crossing
text: Crossing a high pass began as a matter of need, never of pleasure. The first ways over were opened by carriers hauling salt and wool, who followed the lines of least effort that the herds had already worn into the ground. Bridge-builders came after them, able to throw an arch over a torrent and cut weeks from a journey. Even so, the route stayed the business of merchants and of the men who carried letters. Then came scholars who set out to climb the summits from curiosity alone, with instruments and notebooks, and who were taken at first for men who had lost their way. Their accounts, once printed and passed round, gave rise to a fresh taste for broken country that their fathers had thought plainly ugly. In the end the mountain was bored through, and the pass stopped being an ordeal.

units: the clearness of a high lake comes from what its water carries
lowland rivers drag along silt torn from farmed banks
those fine grains hang in the water and get in the way of sight
high up, the ground feeding the lake is short and the rock is hard
the water therefore lifts very little material
the cold holds back the spread of microscopic plants
that scarcity of algae raises the clearness of the water further
a walker sees the stones on the bottom and misjudges the depth
the want of food makes living things rare and fish grow very slowly
works upstream can cloud the water for a whole season
text: A mountain lake looks clear for one reason: what its water is carrying. Rivers down in the lowlands drag along silt torn from farmed banks, and those fine grains hang in the water and blur whatever you try to look at. Higher up, the ground that feeds the lake is short and the rock beneath it hard, so the water lifts almost nothing on its way down. The cold up there plays its part as well. Microscopic plants barely multiply, and their scarcity clears the water further still. A walker can pick out every pebble on the bottom and takes a deep basin for a shallow dip. There is a price for that clearness: with so little to feed on, living things are few and the fish put on weight at a crawl. One dig upstream, stirring the mud of an old deposit, will cloud the lake for a whole season.

units: two walkers meant to cross a flat windswept expanse without a halt
they had set out with little gear
a thick veil of vapour came down halfway across
the route was marked by small piles of stones
those markers became impossible to see
one of the two was for pressing on by guesswork
the narrator refused because of holes where one can be hurt
they worked out a way of moving in which one waits while the other explores
the one going ahead calls out as soon as he makes out the next marker
the veil lifted by a grassy hollow, close to the shelter
text: We had it in our heads to cross the windy tableland in one go, light packs, the map folded in a pocket. Bad reckoning: halfway over, the fog dropped all at once and the line of small stone piles that marked the route simply went. My companion was for pressing on by guesswork. I would not have it, because ground like that is pitted with holes, and a foot goes into one and a bone goes with it. So we made up a method of our own. One of us stayed put at the last marker he could see while the other walked straight ahead to the edge of the murk, shouting as he went. The moment he made out the next pile he called, and his mate came up to him. We worked our way across like that, relay by relay, all afternoon. The fog lifted at a grassy hollow, and the hut stood there within earshot.

units: a living culture forms from flour and water left open to the air
yeasts carried in the air settle in the mixture
the baker takes out a portion and tops it up with fresh flour at regular intervals
after a week the culture holds steady
a sour smell shows that the culture is ready to use
the flour is sifted before the warm liquid goes in
the dough is folded over itself between two rests
the fierce heat of the oven sets the structure and colours the outside
the loaf keeps for a week without drying out
text: Leave flour and water in an open bowl and something living begins. Within two or three nights, yeasts drifting through the air settle in the mixture and lift it. From then on the baker keeps the culture fed at regular intervals: a portion is taken out and thrown away, fresh flour goes in to replace it. A week of that and it holds steady, giving off a sharp, sour smell which means it will raise a whole dough. Sift the flour, pour in warm water, work the starter through with a spatula, then knead until the mass turns supple. Let it rest, fold it over itself, let it rest again. In an oven at its fiercest the structure is fixed for good and the crust takes on its colour. Nothing about the method is quick, and yet it yields a close, fragrant loaf that will sit on the board for a week without drying out.

units: an inn worker leaves her pot on faint embers before going up to bed
she meant to lift it off before sunrise
tiredness keeps her from coming back at the hour she intended
the liquid drops by half and the meat falls apart into threads
the cook skims the surface and then tastes what is there
the sauce turns out thick and faintly sweet
low heat held for a long time altered the tissue of the meat
the customers ask for the same dish the next day
the cook repeats the accident on purpose every evening
text: A cook at a roadside inn set her pot over dying embers and went up to bed, sure she would lift it off before sunrise. Tiredness settled the matter for her. She came down long after first light, and found the liquid halved and the meat fallen loose into soft threads. Thinking the dish ruined, she skimmed the surface, tasted from the ladle, and found a sauce that was thick, dark and faintly sweet. Because the heat had stayed low right through the night, the tough tissue had melted instead of tightening. The travellers at her tables asked for the very same thing the following day. Unable to account for what had happened, she chose to repeat it: every evening she banked the fire down and left the pot to look after itself. A recipe born of forgetfulness made the name of the house.

units: lumps form in a sauce while it is cooking
the pan has to come off the heat straight away
leaving the sauce on the heat gives a burnt taste
adding a cold liquid and then whisking hard breaks up most of the lumps
the sudden change of temperature makes the lumps give way
a fine sieve holds back the pieces that are left
you crush what stays behind with the back of a hollow tool
the mixture then goes back over a gentle flame with constant stirring
slackening the flour in something cold keeps it from happening again
text: Your sauce has gone wrong and lumps are bobbing about in it? Don't tip it away, it can be saved. Get the pan off the heat straight away, or the flour will keep catching on the bottom and the whole lot will taste burnt. Splash in a little cold water and whisk hard: the sudden drop in temperature breaks most of the lumps apart. Any stubborn ones that refuse to give can be tipped through a fine sieve, and you crush what stays behind with the back of a ladle. Then back on a gentle flame, and keep stirring all the while, right out to the edges of the pan. Another time, slacken your flour in something cold before it ever meets anything hot. A smooth sauce hangs on that one habit, not on some knack nobody ever taught you. Keep a whisk within reach; it is the tool that rescues supper.

units: two cooking counters stand facing each other in a covered market hall
the first counter cooks everything by dropping it into hot fat
the queue at the first counter moves quickly
the second counter has had its pots simmering since early morning
customers in a hurry go for the quick method
the two counters charge much the same prices
their outgoings fall on different things
the woman who runs the hall notices that the custom swaps sides as the week goes on
neither counter tries to copy the other
text: Under the roof of a covered market, two cooking counters stand opposite one another and argue for opposite methods. On one side everything goes into hot fat: the fierce heat seals the outside in seconds, and the queue never stalls. On the other, a cook has had her pots simmering since first light, and her service moves at a walking pace. Anyone in a rush turns to the fryer; anyone who sits down waits for the pot. The prices sit close together, though the money goes elsewhere, since one counter gets through oil while the other burns energy hour after hour. The woman who runs the hall notices that the custom swaps sides as the week wears on, hurried at the start, patient towards the end. Neither trader shows any wish to copy the other, and the quiet rivalry keeps the hall full.

units: the goods on the stall are sorted by shade
the first group gathers dried roots and curls of bark
the red goods give off a smell that catches at the throat
the green goods are kept at the back of the stall
a stone vessel stands in the middle of the stall
the inside of the vessel is stained by mixtures made long ago
a worn grating tool is used for hard dried nuts
the trader will not sell anything that has already been ground to powder
he says that powder loses its scent within one season
text: On the spice trader's stall the shades are kept in families. The ochres come first of all: dried roots, curls of bark, powders that smell of resin and of warm, dusty wood. The reds follow, harsher by far, catching at the throat as soon as a hand goes anywhere near. The greens hold the back of the stall, crumpled leaves, minute seeds, stems tied into tight bunches. A stone mortar stands in the middle, its pestle laid across at an angle, the inner wall stained by mixtures made long ago. Beside it a worn grater waits for the hard nuts, which the trader will on no account sell ready ground. Powder, he says, goes flat within a season, while the whole seed keeps its soul. Behind him the cloth sacks sag open on brown treasures nobody can name and no customer ever thinks to ask for.

units: cooking once rested on what the cook could sense
measuring probes changed the nature of the trade
each ingredient can now be given a set band of heat
baths of regulated heat came along afterwards
food sealed under vacuum never climbs past the value aimed at
the writer takes this shift to be a gain
those against it read in it a loss of feeling
the writer argues that the device strips out crude error without deciding the seasoning
what the writer fears most is that results will all come out the same
text: For generations on end, cooking was done by guesswork of a skilled kind: a palm held over the embers, an ear tuned to the sizzle, an eye on the colour. Then came measuring probes, and the trade turned into something else. It grew possible to set a narrow band of heat for each ingredient and hold to it without drifting. The same logic led on to baths of regulated heat, where a sealed piece cooks under vacuum and never climbs past the value aimed at. I take that shift to be a gain, whatever is said by those who read in it a loss of feeling. Measuring forbids nobody to taste: the device strips out the crude failure, it does not decide the seasoning. What troubles me a good deal more is the steady pull towards sameness. A flawless result repeated exactly soon manufactures a flawless boredom.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: the pastry cook comes from a line of millers
her father sorted grain in front of her all through her childhood
she could tell one grind from another by touch before she read a recipe
that early familiarity settled the trade she chose
she started as an apprentice in a neighbourhood bakehouse
the hours worked at night built her stamina
an injured wrist took her away from kneading
that accident turned her towards light work
she sifts her flour twice over to get her layered pastry
she will not enlarge her house now that a trade journal has mentioned it
text: Born into a line of millers, the pastry cook of a small guest house inherited an unusual relationship with flour. Her father sorted grain in front of her, so she could tell one grind from another by touch long before she read a recipe. That early familiarity accounts for the trade she chose. She started as an apprentice in a neighbourhood bakehouse, where the demands of night work built her stamina. An injured wrist then took her off the kneading bench, and the accident turned her towards light work, which asks less of the arms. There she found her signature: pale layered pastry whose lightness comes from flour sifted twice over. Her own apprentices remember one rule above all, to weigh the gesture rather than hurry it. Since a trade journal mentioned her house, she has refused to grow.

units: the room wins the visitor over at once
the menu offers a narrow choice
the vegetables come lukewarm although their dish should have kept them hot
the reviewer works out that the plates waited under a source of heat
the main dish is cooked correctly
the sauce has split for having been brought together too early
the fault lies with the way the work is arranged and not with skill
moving the serving bench nearer the stove would do away with the wait
sending out fewer plates at a time would improve the service
the pudding made to order arrives faultless
text: The room wins you over at once, and the menu is short, which usually promises a kitchen that knows its own mind. The trouble starts with the first course. The vegetables come lukewarm in a cast-iron dish that ought to have kept them scalding; plainly they had been standing under a lamp. The main plate confirms the weakness: the cooking is judged well, but the sauce was brought together too early and had already split. The remedy has nothing to do with talent and everything to do with the way the work is arranged. Bring the serving bench nearer the stove, send out fewer plates at a time, and the delay that spoils the kitchen's own effort goes away. The pudding proves the point, made to order and arriving clean, taut, exact. A kitchen this able should not let a meal begin cold.

units: the reader had asked whether the writer eats better since the move
the writer finds the food different without finding it better
her aunt cooked everything in a single pot
she tipped the leavings of the day before into a broth
the flatmate gives every ingredient a tool of its own
at her aunt's the helpings were generous and piping hot
proportions were never argued over there
in the present home they taste and adjust before serving
the writer misses the smell that used to fill the hallway
the writer asks the reader to come and judge for himself
text: You asked whether I am eating any better since the move. Honestly, it is different, not better. At my aunt's everything came out of one pot; she tipped yesterday's leavings into a broth and out came a meal. My flatmate works the other way round, and every ingredient gets its own pan, its own timer, its own seasoning. At hers we ate hot and we ate plenty, and nobody ever argued about proportions or weighed a thing. Here we taste, we adjust, we start again, and supper lands late. I like both, for opposite reasons. One fed you, the other entertains you. What I miss is the smell that filled the hallway the moment I opened her door. This flat smells of clean. Come over one evening and judge for yourself; I promise not to pick the menu, we will decide together in front of the cupboard.

units: the woman who runs a preserving workshop answers questions about the commonest mistakes
she holds that the quality of the seal matters more than the thickness of the glass
a seal used a second time often gives way as things cool
the water has to cover the jars completely while they are being heated
the top of the contents spoils with nothing to show for it if it stands proud
she points out that salt preserves but also hides the faults of poor produce
the foam that rises on fermenting vegetables is no sign of failure
that foam belongs to the start of the process
she will give no general rule about how long things keep
text: We put the commonest mistakes to the woman who runs a preserving workshop. On choosing jars, she answers that the seal matters far more than the thickness of the glass, and that a seal used a second time will often give way as the jar cools. On heating she is firm: the water has to cover the jars completely, or the top of the contents spoils with nothing to show for it. Asked about salt, she qualifies her answer, since it preserves, yet it also hides what is wrong with poor produce. On fermenting vegetables her reply surprises: the foam that rises is no sign of failure, it belongs to the start of the process. On how long things keep she will give no general rule, and sends you back to the smell, the sound of the lid, the look of the liquid. A careful nose, she ends, beats any label.

units: an experienced cook takes his apprentice to task over the state of his cutting tool
the blunted blade crushes the herbs instead of severing them
the crushed leaves give up their sap too early
the colour of the preparation turns dull as a result
the scent of the preparation is weakened by it
the apprentice claims he sharpened the tool the day before
the fault comes from an angle poorly held during sharpening
the superior asks for the operation to be done again in front of him
text: The head cook took his apprentice aside and spoke plainly about the state of the chopping blade. Blunt as it had become, it crushed the herbs rather than severing them, and crushed leaves give up their sap far too early. Colour drains out of the preparation, he said, and the scent thins away to almost nothing. The apprentice protested that he had put the tool to the stone only the day before. His superior held the edge up against the window light and showed him where the metal had gone round. The angle had wandered while the blade travelled over the stone, so the cutting line was lost without anyone noticing. Proof of it sat on the plate: a sauce gone brown where a bright tone had been expected. Care over the upkeep decides the flavour at the end, he concluded, and he asked the young man to sharpen the blade again in front of him.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: meat from animals killed before the cold season spoiled very quickly
the lack of artificial cold left rural households exposed to shortage
salt supplied the first remedy to this problem
a heavily concentrated salt solution draws the water out of the tissues
this drying out stops micro-organisms from multiplying
aromatics were later added to the preserving bath
preserving thus became a way of seasoning as well
smoking added a protective layer at the surface
these methods passed from one person to the next through direct apprenticeship
text: Meat from beasts killed ahead of the cold season spoiled within days, and country households had no artificial cold to fall back on; once the store turned, hunger followed. Salt offered the first way out. Cooks noticed that a heavily concentrated brine drew the water out of the tissues, and that micro-organisms could no longer multiply in what was left. The method grew finer as aromatic berries, dried peel and bitter roots went into the bath, so that keeping the meat came to season it as well. Smoking was added on top, laying a protective film over the exposed surface. None of it was ever written down. It travelled from one valley to the next by watching and doing, an older hand showing a younger one, and it reshaped what people ate wherever regular trade never reached.

units: the difference between the two doughs lies in the microbes living in them
a starter brings together wild ferments and acidifying bacteria
the yeast sold in packets carries only one selected species
starter dough gives a crumb with uneven holes
yeast dough gives a crumb that is more even and more neutral
fermentation with a starter calls for a whole night of waiting
fermentation with yeast reaches its end far sooner
the outer crust of the starter loaf browns more deeply
the acids produced by fermentation feed the browning reactions
text: So what really sets a loaf raised on a starter apart from one raised with shop yeast? It comes down to who lives in the dough. A starter holds a whole crowd of wild ferments alongside acidifying bacteria, while the yeast sold in packets carries a single selected species and nothing more. You taste that crowd in the crumb: ragged, uneven holes, a gentle sharpness, a smell somewhere near hazelnut. Yeast crumb turns out tidier, milder, rather well behaved by comparison, with holes of much the same size all the way through. The rising splits them too. The first wants a whole night; the second is done after a short wait on the worktop. And the crust of the starter loaf goes darker, because the acids thrown off during fermentation feed the browning reactions. Patience or speed, then, and you take your pick.

units: a power cut struck a kitchen team during a banquet
the ovens stopped while poultry was only half cooked
the chilled cabinets stopped holding their temperature
the darkness forced the brigade to work by hand-held lamps
an emergency gas burner served to finish off the meats
tubs of crushed ice took over from the chilled cabinets
a section head improvised a faster form of service
the guests noticed nothing of the incident
text: A power cut caught a kitchen team halfway through a banquet, and the account they give of that evening is worth setting down. Three problems arrived at the same moment, one on top of the other. The ovens died with the poultry only half cooked. The chilled cabinets stopped holding their temperature, putting the creams and the mousses at risk. Darkness left the brigade working under hand torches propped against the shelves. The answer came from three things that lay to hand. An emergency gas burner was lit and the meats were finished off in simmering stock. Tubs of crushed ice took the place of the cabinets. A section head reworked the order of service on the spot, sending plates out one by one rather than by table. The guests, so management insists, never guessed at the scramble behind the swing door.

units: you must choose a vessel of fired clay with a stout handle
the lid has to close without leaving any gap
the aromatic bath is made up the day before
the meat is laid into that bath piece by piece
the resting happens overnight in a cool place
the liquid deepens and the flesh darkens while it waits
the meat is then seared over a fierce heat
the strained liquid serves to moisten the cooking
the covered cooking carries on beside the hearth
the meat is ready when a fork goes in without effort
text: Begin with a vessel of fired clay, one with a stout handle that will not give and a lid that settles down without the least gap. The night before, pour in the bath: a scented oil, a mild vinegar, leaves bruised between the fingers. Lay the meat down piece by piece, unhurried, the way stones are set into a low wall. Then leave the night to do its work somewhere cool and dark. In the morning, lift the lid: the liquid will have deepened, and the flesh will have taken on a duller, quieter shade. Sear it over a fierce heat, then moisten the pot with the bath you have strained. Cover it again and let it be forgotten beside the hearth through a long afternoon. Serve at last, when a fork slides in and meets nothing at all, and when the thickened sauce coats the back of a spoon with a bright film.

units: a cooperative plant records a rise in rejected products
the line in question packs soups
the cooling that follows heat treatment starts too late
the product stays in a temperature band that suits resistant spores
this exposure makes the closures bulge
a souring becomes noticeable in the product
fouling of the plate exchanger cuts down heat transfer
chemical cleaning spaced too far apart is held to blame
management plans an additional washing cycle
probes will be fitted at the entrance to the tunnel
text: Technical management at a cooperative processing plant reports a rise in rejected units on the line that packs soups. The analysis points to a single cause. Cooling after heat treatment begins with a measurable delay, so the product lingers in a temperature band where resistant spores thrive. That drawn-out exposure shows up as bulging lids and a souring that comes through in the taste. The plate exchanger stands accused: fouling has built up little by little and the transfer coefficient has fallen with it. Chemical cleaning has been spaced too far apart, and the flow of chilled water no longer makes up the loss. Managers have announced an extra washing cycle, and probes are to be fitted at the entrance to the tunnel. A check on how the vats close will round out the measures.

units: the ripening room lies in a cellar beneath a stone vault
the cheeses rest on boards of resinous wood
the level of moisture falls when the way in is left open
the surface of the cheeses hardens because of this drying
a shallow basin of water was set along a cold wall
what evaporates from that basin makes good the losses of moisture
the wooden door was replaced by a soft-closing leaf
a hanging measuring device warns the team before the critical threshold
text: The ripening room lies in the cellar of an old building, beneath a vault of grey stone. Spruce boards carry the wheels, sorted by size, and the air smells of hazelnut and damp straw. One difficulty threatens the place, all the same. As soon as the way in is left open, the moisture in the air falls away, and the rind hardens over the surface until ripening stalls beneath it. Two remedies were adopted by the people who look after the cellar. A shallow basin of water now runs along the coldest wall, and what evaporates from it makes good the losses. The old wooden door gave way to a soft-closing leaf with a low handle that can be worked with an elbow. A gauge hung from the vault warns the team before the critical threshold is crossed, and the wheels nearest the doorway are turned more often than the rest.

units: the defence of cooking at home often rests on an emotional attachment
the writer suggests comparing two meals of equivalent worth
the meal made at home costs little in raw ingredients
the amount of salt in it depends on whoever does the seasoning
this meal calls for someone to keep watch over the stove
the ready-made dish hands back a whole evening
the ready-made dish keeps without any special care
the ready-made dish imposes a fixed recipe and additives one has to accept
the decisive gap concerns control, not taste nor price
text: Standing up for cooking at home against the sealed tray tends to come from the heart, which is exactly why the argument deserves a cooler look. Set two comparable meals side by side. The first comes out of a family pan: the ingredients cost little, the salt in it depends entirely on the hand doing the seasoning, and it asks for someone to stand over the stove and watch. The second comes out of a sealed tray: it hands back a whole evening, it keeps with no special care, and it settles the recipe and the list of additives without asking the eater. Neither the flavour nor the price decides the matter in the end. What decides it is control. Cooking for yourself means keeping a say in what you swallow. That freedom is paid for in attention, and each of us can judge whether the trade is one worth making.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: the pastry cook reaches her workshop before the sun comes up
she grates the coloured skin of citrus straight over the dough
she keeps the candied peel in jars
her dented mould came down to her from her mother
she carries her scoring knife on her at all times
she turns away any machine she could not take apart herself
she trains one apprentice every season
she hands the baking over to her apprentices very early
she says she listens to the dough instead of imposing her will on it
text: You want to catch her pushing the workshop door open before the sun is up, apron tied high, sleeves already shoved back. The pastry cook along the road has three passions, and she will talk about every one of them without being asked twice. Citrus first: she grates the coloured skin straight over the dough so the scented oil falls where it belongs, and the candied peel goes into jars lined up on a shelf above the bench. Then old tools: the dented mould came down from her mother, the scoring knife never leaves her pocket, and she turns away any machine she could not take apart herself. Last, the apprentices. She takes one on every season, with no elaborate contract, and hands them the baking almost straight away. Ask her the secret and she shrugs: she listens to the dough rather than laying down the law to it.

units: the plain look of the room gave no hint of the quality of the meal
the first course is a clarified broth of root vegetables
this broth is striking in its depth despite being clear
the second course pairs a fish with crisp skin and a purée of bitter herbs
the cooking of the fish is judged remarkably precise
the main course disappoints because of a sauce reduced too far
the meat in that dish was nonetheless of good quality
the dessert puts the whole meal back on course
the dessert pairs an ice scented with citrus and a crisp wafer
the service is described as discreet and assured
text: Nothing in that plain room, as you push the door open, hints at how carefully the meal ahead has been built. The opening course arrives without announcement: a broth of root vegetables, clarified, clear to the bottom of the bowl, and startling in its depth. Then a piece of fish with crackling skin, set over a purée of bitter herbs; the cooking is timed to the second and deserves saying so. The central plate lets things slip, for a sauce reduced too far flattens meat of real quality and buries the aromatics under it. The dessert puts the evening back on course, a cream ice scented with sharp peel on a thin wafer that snaps under the spoon. Portions stay measured throughout, which keeps the whole thing light. The service is quiet and sure, following the rise without ever running ahead of it.

units: the writer of the message is taking a baking course
the mixture rises properly while it rests
the mixture sinks once it goes into the oven
the writer states that the instructions received were followed closely
the writer has tried a different raising agent
an experienced acquaintance puts forward an explanation
that explanation blames the fault on too much handling
the neighbour advises cutting the last rise short
the writer asks for a meeting before changing method
text: I am writing about the baking class you run in the community room. Since I joined, one problem has defeated me and I cannot work it out on my own. My dough rises beautifully while it rests, then sinks the moment it goes into the oven. I have followed your instructions to the letter, weighed out every ingredient, and even switched to a different raising agent. A neighbour of mine, who has been making bread since she was a girl, offered me an explanation. The dough is worked too hard, she says, and the structure holding it up gives way in the end. Her advice is to knead more gently and to cut the second rise short. I would rather hear your view before I try anything, since nobody knows the ovens in that room as you do. If you could spare me a few minutes after the next session, I should be very grateful.

units: the text sets two ways of cooking fish against each other
cooking over coals dries the surface and colours it
cooking with steam keeps the flesh moist
coals add a smoky aroma that the other method lacks
steam lets the clean smell of the food come through
cooking on a grill calls for a thin coating of fat
cooking under a lid needs no fat at all
firm flesh suits fierce heat better
delicate flesh falls apart and needs close watching
text: Should a fish go over the coals or into the steamer? The two methods stand less far apart than people assume, though they never end in the same dish. Coals dry the outside and colour it, and they drive the juices back into the flesh. Steam swells the fibres instead and holds the moisture where it is. What about flavour? Cooking over charcoal brings a smoky note that steaming will never produce, whereas steam lets the clean smell of the fish itself come through, with nothing laid over the top of it. And fat? The grill wants a thin coating, or the skin takes hold of the bars. Cooking under a lid asks for none at all. So which of them? Whichever suits the piece in hand. Firm flesh takes the flame well, while delicate flesh breaks up above boiling water and has to be watched closely.

units: a vegetable seller gives advice on cutting
he says the size of the cut changes with the plant
onion must be cut into thin slices so that it melts down
herbs are cut finely without being crushed
garlic is worked almost to a paste so that it spreads better
carrot is prepared either in shreds or in even dice
he advises against anything in between for that vegetable
he warns that a blunt blade damages the vegetables
he recommends sharpening the blade before a long session
text: You do not cut everything the same way, the man on the vegetable stall told me yesterday evening, over his crates. That, he reckons, is where most people go wrong. Onion has to be sliced very thin, otherwise it will never melt down properly in the pan. Herbs you cut with the very tip of the blade, lightly, never crushed, else they blacken and lose their scent altogether. Garlic he likes worked down almost to a paste, because only then does it spread right through the sauce. And carrots? He laughed at that one. Grate them, or cut them into perfectly even dice, but never anything in between. Then, as he handed me my change, he threw in one last piece of advice. A blunt blade bruises vegetables far worse than the clumsiest hand ever will, so put a proper edge on it before any long stretch of chopping, on a wet stone, and never in a rush.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: keeping food comes long before any way of making cold
drying in the air was the first method
salt draws the water out of flesh and halts decay
smoke above a fire makes meat keep longer
smoked meat takes on a harsh taste
travelling traders carried these stores along long roads
distant kitchens took up identical methods
sinking meat in melted fat seals it away from the air
these methods live on in the recipes of today
text: Long before anyone could make cold, keeping food edible meant a running fight against damp and rot. The earliest cooks hung their catch in the wind to dry it out. Then came the discovery that salt pulls the water from flesh and stops decay in its tracks. Smoke followed. A joint left hanging over a fire took on a harsh, biting taste and would keep for whole seasons. Traders on the move carried such stores along steadily longer roads, until kitchens far apart from one another had settled on the very same methods. Later still, cooked meat was sunk in melted fat and sealed away from the air in a pot. Every one of those steps pushed back the day a food would turn, and every one has left a mark on the way we cook now, repeated by cooks who never stop to ask where it came from.

units: a pale foam appears on the surface of a cooking liquid
that foam comes from proteins freed by the heat
the particles set loose are too light to sink again
the bubbles carry those particles upwards
leaving the foam clouds the broth
a clouded broth turns grey and tastes heavier
the cook lifts it off with a ladle again and again
beating an egg white stretches those same proteins
the mesh that forms holds air
a trace of salt weakens the bonds and firms the foam
text: As the water begins to tremble in the pan, a pale foam climbs to the surface and clings to the sides. It is made of proteins that the heat has driven out of the food. Cooking loosens the fibres and frees particles too light to sink again, and the rising bubbles carry them up. Leave that foam where it is and it falls back into the broth and clouds it. The liquid greys, the taste turns heavy. This is why a careful cook lifts it away with a ladle, over and over, for as long as it keeps forming. Something close to it happens under the whisk. Beating an egg white draws those same proteins out into a supple mesh, and the mesh takes hold of the air. A pinch of salt hurries the whole thing along, since it weakens the bonds and lets the foam rise sooner, firmer and far steadier.

units: a fish stock carried a metallic bitterness
the cook first suspected an acid ingredient and then his pan
he went back through every step of his preparation
the bones had boiled for far too long
a short infusion with no rolling boil is what is needed
a long extraction sets sulphur compounds loose
the gelatine breaks down beyond that limit
he now rinses the bones and takes out the gills
he keeps the pan below boiling point
the stocks that come out are clear and free of bitterness
text: It began with a fish stock that gave off a metallic bitterness, the day before a service in a staff canteen. The cook blamed the vinegar first, then the pan he had used, and only afterwards went back through his own recipe step by step. The fault lay with the bones. He had let them boil for close to an hour, when a frame will stand nothing more than a short, barely moving infusion. Past that point the bones give up sulphur compounds and the gelatine breaks down. So he rewrote his method altogether. He now rinses the bones in cold water, pulls out the gills, brings the pan up short of boiling, and stops the extraction before the liquid ever heaves. A fine cloth strains the rest. Since that correction his stocks come out perfectly clear, the bitter note has gone, and his team report nothing amiss.

units: the recipe offers two implements for crushing herbs
the leaves must be washed dried and stripped of their stalks
with the mortar the salt and the garlic are crushed first
the leaves go in gradually and are not struck
the mortar gives a thicker and more fragrant texture
the colour holds better by that route
the electric device is used in short pulses
the bowl must be chilled so that heat does not cook the herbs
the oil goes in as a thin stream at the end
a dry cheese may be added in fine shreds
text: A herb paste may be made with a mortar or with an electric bowl, and the choice matters, since the two do not give the same texture. Begin by washing the leaves, drying them thoroughly, and stripping away the tough stalks. Working with the mortar, crush the salt and the garlic first, then add the leaves a handful at a time, turning the pestle rather than striking with it. The paste comes out thicker and more fragrant, and its colour holds far longer. Working with the electric bowl, use short pulses only, and chill the bowl beforehand, or the heat of the blades will cook the leaves and dull the whole preparation. Either way, pour the oil in at the end as a thin stream. A dry cheese may finally be grated over the top and folded in with a fork, lightly, until the paste is even.

units: a covered market has reopened after renovation work
the hall takes its light through the roof
the vegetable stalls now hold the middle ground
the fishmongers’ aisle has cooling that works without ice
part of the building is set aside for makers who process on site
a baker shapes his dough in front of the customers
a shared kitchen is offered to let by the hour
the traders approve of the ventilation and the drainage of water
those two faults used to bring repeated closures
future rents worry the sellers because the sum is not yet known
text: The covered market in the northern quarter reopened this week, after building work that ran almost a whole season. Visitors step first into a hall lit from the roof, where the vegetable stalls now hold the middle ground. Beyond them runs the fishmongers’ aisle, cooled in silence by a system that has done away with trays of melting ice.
