A third of the floor has gone to traders who process on the spot: a baker shaping dough in full view of his customers, a seasonal bottling bench, a cutting room. The management is also offering a shared kitchen, let by the hour, for caterers with no premises of their own. Stallholders praise the ventilation and the drainage, the two failings behind a string of earlier closures. What worries them is the rent, whose final level has still not been announced.

units: the steam stops you seeing as you come into the room
the fat melts in the bottom of the pot
the pieces of meat begin to brown at their edges
a smell of caramel signals that liquid must go in
the stuck juices are lifted off and the flame is turned down
a fragrant steam escapes from under the lid
that smell travels as far as the corridor
the sauce darkens and coats the spoon
the meat comes away with no effort
the heat is put out and the smell lingers in the house
text: You walk into the kitchen and you can hardly see a thing, the steam has taken over. At first the pot says nothing at all. It simply warms, the fat melts down in the bottom, the pieces of meat start to take colour round their edges. A little later comes a smell of burnt sugar, and that is your cue: in goes the liquid, up come the stuck bits off the base, down goes the flame. After that everything slows. The lid shivers, one bubble breaks, another follows, and a thick savoury steam works its way out through the gap and drifts as far as the corridor. Towards the end the sauce has darkened, it coats the back of the spoon, the meat gives way under a fork with no effort at all. Then you kill the heat, leave the pot alone under its lid, and the smell goes on filling the house until morning.

units: the writer refuses to treat home cooking as an optional pastime
where the handing down stops industrial food takes the room
the consequences show up later at the doctors
with no adult to pass it on the child never handles a blade
the child does not learn to judge when something is cooked
grown up he buys dishes that only need reheating
spending on food climbs
the range of foods eaten narrows
added sugar becomes the taste everything is measured against
the writer holds that the cost at school would be met by savings on care
text: We ought to stop treating home cooking as an optional pastime. Where the handing down of these skills stops, factory food moves into the gap, and the bill is read out later in the consulting room. The chain is almost mechanical. With no adult to pass on the order of the work, a child never picks up a blade, never tastes a dish halfway through, and never learns to judge when something is done. Left to himself as an adult, he buys what can be reheated, because that is the one route he knows. Spending on food climbs, the range on the plate collapses, and added sugar settles in as the taste against which everything else is measured. Making such workshops compulsory at school would cost a great deal, and nobody denies it. But the saving on long-term care would outstrip the bill, and the next generation would win back something it had lost.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: the woman described runs the kitchen of a country inn
she took her first steps at a very cramped cooking station
at the outset she followed written instructions to the letter
she weighed every ingredient then and dreaded getting it wrong
she now trusts her palate rather than a timer
she has given up fierce heat and favours a very gentle simmer
her former manner leant on a profusion of aromatics
her present manner leans on the worth of the raw material
she passes this change on to the beginners she trains regularly
she holds that mastery of the hand comes before mastery of waiting
text: The woman who runs the kitchen of a country inn learnt her trade at a very cramped little stove. In those early months she followed written instructions to the letter, weighed out every ingredient and lived in constant fear of getting something wrong. She trusts her own tongue now, and pays no attention at all to a timer. The fierce heat has gone as well: she keeps the pot barely trembling, because gentleness draws out flavours that haste destroys. What separates the two cooks she has been is not the skill of her hands. Her old way leant on a great heap of aromatics; her present way leans on the worth of what she buys. She hands that shift on to the beginners who come to her for training, and she tells them the same thing every time: the hand is mastered long before the waiting is.

units: the place described stands beside a waterway
the staff bring the dishes discreetly and without explanation
the list of dishes is short and fits on a single sheet
that list changes according to what the suppliers bring
the brevity of the offer suggests nothing is stored for long
the methods of cooking are not of constant quality
the fish is a success on the surface as well as inside
the root vegetables are spoilt by too heavy an accompaniment
the final sweet dish repairs the impression left by the vegetables
the conclusion recommends a visit despite an excess of sauce
text: Three things stand out in this dining room beside a waterway. The service is plain to an unusual degree. Plates arrive, nobody says a single word about them, and the diner is left to work out what is on the plate. The menu comes next. It fits onto one single sheet of paper and shifts with whatever the suppliers bring, and so little is offered that nothing can be sitting in a cold store for long. The cooking is where the kitchen wavers. The fish leaves the pan crisp on the outside and yielding within, while the roots, buried under a thick sauce, lose all their edge. The last course puts that right: a smooth cream, barely sweetened, with a fruit poached in its own juice. The place is well worth the journey, provided you accept that the sauce sometimes takes up more room than it should.

units: the writer of the message recounts a cooking experience of the day before
he browned sliced bulbs in a flat pan
he stirred without stopping so that the fat would not blacken
he then added pulses and water
the dish cooked gently while he cleaned up
the first attempt had no flavour at all
he corrected the seasoning with a sour fruit and crushed seeds
he covered the dish with a soured milk product
someone living in the same building went back three times
the writer admits he improvised the dish with no model
text: You will never guess what I got up to in my tiny kitchen late last night. I began by browning sliced onions in a wide flat pan, stirring the whole time so the fat would not catch and blacken. In went the lentils, then cold water over the top, and I left it all ticking over gently while I dealt with the washing up. Then I tasted it. Nothing. No flavour at all. So I squeezed in a good deal of sharp citrus juice, threw in a pinch of crushed seeds, and the whole pot woke up. I poured off the extra liquid, spooned soured milk over the lot and carried it to the table without much hope. My neighbour from upstairs, asked round at the last minute, went back for a third helping and wanted the recipe. I had to admit I had made it up as I went along. Come round next week and I shall do it again.

units: the text explains where the golden tint of a bread crust comes from
the colour is born of an interaction between sugars and proteins
very dry air sets that interaction off
a pale surface signals an oven that is not hot enough
too much water in the dough also delays the colouring
damp keeps the surface from reaching the temperature required
excessive heat turns the sugars black
that drift brings a bitter taste
a very dark crust is not necessarily a fault
the same change yields pleasant aromas and burnt ones alike
text: What gives a crust its amber colour? Apprentice bakers put that question constantly, and the answer lies in a meeting between the sugars and the proteins of the dough, set off by the dry heat inside the closed oven chamber. And when the surface stays pale? Usually the air is not fierce enough, or the dough carries too much water, and the steam holds the colour back, because damp keeps the surface below the point at which the reaction begins. What happens if the heat is pushed further still? The sugars caramelise, then they blacken, and bitterness settles in for good. Does a dark crust therefore betray a mistake made along the way? Not at all. The shade you aim for depends on the smell you want, since one and the same reaction yields the scent of toasted nuts and the smell of burning.

units: a trader in spices observes that his shop is declining
visitors smell the goods but leave with empty hands
their restraint comes from not knowing how to use these products
his pupil reckons that a scent alone does not bring about a purchase
she suggests setting a tasting pot on the counter
vegetables would steep in it in a scented liquid
the trader fears at first that there is no room
he ends by accepting the proposal
sales rise from the following week
visitors come back asking more precise questions
text: One wet evening the spice seller complained that his shop was dying for want of custom. He told his apprentice that people came in, leant over the jars, breathed deeply, then went out again with nothing, put off by powders they had no idea how to use. A smell on its own persuades nobody, she answered, not when it belongs to no particular dish. Why not keep a pot at one end of the counter, she said, with roots steeping in a scented broth, so that anyone could taste before buying? He hesitated, muttering about the room it would take, and then gave way. By the second week he admitted that the jars were emptying and that visitors came back with sharp, precise questions. His shop, he said with amused solemnity, had stopped selling powders and started selling ideas for supper.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: the text contrasts two great methods of preserving food that came before mechanical cold
the first method consists in drawing the water out of food
salt, sugar and exposure to dry air belong to that method
depriving micro-organisms of water prevents them from multiplying
the second method changes the matter by souring or fermenting it
the ferments themselves create surroundings hostile to germs
drawing out water stiffens the texture and forces a soaking before use
the change alters the taste of the product markedly
it brings out aromas the raw matter never held
cold halts spoiling without enriching the flavour
text: Long before mechanical cold, two families of technique competed to keep food edible, and setting them side by side still explains a good deal about the way we cook. The first works by taking away. Salt, sugar and drying in open air pull the water out of the tissues and leave micro-organisms without the medium they depend on. The second works by changing the food itself. It is steeped in a sour brine, or handed over to ferments that build their own surroundings, hostile to any intruder. Taking water away hardens the texture and forces a long soak before use. Changing the food goes further and rewrites its flavour, sharpening it, rounding it, raising scents the raw matter never held. Cold came later. It halts decay and creates nothing, which explains both its reign and its blandness.

units: the text sets out four ways of carrying heat in cooking
boiling water spreads an even and limited heat
it softens the tough parts and draws out the soluble aromas
cooking by steam avoids washing the substances out of the food
it keeps the colour and the firmness of vegetables
a heated fat reaches a temperature higher than that of water
it serves to colour the surface before the heat is lowered
the dry heat of the closed chamber dries the outside and concentrates the sugars
the piece must be moistened with its own cooking liquid
linking these methods in a considered order gives results no single one can reach
text: Four ways of carrying heat cover very nearly everything that is done in a domestic kitchen, and each obeys a logic of its own. Boiling water gives an even, moderate warmth that can climb no higher. It softens tough tissue, dissolves the aromas that will dissolve, and suits any dish meant to yield a broth. Steam is gentler still, and it cooks without washing the food, so vegetables keep their colour and their bite. Hot fat carries far more heat than water ever can, which is why it is used to colour a surface before the flame is turned down. The dry air of a closed oven dries the outside and concentrates the sugars, so long as the joint is moistened now and then with its own juices. Set these four ways in a considered order and you reach textures that none of them ever reaches alone.

units: a large wedding reception is threatened by an accident of cooking
the cook in charge of the sauces left her pan on a source of heat
she had gone away to tend an assistant hurt in the hand
the bottom of the pan had become covered with a blackened deposit
the guests were already waiting to be served
she recovered the deposit by pouring pale wine over it
the deposit gave off a smell of nuts
she strained the liquid and enriched it with a cold fat
a relative of the bride asked how it had been done
she refused to set the method down in writing
text: A wedding feast came close to collapse because of a forgotten pan. The cook in charge of the sauces had left her reduction on a hot plate while she saw to an apprentice who had opened his finger on a blade. She came back to a dark sticky crust on the bottom of the pan, and the guests were already seated. Rather than start again, she poured in a glass of pale wine, scraped the base with a spatula and found that the burnt layer was giving off an unexpected smell of toasted nuts. She strained the liquid, beat in a knob of cold butter and sent it out without a word to anyone. The bride's father asked how it had been done before the pudding arrived. She told the tale to her colleagues at length, yet she would not write the method down, on the grounds that an accident cannot be ordered.

units: the instructions concern the cooking of a whole farmyard bird
it must be taken out of the cold well before it is cooked
without that rest the outside would be done before the middle
the skin must be wiped because water blocks the colouring
as long as water is evaporating the surface does not grow hot enough
the bird must be set on a support with holes in it
laid in its own juice the underside would cook in water
the piece must be moistened with its fat while it cooks
a rest after cooking is needed before carving
carving too soon loses the liquid and dries the flesh
text: Take a whole bird and get it out of the cold a good while before you mean to cook it, or the outside will be done long before the middle has even warmed through. Wipe the skin properly dry with a cloth, because damp stops it browning: while water is still evaporating, the surface never climbs to the temperature that turns it golden. Salt the skin generously, then sit the bird on a rack, never flat in its own juices, or the underside boils instead of roasting. Baste it with its own fat as it cooks, since hot liquid carries heat into the hollows the air struggles to reach. Then let the bird rest away from the heat for a while before you carve. The fibres tighten in the heat and give their juices back as they cool, and if you cut too soon it all runs onto the board and the meat comes out dry.

units: quantities of damaged vegetables were thrown away at the end of the market
the traders regretted that loss without being able to prevent it
the goods were still fit to eat despite how they looked
no arrangement allowed them to be recovered before closing
a group of local residents put forward an answer in three steps
the unsold goods are gathered just before closing
a room made available by the local authority is used for sorting
the vegetables are cooked and put into jars the same evening
the preparations are handed to households named by the social services
the lack of space and the absence of refrigerated equipment hold the project back
text: Whole crates of battered vegetables went into the skip week after week when the covered market shut, under the eyes of traders who minded but could do nothing about it. The produce was sound, merely bruised or a little too ripe to sell, and no arrangement existed for taking it away before nightfall. A group of residents from the neighbourhood came up with an answer in three moves: gather the unsold crates in the last hour of trading, sort them in a room lent by the local authority, and turn them into soup and preserves straight away. Volunteers simmer the vegetables that same evening, sterilise the jars and pass them on to families sent their way by the social services. Space is now the real sticking point. The room they were lent is full to bursting, and there is still no cold store to be had.

units: a short cooking time is needed to obtain a firm bite
too much sauce softens a firm preparation
gentle, lengthy heat loosens the fibres without drying them out
patient sieving gives a smooth preparation that coats the palate
a smooth texture takes the edge off harsh flavours
liquid poured in cold causes lumps in a purée
flesh full of fibres signals a badly chosen cut
an over-wet batter gives a cake that sinks like a sponge
texture is judged before taste
text: Three textures rule the plate of a careful cook, and each answers to rules of its own. Crispness comes first. It demands a brief cooking time, firm ingredients and a restrained dressing, since a generous sauce softens it at once. Meltingness takes second place, born of low heat held over a long stretch, which loosens the fibres without drying them out. Smoothness closes the set: won by patient sieving, it coats the palate and rounds off flavours that would otherwise cut too sharply. Alongside these three families sit the mishaps every cook dreads. A lumpy purée gives away liquid poured in straight from the cold. Stringy meat announces a badly chosen cut. A spongy cake reveals a batter swollen with damp. Knowing these faults counts for as much as mastering the successes, because texture is judged before flavour ever comes into it.

units: talk about cooking has shifted as households cooked less
speed was praised first
industry claimed to set free whoever prepared the meals
ready-made dishes were then taken to task for tasting of nothing
they were blamed for carrying too much salt
cooking programmes put the working hand on show
home kitchens never followed that display
a newer line of argument weighs a plate by its price and its origin
each phase corrected what the one before had overdone
text: The way people talk about cooking has shifted, and it shifted as households cooked less and less. Speed came first: a meal had to fit into a narrow gap in the day, and industry pledged to set free whoever stood at the stove. The mood then turned. Ready-made dishes were taken to task for tasting of nothing much at all, and the salt they carried was called excessive. Cooking programmes answered by putting the working hand on show, though what went on in home kitchens never really followed the display. A newer line of argument now weighs a plate by its price and by where its contents came from. None of this sequence is absurd: each stage corrected what the one before had overdone. It leaves a question nobody has settled, all the same. Who still has the room to cook without pressure bearing down on them?

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: the baker puts her skill down to a childhood spent beside the family mill
she turned down ready-mixed flours
that refusal cost her custom at the start
her dough rises at its own pace
the slow rise thickens the crust
her bread gives off a faintly sharp smell that throws new customers
many disappointed customers come back because the bread keeps for a week
her bake is gone before the middle of the day
she puts her success down to stubbornness rather than a gift
text: Ask the baker down the road where that dense loaf of hers comes from, and she will tell you she can hardly take the credit for it. Her parents ran a mill, so she grew up with her hands in the flour, and the habit settled everything that came after. Because she could tell the grains apart by touch from an early age, she turned down the ready-mixed flours, and the choice cost her custom at the start. Her dough rises at its own pace, so the crust thickens and the faintly sharp smell throws newcomers. Plenty of people leave disappointed, then come back again, because a loaf like that keeps for a whole week. She has never needed a sign above the shop: the bake is gone before midday and the queue spills out onto the pavement. Stubbornness, she says with a laugh, is what did it, not a gift.

units: this establishment listed more dishes than its kitchen could handle
the broth came through with no flavour at the first service
a heavy sauce flattened a delicate fish
the chocolate pudding felt rough under the spoon
the front of house did its job properly
the manager cut the menu in half
a cook brought in from a country inn took over the slow cooking
plates went out hotter and the wait shortened within the week
a short menu is presented here as the condition of decent cooking
text: The place that has just opened at the far end of the busy shopping street was suffering from a common complaint: a menu far too long, listing dishes that its own kitchen could not handle. The first service made that plain enough. The broth came through with no flavour at all, a heavy sauce flattened a delicate fish, and the chocolate pudding felt rough under the spoon. The front of house, in fairness, did its job well. The manager took the knife to the menu and cut it in half, then handed the slow cooking over to a cook brought in from a country inn. The difference showed within the week: plates went out hotter, the wait shortened, and the evening service coped without extra hands. A short menu is no confession of poverty. Here it is the very condition of decent cooking.

units: the woman written to describes her new kitchen as nothing like the old one
the old kitchen smelt of damp wood and baked fruit
the new one gives off a smell of metal and soap
the copper pan heated unevenly
the sauce had to be watched the whole time
the newer hob answers the dial at once
the writer reads this as a trade rather than an improvement
the old soups had a cloudy colour and a strong flavour
vegetables cooked in the new kitchen keep some firmness
text: You write that the kitchen you cook in now bears no likeness to the one we once shared, and I think I follow you. Ours smelt of damp wood and baked pear; yours, you say, smells of metal and of soap. With us the copper pan heated unevenly, and a sauce had to be watched the way one watches a child. With you the hob answers the dial at once and nothing boils over. I read that as a trade rather than an improvement. You have gained precision and you have lost the waiting. Our soups took on a cloudy colour and a deep flavour that your bright kitchen will never draw out; yours, on the other hand, leave the vegetables a firmness we knew nothing about. Write and tell me what you make in the evenings. I should like to picture the steam on your windows as I still see it rising from ours.

units: the hold of an emulsion rests on three separate things
an egg yolk or mustard wraps the droplets of fat
that coating keeps the droplets from running together
oil trickled in slowly gives the binder time to work
a sudden pour of oil breaks the mixture
very cold liquid sets part of the fat and leaves lumps
a split sauce is rescued by starting again from a fresh yolk in a clean bowl
the failed mixture is worked back in a little at a time
an emulsion that has held looks almost clear at the edges
text: What separates a stable emulsion from one that has split? Its hold rests on three things, and each of them can be looked at on its own. The first is the binder: an egg yolk, or a touch of mustard, wraps the droplets of fat and keeps them from running together. The second is the pace of the mixing. Oil trickled in slowly gives the binder the time to do its work, whereas a sudden pour breaks the whole thing at once. The third is temperature: liquid straight from the cold sets part of the fat and leaves a lumpy mass behind. And how is a split sauce rescued? Start again from a fresh yolk in a clean bowl, then work the failed mixture back into it a little at a time, without hurrying. An emulsion that has held together looks almost clear at the edges and velvety at the centre.

units: the head waiter tells the junior cook that every table will be taken
the junior cook says he prepared the garnishes as soon as the doors opened
only the herbs are missing
the buyer reports that the delivery will arrive late
she suggests using a spiced relish kept in a jar
the head waiter agrees on condition that the menu says so
a guest finds his dish too salty in the middle of service
the junior cook accepts the mistake and offers to make the plate again
not a single order was lost in the end
text: At the start of service the head waiter reminded the junior cook that every table would be taken. The junior cook replied that he had prepared the garnishes as soon as the doors opened, and that only the herbs were missing. The buyer then announced that the delivery would arrive late, and she suggested a spiced relish kept in a jar in place of fresh leaves. The head waiter hesitated before agreeing, on condition that the menu said so. Around the middle of service a guest remarked that his dish tasted too salty; the junior cook owned the mistake and offered a fresh plate at once, which the room carried out with no noticeable delay. At the close of the evening the buyer summed matters up before the assembled staff: not a single order had been lost, and everyone had been equal to the work.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: keeping food once rested on salt, smoke and sugar
these constraints shaped tastes that lasted
salt drew the water out of flesh, so it had to be soaked out before cooking
root vegetables were added to broths to balance a flavour that came through too strong
smoke left sharp compounds on the surface of the joints
cooks rubbed those joints with herbs and fat to soften the attack
sugar was kept for fruit because it was scarcer
mechanical cold made these methods unnecessary
the methods lived on as tastes people look for
text: Long before mechanical cold reached the kitchen, keeping food rested on salt, on smoke and on sugar alone. That constraint went on to shape whole tastes. Because salt drew the water out of flesh, it had to be soaked out again before cooking, and broths filled up with root vegetables to balance a flavour that came through far too strong. Because smoke left sharp compounds on the surface of a joint, cooks learnt to rub the outside with herbs and fat and soften the attack. Sugar, being scarcer, went to fruit, whose flesh it turned clear and yielding. When the ice box and then the cooling machine spread, none of these methods was needed any more, yet none of them died out either. They had become tastes that people look for, and they now cost a good deal more than something fresh.

units: sticky rice turns into a pasty lump as it cooks
the pan is rarely the main cause
the grain gives off starch the moment it heats in water
that starch behaves like glue
rinsing the grain until the water runs clear solves part of the problem
measuring the water avoids a longer cooking time
a longer cooking time crushes the grains
cutting the heat before the end lets the steam finish the job
salting the water at the start puts right a flavour that is too faint
text: Rice sticking together in a pasty lump? It happens far more often than you would think, and the pan is rarely the one to blame. The grain gives off its starch the moment it heats in water, and that starch behaves like glue. First thing to do: rinse the rice under cold water until what runs off it is clear, then leave it to drain. Second: measure the water instead of splashing it in, because too much of it means a longer cooking time, and a longer cooking time crushes the grains. Third: cut the heat before the stated end, put the lid on tight and let the steam finish the job without stirring. If it still tastes flat to you, salt the water at the start rather than the plate at the end. You will get separate grains, firm to the bite, that will take any sauce without falling apart.

units: a broken oven turned a caterer's evening upside down
the team shifted the whole menu onto fierce direct heat
the guests compared two ways of cooking without meaning to
root vegetables roasted the day before had a soft centre and a sweet surface
the same vegetables seared in the pan held a marked firmness and a plain bitterness
fish cooked in the oven had soft, airy flesh
fish cooked over the flame had brittle skin and denser flesh
the guests who were asked split into two camps of much the same size
the caterer now offers both ways of cooking
text: A broken oven turned a caterer's evening into an experiment that nobody had planned for. With no dry heat left to work with, the team shifted the whole menu onto fierce direct flame, and the guests found themselves comparing two ways of cooking without meaning to. The day before, the same root vegetables had roasted slowly: soft at the centre, sweet on the surface, rounded in smell. That night, seared in the pan, they held a marked firmness and a plain bitterness closer to the raw plant. The fish went the same way. From the oven it gave soft, airy flesh; over the flame the skin turned brittle and the inside came out denser. Asked on the way out, the guests split into two camps of much the same size. The caterer took the point and now offers both, letting the room decide.

units: a hard surface sends a short jolt back into the foot as it lands
the jolt travels up to the ankle joint and then to the joints of the leg
the muscles soak up part of the impact, which brings tiredness on sooner
stride length shortens of its own accord on that kind of ground
the foot then lands closer to the hips
a shorter stride covers less ground and brings the pace down
the body quickens the rate of the steps to make up for it, at the cost of more breath
coaches advise alternating the surfaces trained on
repeating an identical movement on an identical surface injures more than the distance covered
text: Land on hard ground and the ground answers with a short, sharp jolt. It travels up through the ankle, then into the knee and the hip. Muscle soaks up part of it, so tiredness arrives sooner than it would on a yielding surface. The stride shortens of its own accord: the foot comes down closer to the hips, and the joint takes less strain. Pace drops as a direct result, since every step covers less ground. To make up the difference, the body quickens the turnover of the legs, and that costs more breath. Coaches therefore ask their runners to alternate the surfaces they train on. A soft one gives the tendon room to recover, while a firm one builds bone. What breaks a runner is rarely the distance covered. It is the same movement, laid down again and again on the very same surface.

units: the club coach warned that ankles would give out before breath did
ground hardened by the cold stopped the boots from gripping
half the squad was limping when the season started again
the players blamed their kit, then the man who ran the sports hall, then bad luck
a player who worked as a physiotherapist suggested a balance drill on one foot
the drill is done on a soft cushion, with no hand on the wall, before every session
the players thought the drill ridiculous at the start
the sprains grew rarer once the habit had been taken up
the routine now opens every session, whatever state the ground is in
text: Our coach kept telling us our ankles would give out long before our lungs, and he was right. The moment the cold hardened the pitch, the studs stopped biting, and half the squad was limping by the time we started again. We blamed the boots first, then the man who ran the sports hall, then plain bad luck. One of the players, a physiotherapist by trade, put a deal to us: a spell of balancing on one foot before every session, on a soft cushion, with no hand on the wall. Nobody believed a word of it. At first we laughed at ourselves, wobbling about like badly planted posts. Then the sprains thinned out, and coming back after the break stopped feeling like a sick bay. The drill opens every session now, frozen pitch, soaked pitch or dry. Our coach has yet to admit it was not his idea.

units: three families of sole stand apart at the moment of buying
the thick, soft sole damps the impact and suits long outings on the road
the thick sole wears through quickly and leaves the foot unsteady on descents
the thin sole brings the foot nearer the ground and passes the push on better
the thin sole leaves the tendon exposed to repeated jarring
the studded sole is meant for soft ground and turns uncomfortable on a hard track
it is worth trying models on once the foot has already swollen
one should jog on a firm surface before completing the purchase
how well the joint is held is tested by turning on the spot
text: Buying a sports shoe comes down to weighing up three families of sole, say the assistants trained to advise on them. The first is thick and soft: it damps the impact and suits long outings on tarmac, but it wears through quickly and leaves the foot unsteady on a descent. The second is thinner. It brings the foot nearer the ground and passes the push on more faithfully, though it leaves the tendon open to repeated jarring. The third carries studs and belongs on soft ground; on a hard track it turns noisy and awkward. The method itself holds no mystery. Try the models on once the foot has swollen after a long walk. Jog on a firm surface before you reach for your card. Then turn on the spot to compare how each one holds the ankle. A shoe that suits you draws less notice than one that rubs.

units: the sports hall reopens after its fittings were put back in order
the tumbling track has been laid again from scratch
a springboard stands in front of the vaulting table
the bars carry the trace of the chalk left there by those who train
the hanging rings serve mostly for strength work in the upper body
a pit filled with foam blocks catches the falls of those learning
beginners turn up at the end of the evening
attendance has risen since the reopening
those who run the place put the rise down to the renewal of the apparatus
text: A smell of varnish still hangs over the mats in the hall that has just been put back in order. The tumbling track, laid again from scratch, gives out a dull note under the visitors' shoes. Then comes the springboard, a curved plank set before the vaulting table, which jumpers test with the heel before trusting themselves to it. Further on, the bars carry the white trace that every gymnast leaves behind in chalk. The rings hang from the ceiling on long cables and serve mostly for strength work in the upper body. At the far end, a pit filled with foam blocks catches the falls of those still learning, and the soft thud of it keeps time through the evening. Beginners come late on, when the room still belongs to the quiet. Attendance has climbed since the reopening, and the people who run the place put that down to the renewal of the apparatus.

units: the run-up settles the speed at which the board is reached
the jumper builds speed gradually, keeping the chest upright
the second to last contact serves to drop the centre of gravity
the last contact with the ground lasts less time than the ones before it
that last contact turns forward speed into a drive upwards
the board bends under the load and then hands back the energy it has stored
the arms rise at the moment the board sends the jumper away
rotation starts during the climb and not after the highest point
a landing that is too stiff passes the shock into the joint of the foot
text: It all starts with the run-up, whose length settles the speed at which the board is reached. The jumper builds that speed gradually, chest upright, stride even. On the second to last contact he drops his centre of gravity, bending the supporting leg further. The last contact with the ground lasts less time than any before it, and it is the one that turns forward speed into lift. The board bends under the load, then hands back the energy it has stored. The arms rise at that exact moment; otherwise the drive leaks away. Rotation starts during the climb, never after the highest point of the flight. The landing is taken on both feet, knees bent, chest a little forward. A landing that is too stiff sends the shock straight into the ankle and the tendon, which accounts for most of the injuries seen at this stage.

units: nothing obliges a child to settle on one discipline before adolescence
early specialisation loads the same movements onto the same joints
that loading brings on tendon overload before growth has finished
a narrow range of movement makes adapting hard when the ground changes
weariness is given as the chief reason for giving up
clubs push towards specialisation because early results draw funding
the writer proposes delaying selection in the junior ranks
he recommends requiring a second activity of every competitor
text: Nothing obliges a child to settle on one discipline before adolescence, and yet the clubs press for it, with effects that can be measured. Early specialisation loads the same movements onto the same joints, so overload of the tendon shows up before growth has finished. It also thins out the range of movement a young athlete owns: a teenager who has known one apparatus, or one way of landing, adapts badly the moment the ground changes. Then comes weariness, the chief reason for giving up somewhere between late childhood and adulthood. If clubs hold to their course, it is because results won early draw funding. We would do better to delay selection in the junior ranks and to ask a second activity of every competitor. A sporting life is built on the variety of the movements met, not on their repetition.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: the strength coach swam in competition when she was young
a torn tendon brought her sporting career to a halt
she went back to studying after that injury
she noticed that injuries came above all on the return after a break
she brought in a build-up spread over three weeks
that build-up starts with light loads and slowed movements
heavy loads come in only at the end of that period
the number of injuries in her club has fallen
neighbouring clubs have taken up her method
text: The club calls her its strength coach, and her whole office fits into a kit bag left on the tiles at the edge of the pool. She swam in competition when she was young, until the evening a tendon gave way and brought that career to a halt there and then. She went back to studying, then came back to the poolside with a question in mind. Watching her athletes, she noticed that injuries seldom struck in the thick of the season: they came on the return, after a break. So she brought in a return to training spread over three weeks, built from light loads and movements deliberately slowed down. Heavy weights enter only at the end of it, once the ankle and the shoulder have their range back. The number of injuries has fallen since, and clubs nearby have taken up the same method.

units: the writer used two gyms over the same season
the first gym is fitted with guided machines and screens
guided machines force a fixed path on the movement
the second gym sits in a badly heated shed
the second gym offers mostly bars, free weights and apparatus
the coach at the second gym corrects your position without being asked
the writer made more progress in the less comfortable gym
he still recommends the smart gym to anyone the weights frighten
text: I used two gyms over the same season, and they have almost nothing in common. The first one gleams: guided machines, screens on every wall, soft music, carpet that swallows the sound of the weights. It is a pleasant place to be, except that the machine settles the path of the movement for you, and the shoulder never learns to hold itself. The second sits in a badly heated shed, with bars, free weights and a couple of frames that creak. The floor bangs, people talk loudly, and the coach comes over to correct your position without being asked. Guess where I made progress. In the shed, of course, because a whole movement is worth more than one that is steered for you. Even so, I would send anyone the weights frighten to the smart gym: a machine that reassures beats giving up within a week.

units: the writer of the message reports to her reader on the club she has joined
sessions in the adult section run an hour and a half
warming up takes up the first third of the session
the equipment includes thick mats, a springboard and two sets of weights
the membership fee covers the loan of studded boots
the staff are two volunteers and one paid member of staff
the paid member of staff follows up the athletes who are injured
newcomers sit in on two sessions before paying
the writer invites her reader to come along one evening early in the week
text: Dear neighbour, you asked me for an account of the club I have joined, so here it is. Sessions in the adult section run an hour and a half, and the first third of that goes on warming up, which took me aback at first and won me over afterwards. The equipment is sound: thick mats, a springboard in good order, and two sets of weights, from the lightest to the heaviest. The membership fee covers the loan of studded boots, worth knowing if you would rather not buy anything before you are sure. Two volunteers and one paid member of staff look after us; she is the one who follows the injured, a twisted ankle, an angry tendon. Newcomers sit in on two sessions before paying a thing. Come along one evening early in the week, the hall is quiet then and I will introduce you to the whole group.

units: the first question is about what happens on the approach to the wall
the swimmer judges the distance left without lifting the head
she adjusts the reach of her arm strokes to arrive at the right spacing
the somersault begins with the chest tipping towards the bottom
the feet come to rest against the wall, set about hip width apart
the push off the wall gives a speed higher than that of swimming
the tucked position underwater holds on to that speed
swimming has to start again before the speed falls away
a foot placed badly costs more than a length swum badly
text: What happens to a swimmer in the second before the wall? Without lifting the head, she reads off how much water she has left before the wall, and she adjusts the reach of her arms so as to arrive neither cramped nor short. And what comes next? The chest tips towards the bottom, the somersault takes hold at once, and the feet come to rest against the wall, set about hip width apart. Does that turn really count for as much as people claim it does? It does, because the push off the wall sends her away faster than she will ever swim. The tucked position underwater holds on to that speed, so long as nothing sticks out to catch the water. When should she start swimming again? Just before the speed falls away. A foot badly placed on the wall costs more than a whole length swum badly.

units: a sports coach questions her pupils about their recurring aches
a boy describes a burning feeling in his thighs two days later
that boy often gave up on the sessions at the end of the week
another pupil reports a comparable discomfort in her upper back
the coach puts these aches down to sudden demands on an unprepared muscle
she recommends a longer warm-up, starting with brisk walking
she advises closing the session with stretches free of sharp movement
after a fortnight the aches ease and absences stop rising
text: At the end of practice the coach asked her group what kept on hurting once the training was over. One boy said that his thighs burned two days later, and that he often dropped the sessions at the end of the week rather than face them. A girl in the same class had much the same trouble, though hers sat high in the back. None of this surprised the coach. Soreness, she told them, comes of asking a cold muscle to work hard before it is anywhere near ready. So she stretched the warm-up out: brisk walking first, then slow circles of the arms and shoulders, and only after that the harder work. She asked them, too, to finish every session with quiet stretching, nothing sharp and nothing forced. The group trained that way for a fortnight. The aching eased off, and the register stopped filling up with absences.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: old contests were held with no measuring instrument and no markings on the ground
an elderly villager acted as judge through his word alone
the end of a game depended on the players wearing themselves out
in matches today the smallest irregularity is spotted and checked on video
sportspeople of the past began play with no muscular preparation
that lack of preparation brought repeated damage to the joints
sportspeople today set aside a sizeable part of their training for warming up
the appeal of movement and the wish to outdo others have not changed
text: Picture for a moment a sporting contest from long ago. No stopwatch, no whistle, not one chalk line anywhere on the ground. An old man from the village settled every argument that came up, and his word was the whole of the rulebook. A game ended when the players had nothing left in their legs. Set that beside a match today, where the smallest shove is caught, weighed and played back on a screen. The other gap is preparation. Players once walked straight into a game with their muscles cold, and they paid for the hurry with joints that gave way again and again. Anyone who plays now gives a serious slice of every session to waking the body up before asking anything of it. One thing has not shifted, mind you: the pull of running about, and the itch to beat the person alongside you.

units: three signs give warning that an effort is outrunning the resources available
the involuntary clenching of a muscle comes above all from a shortage of water and minerals
a sharp pain under the ribs comes from poorly managed breathing
trembling in the legs reveals a store of energy almost spent
each of these signs calls for a different response
the first is answered by drinking and lengthening the muscle gently
the second is answered by slowing the pace and breathing more deeply
the third is answered by stopping, taking food and waiting
neglecting these warnings risks an injury that is slow to heal
text: Three separate signals tell a runner that the effort under way has outrun whatever is left in reserve. The first is cramp: a muscle clenches on its own and will not let go, usually once the water and the mineral salts have run low. The second is a stitch, that sharp jab under the ribs, which comes of breathing that has fallen out of step with the pace. The third is a shake in the legs, the mark of a body that is running on almost nothing. Each one asks for its own answer, and treating them alike only drags the recovery out. For cramp: drink, then lengthen the muscle slowly. For a stitch: ease off and pull the breath deeper. For the shaking: stop, eat something, then wait. A pause costs a few minutes. Brushing the warning aside often costs an injury that takes months to mend.

units: a smell of chalk and warm rubber fills the hall as the player comes in
this player had been left unused for the whole season
the person in charge of the team sends her on with a simple wave of the hand
her first attempts fail and she misses two catches
a deflected ball strikes the edge of the hoop and drops back high in the air
she recovers the ball after its bounce by throwing herself to the floor
her roll ends with the ball returned one-handed
the move earns her a point without altering the gap on the score
from that moment she stops staring at the floor and feels lighter
text: The hall smelled of chalk and warm rubber when the substitute stepped onto the boards. She had spent the whole season on the bench, counting other people's passes and warming her calves for nothing. After the break the man in charge sent her on with a flick of the hand, saying not a word. She hurried, and it showed: she fumbled two catches and felt the quiet close in around her. Then a ball came off a hand at the wrong angle, clipped the rim and floated up. She followed the bounce, threw herself down, rolled across her shoulder and pushed the ball back one-handed. The point was given, and the gap on the board stayed exactly where it had been. But she stopped looking at her feet. The rest of the match went by quickly, almost lightly, as though the floor had at last taken her weight.

units: the support must be pulled onto a straight limb and not a bent one
a support fitted over a bent joint slips from the first strides
the sleeve is drawn up from the lower leg without being rolled
a fold of fabric hinders the circulation and numbs the end of the limb
the opening in the middle must ring the kneecap without pressing on it
weight resting straight on the bone brings on a dull ache after exercise
the straps are tightened working from the bottom upwards
tightening done the other way round makes the lower joint of the leg swell
wearing it for long stretches without cause weakens the muscles concerned
text: Pull the support on with the leg held straight, never with the joint bent. Fitted over a bend, it works loose within the first few strides and holds nothing at all. Draw the sleeve up from the lower leg, smoothing it as you go, and do not roll it: a ridge of fabric presses on the vessels underneath and leaves the foot numb. Check that the opening in the middle rings the kneecap without resting on it, since weight sitting straight on the bone brings on a dull ache once the session is over. Now pull the straps in, working upwards from the lowest of them. Fastened the other way round, they drive the blood downwards and the ankle swells up. Take the support off as soon as you have finished. Worn for days on end with no cause, it does the work the muscles should be doing, and they weaken.

units: the management of a sports facility closes two halls for the time being
the warped coverings underfoot had caused accidents
the families of the children enrolled protested against this decision
the neighbouring bodies had no free slot available
a meeting open to the public was arranged
specialists named an old water leak as the source of the trouble
that leak made the boards lift under the impact of landings
the games played with a racquet or over a net move to a hall brought back into use
the dance and strength classes are held in a multi-purpose room
text: Two of the halls at the sports centre have been shut for the time being, after the boards warped underfoot and brought about a run of falls. Families whose children train there objected almost immediately, all the more so as not one of the clubs round about had a single free slot to offer them. A meeting was called, open to anyone who wished to come. Engineers set out what lay behind the damage: water had leaked in years earlier and had never been traced, so the timber lifted each time a landing shook the floor. The answer they settled on comes in two parts. Racquet games, and anything played over a net, move to a hall that volunteers have brought back into use. The dance and strength classes go into the multi-purpose room. The slots that were lost will be handed back to the families.

units: two kinds of surface are laid in most sports halls
these two surfaces answer differently under the weight of a foot
the floor set on flexible battens sinks slightly at each step
that floor hands part of the energy back to the leg
it spares the joints and forgives inexact landings
its pale shade keeps the marks of shoes and calls for regular upkeep
the synthetic surface grips harder and helps the push at the start
it puts up with water, with wheels rolling over it and with shoes from outdoors
it makes sliding painful and does not absorb impact
text: Most sports halls are laid with one or other of two surfaces, and a foot coming down on them meets a very different answer. Wood set on flexible battens gives a little under each step, then hands a part of that energy straight back to the leg. Awkward landings are forgiven, and the joints take far less of a beating. The pale boards keep every scuff left by a sole, which means they have to be cleaned again and again. A synthetic surface grips harder and gives a cleaner push at the start of a sprint. Water does it no harm, trolley wheels roll over it and shoes worn in from outdoors leave it untouched. What it will not do is soften a landing, and sliding across it hurts a good deal. The choice follows the use, then: a floor that cushions on one hand, sharp changes of direction on the other.

units: the writer holds that the mania for counting spoils the pleasure of physical activity
he sets out the effects of that mania one after another
he likens running to a graded test because of the devices worn on the arm
he notes that the pitting of one against another reaches even friendships
an easy outing thus turns into a contest with figures
whoever falls short of the weekly target feels at fault despite having been active
night-time rest too is put through the reading of graphs
the writer does not reject the measures but blames them for filling the whole space
he wants physical activity to remain a wish and not an obligation
text: Honestly, all of this counting has taken the fun out of moving about. Look at what it has brought about, one thing at a time. Running has turned into an exam: off you go with a device strapped to your arm, and home you come with a mark. Then comes the ranking, which has crept in everywhere, friendships included, so that an easy outing ends up as a contest with figures attached. Then the guilt: fall short of your target for the week and you feel at fault, never mind that you walked, swam and laughed with the people near you. Even sleep is fed through the graphs now, as though the night were a test to be passed. I am not saying the figures are useless. I am saying they have swallowed everything else. Moving ought to stay something you fancy doing, not a debt that hangs over you.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: this practitioner began her working life in a small local facility
there she eased the shoulders of swimmers during their training
she specialised in shoulder injuries, a field little sought after at the time
a women's side at the top level then took her on
she watched the throwing movements for a full season before stepping in
her way of going about it rested on video, on comparison and on talking things over
shoulder injuries fell within the group
she now leads the medical staff of a training centre
she puts her results down to listening to injured players and checking what they say
text: The club's physiotherapist started out at a small local pool, easing the shoulders of swimmers between lengths. Shoulder injuries were what she went on to study, at a time when hardly anyone chose that corner of the field. A women's side at the top level took her on, and she spent an entire season watching how the players threw before she put forward a single exercise. Her way of going about it raised eyebrows: she filmed, she compared, she talked things over with the squad instead of handing down instructions. Shoulder trouble within the group fell away sharply. She now runs the medical staff at a training centre and teaches those coming up behind her. She insists she invented nothing. She listened to the players in pain, then checked each complaint against what she could see.

units: the performance leaves the spectator with an unsettling feeling
the performers were trained in sport and not in the theatre
that background gives them an uncommon physical stamina
they dance for a full hour without their breathing betraying any tiredness
that reserve lends an unexpected scale to the closing part
the same background produces the flaw of the evening
trained to reach a target, they favour movements that make a show
gestures that serve no purpose, with nothing to prove, are missing from their work
the string of feats leaves no room for a pause
the audience comes away impressed but hardly moved
text: There is something unsettling about this piece, and the reason for it shows within minutes: the performers were trained on the track, not on the stage. From that background comes the great strength of the evening, a stamina of a kind you very rarely see. They dance for a full hour and the breath never once gives them away, and that held-back reserve lends the closing section a scale which technique on its own would never reach. The same background explains what is missing. Taught to aim at a target, the performers go for what shows: the high leap, the fall caught clean, the shape that draws a gasp from the seats. The gesture that proves nothing escapes them entirely. And so one feat follows another with nowhere at all to breathe. You come away admiring, and oddly little moved.

units: the writer sends his message straight after a training session
he used to believe the two disciplines called for identical abilities
both practices demand holding a steady rhythm
the burning breath of the first minutes turns up in both activities
when running, the joints absorb the impacts against the ground
when swimming, the sense of weight fades away
the runner's obstacle is the slope of the ground
the swimmer's obstacle is the resistance of the water
alternating the two practices has eased the writer's joint aches
the writer invites his correspondent to try it for himself
text: I am writing with my hair still wet, straight off the back of a session, because something I had wrong for a very long while has finally come clear. For years I lumped running and swimming together, sure they asked for the same qualities. They do share one thing. Both make you hold a steady rhythm, and both begin with that raw burning in the chest until the breath settles down. After that they part company. On the road my joints take every landing, shock upon shock. In the pool my weight simply melts away, leaving nothing but the pull of the shoulders. The runner's adversary is the gradient of the ground; the swimmer's is the water pushing back at him. Since I started swapping one for the other, the old aches in my knees have gone quiet. Give it a go yourself, and write back to tell me how it feels on you.

units: the text answers the questions beginners ask most often
the warm-up must mobilise the ankle and the hip
expensive shoes are not necessary
a sole that grips guards against slipping on wet ground
the breathlessness of the opening minutes clears on its own
a sharp pain signals damaged tissue
muscle repair happens during rest
outings should be lengthened in small weekly steps
the pace chosen must leave room for conversation
text: So you want to move about considerably more without wrecking a knee in the process. The same handful of questions come round week after week, so here they are, in order. Do I need to warm up? Yes, and not with a token wiggle either: the ankle and the hip want waking properly before you set off. Do I need pricey shoes? No. You do need a sole that grips, though, or the first wet pavement will have you over and your ankle with it. Should it hurt? Never. The breathlessness of the opening minutes clears on its own; a sharp, stabbing pain is telling you something has been torn. Should I train flat out every day? No: muscle rebuilds itself while you rest, not while you labour. And how do I get better? Lengthen the outing slightly each week, and hold a pace you could still chat through.

units: the coach breaks the race down into three passages
the favourite set off at an excessive pace
the chasing group let the favourite go without reacting
the turn came on the steep climb of the second lap
the coach's runner passed her rivals one by one
the chaser went into the lead at the top of the climb
she opened up a gap on the downhill section
she accepted a slide in a muddy bend that the others refused
she broke clear of her last rival in the closing stretch
the coach puts the win down to composure rather than power
text: The coach we caught up with just past the finish breaks the race into three passages. At the start, as she tells it, the favourite went off far too hard, and the chasing group let her go without so much as a flicker. Then, on the steep climb of the second lap, the whole thing turned over. “I watched my runner pick them off one by one, and I knew she would close on her,” she says. Her athlete came over the top of the climb in front, then stretched the gap on the way down, where the others were braking out of caution. “She let herself slide through that muddy bend. The rest would not,” the coach adds. Along the closing straight the young woman broke clear of her last rival, with the crowd roaring her home. “She did not win on strength. She won on nerve,” she finishes, her voice catching a little.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: running was first of all an obligation tied to survival
it served to chase game, to carry news or to escape a threat
the reliance on stamina favoured limbs able to hold a lasting pace
that constraint shaped a springy cord at the heel
it also produced abundant sweating
a ligament keeps the neck steady during the stride
the spread of settlements and beasts of burden cut that need back
effort then turned into a measured and rewarded display
our bodies keep the imprint of a use that has become pointless
text: In the earliest days, running was no pastime at all but a plain duty: you ran to bring down an animal, to carry word across country, to get clear of something dangerous. Because survival hung on staying power, human groups kept, without ever choosing to, legs able to hold a modest pace over enormous ground. Out of that need came an odd build, with a springy cord at the heel, a skin that sweats freely, and a slender ligament holding the neck steady stride after stride. Then the settlements spread, roads opened, beasts of burden took up our loads, and the need for running drained away. Effort turned instead into a display: we began to measure it, to compare it, to crown it. That turn of events explains a small strangeness. Our flesh still carries the mark of a use that our lives no longer ask of it.

units: the pain in the side under effort brings many outings to an end
a sheet of muscle divides the chest from the belly
that sheet drives the movement of air in the lungs
short hurried breathing stops it from letting go completely
its prolonged contraction drags on the points where it is anchored
the pain shows up mainly under the ribs on the right side
easing the pace and drawing out the breath is the first remedy
pressing the sore spot while leaning the trunk forwards slackens the anchorage
a heavy meal before setting off encourages the problem to appear
text: A stitch in the side puts an end to more outings than anything else, and its workings are far less mysterious than they look. Below the lungs a sheet of muscle divides the chest from the belly, and it is this sheet that pumps the air. When breathing turns short and hurried, the sheet never lets go completely; it stays contracted and begins to drag on the points where it is anchored. The pain then shows up under the ribs, most often on the right. Three simple corrections settle the matter in nearly every case. First, ease off the pace and draw the breath out long, blowing steadily as the foot opposite the pain lands. Next, press a hand into the sore spot and lean the trunk forwards, which slackens the anchorage. Last, keep off a heavy meal beforehand, since a full stomach shoves the sheet upwards.

units: the sportswoman interviewed now plays in goal
she had begun her career in an attacking position
it took her seasons to see how far apart the two jobs are
the forward moves towards the open spaces
the forward has to forget her failures at once
the keeper falls back towards her goal
the keeper must hold on to every detail because her mistakes are paid for immediately
in her first match in goal she turned away a low shot
the crowd rose to its feet after that save
she holds that the two positions ask for equal courage
text: A goalkeeper once told me a memory of hers that lights up her whole trade. She had begun her career up front, and it took her several seasons to see that the two positions obey opposite logic. A forward, she explained, moves towards the open space: she must spring at the right instant, slip past a defender, and forget her failures immediately. The keeper falls back towards her goal, and must instead hold on to every detail, because a botched move there is paid for at once. On the evening of her first match in goal she dived at a low shot and turned it away with her wrist. The entire crowd rose to their feet. She understood then what attacking had never given her: the thanks of a side for an act of defence. Since that night she has maintained that both roles demand identical courage.

units: preparing a session runs through four successive stages
the first stage covers the kit and its condition
a seam that rubs or careless lacing brings on a skin injury
the second stage is getting the body going
getting going combines brisk walking, joint rotations and short bursts of speed
the third stage alternates fast stretches and calm ones
the pace chosen must stay bearable without clamping the breathing
the fourth stage means coming back down, drinking and stretching the legs
writing down the tiredness felt in a notebook records the progress made
text: Build your session in four stages, and keep them in this order. Stage one is the kit and the state it is in. Check the lacing, check that the sole is still sound, and feel round for any seam that rubs, because a blister grows out of some neglected detail. Stage two is getting the body going. Walk briskly, roll the joints of the legs through their range, then finish with a few short bursts of speed before you truly set off. Stage three is the body of the work: fast stretches alternating with calm ones, at a pace you can carry without clamping down on your breathing. Stage four is coming back down. Slow down in stages, drink, then stretch the thigh and the calf smoothly, without jerking. Finally, record in a notebook how tired you felt: week by week that trace will tell you whether you are progressing.

units: rain was falling as the first competitor reached the platform
there were fears the competition would be called off
the wind dropping left the surface of the water still
the organisers then sent off the opening rounds
the swimmer who opened entered the water with almost no splash
the strictest judge gave her a high mark
one competitor skidded on the wet board and chose to pull out
the equipment was wiped down before the restart
the reigning champion brought off a figure never seen at this venue
she finished ahead of the whole field
text: The rain was already coming down when the first competitor climbed onto the platform, and we were honestly wondering whether the thing would go ahead at all. It did. The wind dropped, the water went flat as a mirror, and the organisers sent off the opening rounds. The first dive caught the crowd cold: she went in with barely a splash, and the strictest judge on the panel handed her a high mark. After that it got messy. One competitor skidded on the soaking board, saved himself at the last moment and chose to pull out. The board was wiped down from end to end, and we carried on. Near the end, the reigning champion tried a figure nobody had dared here, a tucked reversal, and she brought it off. Climbing out of the pool she was still laughing: she had just left the whole of the field behind her.

units: a smell of resin and chalk meets the visitor at the door
the climbing wall takes up the full height of the building
the coloured holds trace routes that are hard to read
thick mats cover the floor and smother the noise of falls
nothing is heard but rubber squeaking and the breathing of the climbers
the openings are kept shut to stop the fingers growing cold
keeping the openings shut sends the heat up inside the room
a teenager hesitates then throws herself at a distant hold
her foot skids and the rope catches her halfway up
it is the repeating of the attempts that brings the progress
text: The smell of resin and chalk takes hold of you the very moment you step in through the door. The climbing wall runs the full height of the building, and its coloured holds trace routes the eye follows without ever quite reading them. Because thick mats swallow the floor, a fall makes no noise at all: you hear nothing but rubber squeaking and climbers breathing. The openings are kept shut, to hold off the draughts that chill the fingers, and so the heat builds inside. At the foot of the wall a teenager hesitates a moment, then throws herself at a hold set far out of reach. Her foot skids, she swings round, and the rope catches her halfway up. She comes back down, blows on her palms, and sets off again. It is out of that endless repeating of the attempt, and out of nothing else, that progress comes.

units: the writer holds it wrong to file movement away among amusements
children now spend their afternoons sitting in front of a screen
that stillness tells on the skeleton, the eyesight and the sleep
blaming families is judged convenient and unjust
the streets have closed themselves to play
the yards of teaching establishments have shrunk in size
the adult timetable leaves no free gap at all
the writer calls for places where noise and falling are tolerated
he suggests opening the covered yards outside teaching hours
he argues that physical tiredness is the mark of a life being used
text: We have filed movement away under amusements, and the filing has cost us dearly. The child who used to climb and jump and roll down a bank now spends the afternoon sitting, a screen within reach. The skeleton suffers for it, the eyesight too, and the sleep most of all. Blaming families comes easily, which is exactly what makes it unjust: the street has closed itself to play, the yards of our teaching places have shrunk, and the adult timetable leaves not a single gap. The way out asks for no great budget and no untried doctrine. Give children back places where noise and falling are tolerated. Open the covered yards outside teaching hours. Accept that a journey made on foot beats a parking space won. And stop treating physical tiredness as a mishap: it is the mark of a life being used.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: the specialist works with athletes who practise swimming
she begins by watching the athletes launch themselves off the edge
she looks for the movements that squander strength
she spends the second part of the day in a weights room
she teaches beginners to take hold of the load without tensing the upper back
she finishes with a study of the training logs
she ran middle distance before she took up coaching
she says her craft comes from her own physical injuries
she rejects identical plans for everyone
she reckons that suppleness brings more progress than rigid strength
text: The conditioning coach at a swimming club splits her week between three quite separate jobs. Her mornings belong to the poolside, where she watches the swimmers launch themselves off the edge, follows the way the knees fold before the push, and picks out the movements that squander strength for nothing. The second half of the day goes to the weights room; there she corrects the footing and teaches newcomers to take hold of the bar without tensing the upper back. Evenings are for the training logs, which she reads through and annotates with the patience of a copyist. A stocky woman, once a middle-distance runner herself, she says she learnt the craft by listening to her own injuries. She will not hand two athletes the same programme, and she holds to one idea: a supple swimmer improves further than a strong but rigid one.

units: the narrator recounts her visit to an indoor venue given over to climbing
her first impression of the welcome was poor
the lockers for clothes worked badly
she thought about giving up and leaving
an instructor taught her the right way to take hold of the grips
she lost her balance on the way back down and nobody mocked her
the crowd made the place noisy later on
the way the climbers helped one another made her forget the noise
she finds the price fair and the walls well designed
she criticises the changing cubicles and means to come back
text: Right, let me say it plainly: that indoor climbing centre won me over. The welcome struck me as shambolic, the lockers jammed on every second try, and I very nearly walked straight back out. Then an instructor came across and showed me how to take hold of a grip without crushing my fingers, and the session turned. I climbed an easy route, lost my footing on the way back down, and nobody laughed. Later the place filled up, the noise rose with it, and I grumbled inwardly. But the climbers passed advice around without shoving past one another, and the din dissolved into the effort. I came out with my forearms burning and that daft grin of a beginner who has just worked a movement out. Fair price, walls beautifully set, changing cubicles crying out for a rethink. I am going back next week.

units: the writer sends news to a member of her family
a structure that crosses a waterway has been shut for works
that closure made the training circuit unusable
the man in charge moved the sessions to a disused stone workings
the soft ground there forces the lower joints to bend further
pain at the back of the foot has dropped markedly
the grainy ground cushions the impacts better than the hard surface
passers-by saw the group from the road and signed up
the number of members has doubled
the reader is invited to come and try with borrowed kit
text: Dear cousin, you wanted news of the running club, and the news is good, though the reason for it verges on the comic. The footbridge over the canal has been shut for repairs, which chopped our usual loop into two stretches that lead nowhere. Left without a route, the coach moved the sessions to the old stone workings, where the loose ground forces the ankles and knees to bend a great deal further. The effect showed at once: heel pain has all but gone, since the grit swallows the impact that the hard surface used to throw back at us. And because the place sits in plain view of the road, walkers stopped to watch, then signed up, and our numbers have doubled. I am telling you this because you said you wanted to start again. Come along one morning, and we will lend you a pair of shoes.

units: the text deals with a joint of the upper arm that has been left idle
idleness brings on stiffening, according to the specialists in rehabilitation
the discomfort felt puts the sufferer off moving even more
a violent strain is unwise because it wakes the pain again
the answer put forward is a very small range of movement, repeated
the first exercise lets the limb swing freely
a very light weight is then brought in, such as an empty container
if the discomfort returns, one must go back to an earlier stage
the improvement does not come at a steady rate
whoever hurries the process fails again and again
text: What becomes of a shoulder that stops being used? It seizes up, say the specialists in rehabilitation, and the discomfort that follows puts the sufferer off moving it any further. The circle closes on itself. Should the joint be forced, then? No: a violent pull wakes the pain and drives the shoulder to guard itself all the harder. What remains? A tiny range of movement, repeated without haste, kept up over weeks. You begin by letting the arm hang and swing of its own accord, like a pendulum that nothing is pushing. Then comes a laughably light weight, an empty bottle, and later something barely heavier. And if the ache creeps back? You drop down a stage, without making a drama of it, for progress here rarely runs in a straight line. Whoever accepts that slowness ends up with a working shoulder; whoever hurries replays the same failure without end.

units: a specialist carer describes two techniques for coming back to the ground
the first technique keeps the lower limbs straight
that first option sends the shock right up to the top of the legs
the middle joint of the leg then carries the load
the second technique folds the hips and the knees at the moment of contact
the muscles at the front of the leg then cushion like a spring
the patient finds the second option harder work
the carer grants that tiredness but prefers it to damage of the joint tissue
a noisy return to the ground points to badly controlled cushioning
a quiet return to the ground reveals a movement under control
text: The physiotherapist was setting out for his patient the two ways a body has of meeting the ground at the end of a jump. The first, he said, is to land with the legs straight: nothing breaks the shock, it runs right up to the top of the legs, and the knee takes very nearly all of it. The second asks you to fold the hips and the knees the instant your feet touch, so that the muscles at the front of the thigh slow the drop as a spring would. The patient objected that the second way felt a good deal harder than the first. The therapist granted him that readily, then added that tired muscles cost far less than the wearing away of cartilage. He closed on a distinction that beginners tend to muddle: a loud landing is one that happened to you, whereas a quiet landing is one you steered yourself.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: the physical activities of the distant past are sorted into categories by specialists
the sorting rests on the end that was pursued
the first category sets two wrestlers against each other on a cramped surface
such contests turn up in almost every society that settled for good
the second category gathers the trials of speed over lengths of every sort
those trials put the honour of the community at stake
the third category has to do with sending an object far off
the vocabulary of those movements survives in the disciplines of today
the fourth category brings together the ball games with their local rules
such practices wove together exercise, ceremony and the settling of quarrels
text: The movement games of the distant past sort into separate families, which researchers tell apart by the end each one served. First come the trials of strength, where two wrestlers take hold of each other and try to unbalance an opponent on a cramped patch of ground; they turn up almost everywhere that people settled for good. Then come the races, run over lengths of every sort, often barefoot, with the standing of a whole village riding on the outcome. A third family gathers the throws, where a stone, a shaft or a disc is sent as far as the arm allows, and whose movements have handed their vocabulary down to the sports we watch today.
