A fourth brings together the ball games, whose rules shifted from one valley to the next. These practices, historians add, wove exercise, ceremony and the settling of quarrels into a single thing.

units: the contraction of a muscle follows a strictly ordered sequence
the thinking organ fires an electrical pulse as soon as an intention appears
that pulse travels along a nerve conductor
a chemical is released at the point of contact with the fibre
very fine elements slide past one another and shorten the fibre
the attaching cord then pulls on the piece of bone
the limb moves because of that pull
the filaments let go once the movement is finished
the whole process takes a very short span of time
the breathing quickens when the fibres run short of fuel
text: A muscle that contracts does so through a run of steps whose order never varies. Everything starts in the brain, which fires off an electrical pulse the moment an intention to move takes shape. The pulse runs down a nerve, reaches the point where the nerve meets the fibre, and releases a chemical there. The fibre answers at once: minute filaments slide past one another and the whole of it shortens. The tendon, hauled on from within, drags the bone it is fixed to, and the limb swings into motion. As soon as the movement is over, the filaments let go and the fibre stretches out again. The whole of that sequence lasts no more than a fraction of a second. When it runs on and on, the runner begins to gasp, because the fibres are calling for a fuel that the breath can barely supply.

units: the narrator was coming home from an evening swim
he took a narrow path that runs past a storage building
the recent rain had made the slope slippery
he thought he would gain time going down rather than round the slope
his foot slid on a root he could not see
he fell and landed in the mud
his open bag let his belongings spill out
he had to crawl along the ground to gather his things one by one
a passer-by handed him a towel without a word
he now takes the tarmac route
text: Coming home from the swimming pool the other evening, I had the bright idea of cutting along the narrow path that skirts the warehouse. It had rained, the slope was greasy, and I told myself I would get down it faster than round it. So I let my legs go, and my left foot slid on a root I never saw. I stumbled, flailed my arms like a puppet on strings, and ended up sitting in the mud with my bag hanging open. Out of that open bag my things rolled off in every direction, and I had to crawl about on the ground to gather them up one at a time. A walker handed me my towel without a word, looking terribly busy not laughing. Home I went, soaked through, caked in drying mud and thoroughly put out. Since then I take the tarmac road round, and I put rather less pride into my short cuts.

units: going back to running after an ankle injury worries ordinary athletes
a joint that has been poorly retrained gives way at the first step that lands askew
coaches put forward an approach in four stages
the first stage is to hold yourself up on the injured leg
that posture lasts about thirty calm breathing cycles
the second stage repeats the exercise with the eyes closed
closing the eyes removes the visual cues and calls on the receptors of the joint
the third stage brings in short hops on the spot with a turn of the hips
the last stage offers gentle strides that lengthen little by little
any sharp pain means stopping and going back to the stage before
text: Going back to running after a sprain unnerves most weekend athletes, and the worry is well founded: an ankle that has not been properly retrained gives way the first time a step lands askew. The routine that coaches recommend comes in four stages. Start by holding yourself up on the injured foot, arms loose at your sides, for about thirty calm breaths. Move on to the same posture with your eyelids shut, which strips away every visual cue and forces the receptors inside the joint to wake up. Then bring in short hops on the spot, turning the hips as you land and keeping the heel from drifting outwards. Finish with slow strides on even ground, adding a little distance from one session to the next. Stop everything the moment a sharp pain shows itself, and pick up again at the stage before, the following day.

units: two groups of runners share the same sports ground at the end of the day
the training goes on as night draws in
the sprinters have a heavy build and thick legs
they put out a violent effort over a short run of strides
they then pull up dead, short of breath
the long-distance runners are leaner and go round without a break
their breathing keeps to a steady rhythm
the speed specialists get their wind back by walking
a woman in charge of the training watches both camps
she notes that one lot stare at the timing device and the other lot at the sky
text: The track smells of wet dust, and as the light goes two groups are sharing it. On one side the sprinters: blocky frames, heavy thighs, waiting quite still, then detonating over a bare thirty strides before pulling up dead, gasping, hands on hips. On the other the distance runners, leaner and looser, going round and round without a break, chests calm, breathing ticking over like a metronome. The first lot spend the lot in one brief flare, then walk it off along the fence to get their wind back. The second spare every movement and hardly ever stop. A coach watches both camps from the finish line and remarks that the sprinters stare at the stopwatch while the distance runners stare at the sky. Their event, she says, shows plainly in the way that each of them carries fatigue.

units: the hall can be entered before sunrise
the person in charge lays the equipment out on the floor before the group turns up
those taking part leave their things beside the partition
the warm-up puts a walk together with a run
clapped hands give the jumps their beat
a ball-returning drill is done in pairs
the session closes with seated stretching
each pupil's progress is written down
text: The doors of the sports hall are unlocked before sunrise, and the wooden floor still carries a film of damp. A stocky coach lays out hoops along the centre line, then sets a row of low cones behind them. The pupils file in, drop their bags against the partition and pull on shoes with pale soles. Warming up starts with a long striding walk, arms reaching for the ceiling, and turns into an easy run around the room. Jumps follow, feet together first and then alternating, while the coach claps out the beat. After that come passes in pairs, each player returning the ball without ever holding it. At the end the group sits in a circle and works on the calves. The coach writes down what every one of them has managed, then opens the windows to air the hall before the next lot arrive.

units: the writer finds it contradictory to demand activity while doing away with open space
school play areas are losing ground
empty plots are turned over to parked cars
journeys on foot vanish in the name of road danger
young children are out of breath after one flight of stairs
the writer blames the surroundings rather than any want of will
a child who has never moved on rough ground breaks a fall badly
the fear of falling makes the stillness worse
the writer asks above all for school approaches that can be walked
text: We tell children to get moving, then we take away the places where moving is possible. That is the contradiction that irritates me. Playgrounds shrink year on year, spare ground goes over to parked cars, and getting anywhere on foot disappears because the roads are held to be dangerous. The upshot: youngsters wheezing after a single flight of stairs, tense the moment an unfamiliar effort is asked of them. This is not idleness, it is a consequence. A child who has never run over rough ground has no idea how to break a fall; he lands badly, hurts himself, and takes fright. The fright keeps him still, and round the loop goes again. So yes, add supervised sessions, but make the streets around the schools walkable first. Movement is learnt by walking, by climbing, by stumbling, not only in a slot pencilled on a timetable.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: the woman in charge of the swimming group failed first as a competitor
her uneven stroke cost her ground at every turn
she thought about leaving the sport
a doctor traced the trouble to the set of a shoulder
the fault came of growing too fast
she spent a full season reworking her technique with film to help
her times came down once that was put right
she forbids heavy repetition while the posture is wrong
text: Long before she took charge of a group, the swimming coach at the local club failed as a competitor. As a teenager she swam length after length without improving, held back at every turn by a jerky, broken stroke. Her times stalled and she thought about leaving the water for good. It was a sports doctor who eventually spotted a badly set shoulder, the legacy of growing too fast. Rather than train harder, she gave a whole season to relearning her catch, filmed from below, adjusting the entry of the hand a fraction at a time. The stroke came out long and even, and her times fell away. She now works the same way with the swimmers she looks after: film, show, correct one thing per session. She will not allow endless sets while the position is still wrong, and her group has turned out strong over distance.

units: the writer used two different climbing places in the same season
the first one sits in an old building with little light
its holds have been rubbed smooth by use
the routes there call for balance more than for pulling
the second place is full of colour and its routes are reset every week
the second one draws out leaping, showy moves
the writer prefers the dark one without calling it better
he puts that choice down to the care he must give his feet
text: Two climbing walls took my money in the same season, and nothing about them agrees. The first sits under an old market hall and keeps the gloom of a place nobody thought worth repainting. Its holds are worn, rubbed smooth by countless palms, and the routes ask you to find your balance far more than to haul on your arms. You climb slowly there, almost without speaking, and come down with your forearms on fire. The second wall is a riot of colour: high panels, deep matting, routes stripped out and reset every week. Everything about it invites the lunge, the leap, the move worth watching. A seasoned climber will take patience from the one and pure play from the other. I prefer the dark hall, though I would not call it the better of the two: it makes me listen to my feet, where the other flatters my arms.

units: the writer sets out, as asked, the method he has kept to since taking the sport up again
he records how long each outing lasts and how fast it was
he takes his pulse on waking, lying down
he does strength work twice a week without heavy loads
he uses two pairs of shoes according to how long the outing is
he advises drinking before thirst arrives
he stops building whenever two sessions in a row feel like a burden
he credits this record-keeping with keeping fresh injuries away
text: You asked me to set out the routine I have kept to since I started again, so here it is, heading by heading. Training load: I write down every outing, the time on my feet, the average pace, how the last stretch of it felt. Recovery: I keep an eye on sleep and on my pulse when I wake, taken lying down before I get up. Strength: twice a week is quite enough, side planks, calf raises, hip extensions, never chasing a heavy load. Kit: I rotate two pairs of shoes, a light one for the short outings and a cushioned one for the longer ones. Food: nothing out of the ordinary, beyond drinking before the thirst arrives. Mood, last of all: I stop building the moment two outings in a row feel like a burden. The notebook is an ugly thing, but it keeps me upright and it has kept fresh injuries away.

units: a question is put about the youngest age for carrying a load
before schooling begins no added load is called for
the very young child works with his own weight by climbing
the stage that follows puts the quality of the movement above the resistance
a light implement and a reflection are enough at that stage
the equipment must suit the build of the child
an adult's kit must not be taken over
two short training sessions are worth more than one very long one
the exercise halts as soon as the hold of the back gives way
text: A listener puts the question of the age at which a child may lift a load without coming to harm. The answer follows a progression which ought to be kept to in order. Before school begins, no outside load serves any purpose: the child has quite enough in his own weight, which he shifts about by climbing and rolling. Then comes a stage in which learning the movement counts for more than the resistance, and a light stick with a mirror beats a loaded bar. A second question bears on equipment, which must suit the build of the child and never be taken over from an adult. A third bears on how often, and the answer holds in a line: two short, regular sessions beat one that drags on. Watchfulness comes last, and it must stay keen, for the moment the back gives way the exercise halts.

units: a young athlete reports a pain in the knee after three climbs
he had doubled the length of his outings inside a week
the coach explains that tendons come along more slowly than the lungs
the pain arises from that gap in adaptation
the young man believed he could take on more
the coach adds that the sense of ease arrives before the tissue is ready
they agree on an easier restart and a modest weekly rise
the coach weighs the cost of a neglected injury against that of a short pause
text: A teenager told his coach that a burning came into his knee as soon as he reached the third climb. The coach asked him what had changed in the way he was preparing, and the boy owned up to doubling the length of his outings inside a week. Tendons, the coach said, come along more slowly than the lungs do, and the pain sat exactly in that gap. The boy answered that he still felt able to take on more. He was told that the sense of ease arrives well before the tissue is ready, which is what catches beginners out. So the two of them agreed on an easier restart, with the build kept to a small amount each week. The boy wanted to know how long a thing like that would go on for; a hurt knee left alone costs a season, came the reply, while caution accepted costs a handful of outings.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: carriers of letters once crossed high ground with no path and no pack animal
one man on his own gave out before he reached the end
the letter was liable to come late or to be lost
the answer they found was to hand the load on
shelters were set out at even gaps
each shelter held a rested carrier who left again at once
the overall speed of carriage was doubled
the carriers stopped holding back, their own share being short
this way of cutting up an impossible effort still serves elsewhere
text: Picture messengers who had to cross whole valleys on foot, with no track cut for them and no animal to carry the load. The work broke people, and the snag was easily put: one man on his own gives out before the end, so the letter comes late or never comes at all. The answer they hit on was the handover. Shelters were set out at even gaps, each one holding a fresh runner who took the leather pouch and left again at once. The stretch to be covered in one go turned bearable, and the speed of the whole thing doubled. Better still, the runners stopped holding anything back: knowing their own share was short, they ran it flat out. And there sits an idea we still lean on, from the carriage of goods to races run by teams, which is to cut an impossible effort into portions a body can hold.

units: what tells the two runners apart is the way muscular energy is spent
the sprinter carries mostly fast-contracting fibres
those fibres are powerful but give out in moments
the distance runner carries fine, slow fibres
those fibres burn oxygen without tiring
the sprinter builds up a breathing debt that he pays back afterwards
the distance runner sets his pace so as to avoid that debt
their training differs, repeated starts against long outings
how the fibres are shared out is partly inherited
text: What sets a sprinter apart from a distance runner, if not the way in which his muscles spend the energy they hold? The first leans on fast fibres, thick ones, good for a short and violent contraction that dies away almost at once. The second carries slow fibres, finer and less brisk, which burn oxygen all day without tiring. The sprinter builds his effort with the breath more or less held, then pays the debt back afterwards, gasping. The distance runner sets a pace that never digs such a hole in the first place. The training shows it too: the one repeats his starts and takes his recoveries in full, the other piles up long outings at a held effort. Training tips the balance one way or the other without overturning it, since the share of fibres is partly a thing that you inherit.

units: the narrator recalls a walk along a soaked ridge line
the soles made a sucking noise in the mud
a stone came away down the face during the climb
the walk was led by an elderly woman at a steady pace
the others in the party climbed strung out
the top was reached all at once
a hard wind dried the clothes in an instant
they came down a gentler side and said nothing
text: On the ridge path the mud made every footfall slide, and I remember that outing better than I remember any of the others. There was the noise first of all: the suck of boots pulling free, the shortened breathing, a stone that came away and dropped down the face. There was the woman at the front, a brisk pensioner who climbed without ever altering her pace, as though the slope had nothing to do with her. There was the rest of us strung out behind, each one setting his step by his own tiredness. And there was the crest itself, come upon all at once, with a wind that dried our jackets in the space of a breath. We went down the far side, gentler, telling each other nothing. That silence was worth more than any account of it, and I carry it still whenever a climb looks too steep.

units: a wall painting decays because its support soaks up water
the coloured layer lifts off the wall in flakes
the damage comes from the support and not from the coloured matter
the first step is to draw the damp out of the wall
compresses pull the salts out of the wall
the loosened fragments are refixed with a liquid adhesive
the losses are filled with fine hatching that shows up close to
the missing decoration is not put back by repainting
text: Picture a painted wall flaking away in front of you. The plaster drinks in the damp, the colour lifts, and the wall painting that a workshop once laid down there ends up as dust. The blame rarely sits with the pigment itself; it is the support underneath that moves. So conservators begin by drying the wall out, gently, with compresses that pull the salt out of it. Then they refix the flakes one by one, slipping a liquid adhesive behind every lifted fragment. The brush arrives last, and even then it mainly serves to settle the gaps with fine hatching that you notice only close to. No serious workshop repaints what has gone: they fill, they steady the surface, they leave the loss on show. What you get is a painting that stands up and owns its wounds instead of hiding them under make-up.

units: an exhibition splits the finished work and its preparatory drawings between two rooms
the finished painting hangs alone on a dark wall
visitors lower their voices in front of the finished painting
the preparatory drawings hang close together and show changes of mind
the public stops for longer in front of the preparatory drawings
the preparatory drawings get visitors talking to one another
a teacher reckons her pupils grasp at last how gradual the making of art is
the organiser of the exhibition hesitated before showing the working documents
text: The contrast hit you the moment you walked in. In the first room the finished canvas hung alone on a dark wall, lit like a relic, and visitors dropped their voices in front of it. In the second, the preparatory drawings were pinned up close together, changes of mind and all, hesitant lines, thumbprints from the painter. The attendants say the crowd lingers far longer over the drawings. The finished work commands silence; the working sheets set people talking to one another. A teacher who had come with her class put it plainly: her pupils grasped at last that an image does not arrive whole from an inspired mind, but gropes about, fails and starts again. The organiser of the show admits he hesitated before opening that second room, for fear of stripping the mystery from what he was showing.

units: the modelling material has to be softened under the hands first
the air bubbles are driven out by slamming the lump on a hard surface
a dull sound tells you the air has gone
the thumbs hollow the piece out from the centre
the fingers draw the wall upwards
drying happens in the shade under a damp cloth
draughts are to be avoided while the piece dries
the cut base has to be wider than the piece
a plaster cast lets you copy the shape once the surface is dry
text: Start by waking the clay up. It comes out of the bag cold and closed; worked slowly under the palms, it softens and stops fighting back. Then there is the air to deal with. Slam the lump down onto a hard, unyielding surface, again and again, until the sound turns dull and flat, which tells you the air has gone. Shaping follows immediately: the thumbs hollow out from the centre while the fingers draw the wall upwards. Drying is the thankless stage that impatience invariably ruins. Keep the piece in the shade under a damp cloth that slows the water leaving, and well away from draughts. Last of all comes the base, cut wider than the piece itself, because anything standing needs an honest footing. If you want a copy of your model, make a plaster cast, but wait until the surface is dry to the touch.

units: the window was taken down panel by panel
every element was placed on a measured drawing before it came out
the glass was washed in demineralised water at the workshop
the washing had to spare the dark painted layer
the broken glass was bonded with resin under a magnifying instrument
resin bonding cannot be undone afterwards
a second window was fitted in front of the original to shield it from swings in heat
the new metalwork is finer than the one before
the refitting has to be over before the cold season
text: The undertaking opened with the removal of the window, panel by panel, each piece marked on a measured drawing before it was eased out of its leadwork. The glass then travelled to the workshop, where washing in demineralised water lifted the sulphate deposits without touching the dark painted layer. The most delicate operation followed: bonding the broken glass with resin under a magnifying instrument, a step that cannot be reversed later on. Those directing the site then settled on protective outer glazing, a second window set in front of the original to shield it from swings in heat and from condensation. Rebuilding came after that, with fresh metalwork narrower than the old, so that the drawing could be read again. The refitting will be over before the cold season, the client body says.

units: the performance hall sits on the top floor of an old building
its timber frame is left in view
the wood soaks up part of the lower notes and takes the edge off harsh tones
the side walls lean in slightly
the lean of the walls throws the sound back towards the middle rows
listeners at the back hear almost as well as those at the front
the low ceiling cuts the reverberation short
spoken voices come across more clearly while large ensembles lose their fullness
the place mostly programmes small groups and readings
text: The hall occupies the top floor of an old building, and its exposed timber frame decides how it sounds. Wood resonates with the lower notes, so it soaks up part of the energy in the room and takes the edge off the harsher timbres. The side walls lean in a little, which throws the reflections back towards the middle rows; anyone at the back hears almost as well as those in the front. The low ceiling, on the other hand, cuts the reverberation abruptly short. Spoken voices come across cleanly, while large ensembles lose their fullness. The programming follows directly from all that. Small ensembles, recitals and readings are what the place invites, and the heavy forces that the volume could never carry without muddle are quietly left aside. Here the architecture itself dictates the repertoire.

units: the greater part of museum collections stays out of the display rooms
a shortage of space and of funding explains this
one answer is to digitise the stored holdings on a large scale
digitising makes a piece shut in a drawer visible from a distance
another answer is to lend works out for a limited time
these loans benefit institutions that cannot afford to buy pieces
the writer holds that both answers have to be pursued together
the two answers meet different needs
text: Museum stores hold the vast bulk of what our collections contain, and that bulk never leaves its crates. The imbalance is hardly a secret: only a sliver of what is kept ever goes on show, for want of floor space, of staff and of funding. Two possible remedies are being aired. The first is to digitise on a considerable scale, so that a print shut in a drawer becomes something anyone can consult from a screen. The second is to move works about on temporary loan, towards smaller institutions with no budget for acquisitions. Both deserve to be pursued together, because they answer different needs: one feeds study and curiosity from a distance, the other offers a meeting in the flesh with the object. Refusing to choose between them is costly. Leaving a whole heritage asleep costs a good deal more.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: the craftsman compares his trade to a discipline of patience
he used to draw on a screen
a mistake made on a screen was undone without consequence
the metal he engraves allows no correction
that constraint has made him more demanding, he says
on the screen he worked fast and dropped his difficult ideas
on the plate he thinks before every cut
a cut taken too deep destroys weeks of effort
his daughter is learning to draw on a computer and teases him about his method
text: The engraver in the back workshop talks about his trade as a sport of patience. He used to draw on a screen, where a mistake disappeared at a keystroke and cost him nothing. Since he took up a burin, everything has changed. Copper forgives nothing, he says, laughing, and that is exactly what has made him better. He readily compares the two practices. On the screen he turned out work quickly and in quantity, but he dropped an idea the moment it put up a fight. On the plate he thinks before every cut, because one line taken too deep obliterates weeks of effort. His daughter, who is learning to draw on a computer, teases him and calls him a cave-dwelling craftsman. He tells her he will teach her engraving when she learns to wait, and that she will see then that slowness is a method, not a punishment.

units: the writer picks out three successes and one fault in this exhibition
the low picture rails force the visitor to step in close
that closeness changes how the small formats are seen
the labels are short and free of jargon
the labels set out a technique instead of commenting on a feeling
a quiet sound track plays workshop noises
these noises stand in for ambient music
the lighting is too even and flattens the ridges of thick paint
the writer advises a visit late in the afternoon when the sun comes in through the high windows
text: Three things save this show, and one thing weighs it down. The arrangement comes first: the picture rails have been hung low, so you have to step in close, and that closeness transforms what the intimate formats do to you. Then the labels, written short and mercifully free of jargon, which set out how a thing was made instead of telling you what to feel. Then the sound, kept low, a knife scraping across a palette, an easel creaking as it is shifted: the noise of the work itself, worth immeasurably more than any ambient music. The fault lies in the lighting, too uniform throughout, flattening the ridges of paint on the most heavily loaded pieces. It would be worth returning late in the afternoon, when low sun reaches in through the high windows, to catch what the arrangement failed to bring out.

units: the writer is writing from a performance hall that is still empty
he turned up late to his first class in the autumn
he had sworn never to go back on stage
he came back every week through the cold season
he kept it up out of stubbornness first and then for the pleasure of it
the head of the company gave him the part of an old caretaker
that part says little and watches the others
the performance the night before played to a full house
the person he writes to had urged him to sign up for the class
the writer invites him to the last performance
text: I am writing from the empty auditorium, before the others arrive. Do you remember my first class, back in the autumn? I arrived late with my coat still on, and I swore I would never set foot on that stage again. The cold months went by and I kept coming back every week, out of stubbornness at first, then because I enjoyed it. When the stage sessions began, the head of the company handed me the part of the old caretaker, the one who says little and watches everyone. Last night we played to a full house. I felt the silence close over my first line like still water. I am not writing to boast. I am writing because you were the one who pushed me to sign up, on an evening when I claimed nothing amused me any longer. Come to the last performance; I am keeping you a seat in the front row.

units: old paper browns because of the raw material itself
pulp made from wood holds a substance that oxidises in light and air
that oxidation releases acids which break down the cellulose
the brown ringed stains come from too much damp together with spores
a fungus feeds on the size held in the sheet
washing removes those stains only in part
an alkaline bath neutralises the acids that are there
the bath leaves a protective reserve in the sheet
mounting in a sealed frame limits distortion when the work is moved
text: We are often asked what turns the paper of an old print brown. The cause lies in the fibre itself: as soon as the pulp contains wood, the lignin it contains oxidises in daylight and air, then releases acids that eat away at the cellulose. And the brown ringed stain? That comes from too much damp in the air together with spores. A fungus establishes itself, feeds on the size in the sheet and leaves a mark that washing only partly eliminates. What does a conservation workshop do once it has that diagnosis? It deacidifies in an alkaline bath, which neutralises the acids and leaves a protective buffer reserve in the sheet. And if the work has to travel? It is mounted in a neutral quality window mount inside a sealed frame, since every shift in humidity works the fibre and accentuates the cockling.

units: a neighbour describes an evening spent in a theatre
she sets against each other two venues she attends regularly
in the first venue the scenery is painted onto broad canvases
in the second venue movable panels are shifted in front of the audience
the neighbour prefers the venue that makes her forget she is watching a performance
her brother prefers the venue where the stage machinery is on show
the two of them discuss this question often without ever agreeing
the neighbour ends up granting that each of the two methods calls for a skill of its own
she invites the person she is talking to to come and judge for himself at the next performance
text: My neighbour came back from the theatre the other night and could not stop weighing up the two houses she goes to. At the first, she said, the scenery is painted onto great sweeps of canvas, and the moment the curtain lifts you believe in the old square standing in front of you. At the other, everything hangs on movable panels that the crew shift about in full view, so the audience watches the change happen. She likes the first better, because it lets her forget she is sitting in front of a made-up story. Her brother goes the other way and defends the house where you can see the machinery at work. The two of them turn it over again and again and never agree. In the end she granted that each way asks for a skill of its own. Then she asked me along to the next performance, so that I could settle it myself.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: builders of the distant past handed down a set of forms that architects still reuse
the upright support carries the load and divides the space inside
the rounded vault answers the need to roof a wide room with no support in the middle
the curve of that vault carries the thrust outwards to thick walls
the carved band runs beneath the roof
that band turns into pictures the stories the community wished to hand on
the great staircase serves to stage the arrival of the visitor
specialists explain the spread of these forms by the travelling of masters and apprentices
text: Builders of the distant past left behind a stock of forms that architects still reach for. The column heads that inheritance: it takes the weight above, and it breaks up the space inside, giving the eye something to rest against. The dome came out of a plain need, to roof a wide room with nothing standing in the middle; its curve carries the thrust outwards to the heavy walls that ring it. The carved band running under the eaves does other work altogether, setting out in repeated figures the stories a community wanted handed on. Last comes the great staircase, which does far more than lift you a storey: it turns the arrival of a visitor into an event. Scholars who study these buildings put the spread of such features down to the travelling of masters and apprentices from one workshop to the next.

units: the making of a woven hanging runs through several successive stages
a painter first produces a small drawing that settles the colours and the composition
that drawing is then transferred at very large size onto a guide sheet
the sheet is placed behind the threads to steer the hand of the craftsman
the wools are dyed before the weaving
the craftsman records the recipe of each dye bath so the shade can be found again later
the weaving is done on the reverse of the piece
the threads are cut and the edges strengthened when the piece leaves the loom
the workshop discovers the final appearance only after turning the work over
text: A woven hanging never comes into being at a stroke. It begins small, with a painter's drawing that settles the colours and the placing of the figures. That drawing is then blown up to full size on a guide sheet, an enormous thing the weaver hangs behind his threads to steer his hand. The wools go into the dye vats first, and the craftsman writes down the recipe of every bath, so that the same shade can be found again long afterwards. The weaving is worked from the back, which obliges the woman at the loom to picture a face she will not see until the end. Row after row she goes, unhurried, following the outline showing faintly through. When the piece comes off the loom the threads are cut, the edges bound and strengthened, and the work at last turned over. Only then does the workshop see what it has made.

units: a pupil's instrument had lost its biting tone
the maker first ruled out the heavier faults of the instrument
the belly showed no crack and the pegs were holding the tuning
the examination turned next to the bow, whose hair had been drawn too tight
excess tension reduces the contact between the hair and the string
that reduction makes the attack soft and thins the tone in the upper registers
the maker slackened the frog, rubbed the stick down and laid on fresh rosin
the pupil found the tone again from the first notes
the workshop recorded the case because this fault comes back when a quick adjustment replaces a full examination
text: A pupil's instrument had lost its bite, and nobody could say why the tone had gone so dull. The maker she took it to began by ruling out the heavier faults: the belly showed no crack anywhere, and the pegs were holding the tuning without slipping. He turned next to the bow, whose hair had been drawn far too tight after a rehair. Too much tension lifts the hair away from the string, so the attack turns soft and the tone thins out in the upper register. He slackened the frog off, rubbed the stick down lightly and laid on fresh rosin. From the very first notes the pupil knew again the sound that she had thought lost for good. The workshop wrote the case up in its book, since the same fault comes back again and again whenever a hurried adjustment stands in for a proper examination.

units: playing a stubborn piece through in full deepens the difficulty instead of resolving it
the advised method consists in lifting out the passage that causes trouble
the exact bar where the hand falters must be found and marked
the fragment must be played very slowly and with each hand on its own
attention goes to the position of the fingers and not to the page
the speed is raised in successive stages
one must drop back to the previous stage as soon as a mistake appears
the fragment must then be joined to the neighbouring bars because the difficulty often sits in the join
this approach avoids fixing a faulty movement that would have to be unlearnt
text: Playing a stubborn piece through again and again deepens the trouble instead of clearing it. The advised approach is to lift the awkward passage out and treat it as a thing apart. Find the exact bar where the hand falters, and mark it in pencil so that you cannot mistake it later. Then take that fragment very slowly indeed, each hand on its own, watching where the fingers fall rather than following the page. Build the speed up by stages, and drop back to the stage before the moment a mistake appears. Join the fragment afterwards to the bars on either side of it, because the difficulty very often sits in the join itself. The way of working asks for a good deal of patience, but it keeps you from settling a faulty movement into the hand, one that would later have to be taken apart and unlearnt.

units: two neighbouring concert halls have chosen opposite strategies to renew their audience
the first hall has shortened its programmes and done away with the interval in the middle
tickets there cost less and there is no rule about what to wear
the players in that first hall introduce the works themselves from the platform
the second hall has lengthened its break and turned it into a meeting with the audience
listeners in the second hall may come down and question the performers
both managements report attendance on the rise
the first hall draws occasional visitors whereas the second builds up a body of subscribers
a regional study will compare these results at the close of the season
text: Two concert halls in the same town have taken opposite routes to renewing their audience. The first has cut its programmes short and done away with the interval, on the view that newcomers sit badly through an evening broken in two. Tickets there cost less, nobody is told what to wear, and the players introduce the works themselves from the platform. The second hall did the reverse: it stretched the break in the middle and made a meeting of it, with listeners coming down to the front to put questions to the performers. Both managements report attendance on the rise, though the crowds they draw are not the same. The hall with the short evenings pulls in people who come once out of curiosity, while the other is building a body of subscribers. A regional study will compare the two sets of results at the close of the season.

units: an old market hall has been turned into an arts centre
the entrance holds posters and an upright piano open to everyone
the pottery room houses shelves loaded with half-finished bowls
the makers of those bowls come back to finish them in the evening
the dance room has kept its original floor, which creaks underfoot
a narrow room at the far end serves as a recording studio
rugs fixed to the walls there stand in for soundproofing the place could not afford
the upper floor holds a collection of sheet music lent out against a signature
benches have been fitted on the roof to give people somewhere to rest
text: Push open the door of the old market hall that became an arts centre and the first thing you meet is the entrance, cluttered with posters and holding an upright piano that anyone at all may try. On the left the pottery room smells of wet clay, and the shelves sag under half-finished bowls whose makers come back in the evening to finish them off. Opposite, the dance room has kept its original floor, and the wood creaks so loudly that the pupils count their steps by the sound. At the far end a narrow room does duty as a recording studio, with rugs nailed to the walls in place of the soundproofing nobody could ever afford. Upstairs sits the collection of sheet music, lent out against a signature. And on the roof someone has fitted benches, because people needed somewhere to sit between sessions.

units: in the older forms of song the storytelling part was dominant
the repeated part held a brief and secondary role
broadcasting turned that order upside down
a listener paying half attention had to be able to recognise a track very quickly
the repeated part grew longer until it opened the song
listening platforms have sharpened this shift
their payment is triggered after a very short stretch
the writer of the text judges this shift impoverishing
the writer holds that stubborn creators are already showing that the constraint can be escaped
text: Look at how popular song has shifted since its oldest forms. To begin with, the verse carried the story and the chorus was a place to rest: short, almost an afterthought. Broadcasting then turned that order upside down, since a listener paying half attention had to recognise a track within a handful of seconds; the chorus swelled until it opened the song outright. Listening platforms have pushed the same logic further still, because payment is triggered once a very brief stretch has been heard. What we are left with is a craft where the hook comes before all else and the story fades away. You may welcome that and call it a fresh kind of efficiency. I see mainly a loss: a form that gives up on lasting gives up on surprising us too. The most stubborn writers are already showing that the constraint can be escaped.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: the workshop calls this specialist the restorer of wall paintings
her mother cleaned the display cases of a regional museum
she went along with her mother when she was a child
that early haunting gave her a taste for damaged surfaces
she studied the chemistry of solvents before she came to drawing
she refuses to act until the origin of the damage has been identified
her colleagues complain about how slow she is
she answers that haste has destroyed more paintings than damp
her methods have been spreading among the younger hands since a whole room was put in her charge
text: In the workshop they call her the restorer of wall paintings, and that title says very little indeed about the doggedness the work demands. As a child she went along with her mother, who cleaned the display cases of a regional museum, and that early haunting gave her a taste for damaged surfaces. Because she could not bear to watch faces vanish under grime, she learnt the chemistry of solvents before she ever learnt to draw. The detour explains her manner: she treats each wall like a patient, and will not touch it until she knows what caused the harm. Colleagues complain that she is slow, and she answers that haste has destroyed more paintings than damp ever did. Since a whole room was put in her charge, her way of working has been spreading among the younger hands of the house.

units: a retrospective given over to the art of glass raises an objection of a technical order
the pieces on show stand on low plinths and are lit from above
this lighting flattens the thicknesses instead of bringing them out
the visitor loses the reading of the inner layers of the objects
the cases have been ranged along the partitions
glass calls for a plain ground and light coming from behind
the reviewer proposes drawing the plinths away from the wall and adding diffusing panels
he also advises bringing down the colour temperature of the sources
he recommends reworking the hang before the announced tour
text: The retrospective given over to the art of glass raises a technical objection that the general reviews have passed over in silence. The pieces stand on low plinths and are lit from above; that raking light flattens the thicknesses instead of bringing them out, and the visitor loses the reading of the inner layers, which is the whole point of such work. The fault lies in the layout: the cases have been ranged along the partitions, when glass asks for a plain ground and for light coming from behind. A remedy exists, and it has been tried elsewhere already. The plinths need only be drawn away from the wall and diffusing panels set behind each object, with the colour temperature of the sources brought down at the same time. The hang deserves reworking before the tour that has been announced.

units: the writer of the message answers a question about what he does
a first workshop teaches him to shape hollow figures in clay
the trainer finds his movements still too hurried
a second room is used for moulding and smells of damp material
the writer smooths surfaces there for whole afternoons
one space is given over to making jointed puppets
the back room takes the rehearsals and heats up under its lamp
the writer invites his correspondent to come and see for himself
text: You asked what on earth I get up to at the arts centre, so here is the whole list. The clay workshop comes first. I am learning to shape hollow figures there, and the trainer keeps telling me my hands are far too hurried. Next along is the moulding room, which smells of damp plaster and has buckets lined up against the wall. I spend entire afternoons in there, rubbing surfaces down until they feel soft under the palm. Then comes the puppet corner: heads carved out of soft wood, painted eyes, tiny clothes stitched by hand. Last of all, the back room takes the stage rehearsals, and the lamp above it throws off so much heat that we open the window between scenes. I never expected to grow fond of a place like this, and now I cannot bear to miss a session. Come and join me one afternoon, and you will see it all at once.

units: a restoration specialist is questioned about a damaged painting
she saw the poor state of the work as soon as it arrived
the yellowed protective layer flattened the pale colours
the work begins with a careful examination lasting several weeks
this examination finds the places where the painted matter is lifting
the cleaning moves forward in very small patches
the added retouches can be taken off and do not cover the original
the features of the face became readable again after a single sitting
the work is then put in a space where the damp is controlled
text: When did you realise the canvas was in danger? The restorer says she knew as soon as it came out of its wrapping: the varnish had yellowed so badly that the pale tones were flattened. Where does one begin in a case like that? With examination, she answers, several weeks of inspection under a lens, noting every place where the painted layer is lifting. Cleaning follows, carried out patch by tiny patch, with swabs that are changed over and over. Then the retouching, which never covers the original: fine strokes are laid into the losses and can be taken off again. And did the outcome surprise you? She smiles and admits that the features of the face, long drowned in a brown haze, came back in a single sitting. What becomes of the work now? It goes behind glass, into a room where the damp is watched at all hours.

units: a sculptor breaks off his work to question his pupil
the pupil finds that the block of stone resists her
each of her blows tears off a chip she did not intend
the master explains that stone holds veins running in one direction
striking across those veins shatters the surface
he advises drawing the shape in charcoal first
he recommends taking the matter away in layers while going round the block
the pupil finds this way of working exhausting
the next day the shape comes on and the chipping has stopped
text: The sculptor set down his mallet and asked why the work had gone quiet. His pupil answered that the block was fighting her, since every blow she struck tore off a flake she had never intended. He told her that stone runs in veins, and that striking a vein at an angle will shatter the whole face of it. Because she cut without listening to the grain, the material took its revenge. Draw the outline in charcoal, he said, then take the stone off in thin layers, walking round the block as you go. She objected that working so slowly wore her out. The sculptor smiled. Stone forgives nothing you remove from it, he said, so haste costs more than patience ever does. She picked up her chisel and made no reply. The next day she reported that the flaking had stopped and the shape was rising at last. He nodded without lifting his eyes, for he had heard it coming in the ring of the metal.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: reproducing pictures once called for a draughtsman for every copy
two copies made by hand were never alike
cutting a metal plate settled this failure of fidelity
the ink held in the grooves passes onto the paper under pressure
hollowing the metal with a burin took weeks and a skilled hand
the plate was then covered with a protection and the metal bitten with acid
a light point was enough from then on to open the line
this method made the line suppler and the tones came from the density of the cuts
text: Getting pictures about ran into a physical limit: every copy called for a draughtsman's hand, and no two copies made that way ever matched. Engraving settled the difficulty. A polished metal plate was cut with a burin, charged with stiff ink, then wiped clean, so that only what stayed in the grooves passed onto the sheet under the press. Fidelity was answered, but a fresh trouble came with it, for cutting copper took weeks and a very steady hand. The idea arose of biting the metal with acid instead, under a coat of varnish through which a light needle was enough to trace. A draughtsman who was clumsy with the burin could now print his own line. Contours grew suppler, tone was built up from the density of the hatching, and the picture at last travelled far away from the person who had made it.

units: two separate methods serve to decorate a wall
the first means painting on a coating that is still wet
the colour sets into the lime as it dries
the painter has a single sitting before the surface hardens
his drawing is settled beforehand and carried over from a pierced model
the second method sets coloured fragments into a mortar
the craftsman can break off and take the work up again later
rounded shapes are built there in very small steps
both techniques stand up to damp but decay in different ways
text: Two separate methods share the decoration of walls, and neither asks the same movements or the same patience of its maker. The first is laid onto a coating that is still wet. The colour sinks into the lime and sets there as the surface dries, so the painter has one sitting and no more before everything hardens. The drawing must therefore be settled in advance, then carried over from a sheet pricked with holes. The second method rests on coloured fragments set one by one into a bed of mortar. Nothing presses here: the craftsman breaks off and takes the work up again the following week without harm. Against that, the curve of a face has to be built in minute steps, and a soft gradation is paid for in endless cutting. Damp troubles neither of them, yet one ages by growing pale and the other by shedding its pieces.

units: a group of amateur singers rehearses in an abandoned industrial building
the place brings them three separate discoveries
low sounds hang on there under the iron roof frame
the woman in charge has to slow her entry signals because of that echo
a single lamp leaves half the group in shadow
the singers at the back go by ear without seeing the beat
passers-by come in, listen to one piece and leave in silence
a regular audience forms without any invitation
the group finally chooses to perform there and not in the planned room
text: An amateur choir was rehearsing in a disused factory hall, and the place had three surprises in store for it. The first was acoustic: under the iron roof beams the low voices hung on for a whole second, which forced the conductor to slow every entry she gave. The second was visual. A single lamp, hooked to a girder, cut the group into two halves, one of them lit and the other drowned in shadow; the singers at the back learned to sing without seeing the beat and trusted their ears instead. The third surprise came from the neighbourhood. Passers-by wandered in, sat down on upturned crates, listened to one piece, then left without a word. By the close of the season the hall held a regular audience that nobody had invited, and the choir chose to give its concert there rather than in the room booked for it.

units: the soft plate is warmed first so that it hollows out easily
the design is drawn and then gone over in ink so as not to vanish
the broad zones are taken away with the thickest tool
the tool must be pushed away from the hand holding the plate
the details are opened with a fine tool
the rough edges are smoothed once the relief is there
the ink is spread with a roller until it makes a steady noise
the sheet is rubbed from behind with a smooth curved object
one corner is lifted to check the result before the sheet is taken off
text: Take a plate of lino and let it warm up beside a radiator, because warm material gives way under the tool instead of fighting back. Draw your design in soft pencil, then go over the lines in ink, or you will lose the outline with the very first shaving. Clear the broad areas with the widest gouge you have, pushing away from your free hand. Move on to the fine gouge for the details, the hatching, the edges of each shape. Once the relief looks clean to you, sand the furry ridges down a little. Spread the ink on a sheet of glass, load the roller until it gives a steady hiss, then ink the block, crossing your passes as you go. Lay the paper on, rub the back with the curved bowl of a spoon, and lift one corner to check. If the tone looks thin, drop the sheet back and work at it again before you take it off.

units: a local performance venue reopens after three winters of closure
cracks in the vault had at first raised the fear of destruction
the survey concluded that the structure was sound
damp was rising from the foundations and eating into the ornaments
the work was turned towards drying out and glueing the decorations back
the company was able to rehearse in the entrance hall during the work
the neighbourhood took to attending those rehearsals
every seat of the season is sold on reopening
the management explains this turnaround by the constant presence of the actors
text: Shut for three winters, a neighbourhood theatre has just reopened, and its return rests on a decision the management long hesitated to take. Cracks in the vaulted ceiling had at first raised the fear of demolition. The survey found instead that the structure was holding, but that damp was rising through the foundations and eating into the plaster ornaments. The work therefore changed its aim: rather than build the auditorium anew, the team dried it out and glued the mouldings back one by one. That turn had an effect nobody had foreseen. Since the craftsmen were on site throughout, the company could rehearse in the entrance hall, and the neighbourhood took to coming in to watch. On reopening night the whole season was sold out, though the theatre had shut its doors in front of empty rows. The management puts the reversal down to the actors being there all along.

units: a dirty glass roof leaves the studio in a dull light
this setting falsifies every colour laid on the canvas
the painter only finds her mistakes by taking the picture outside
she gives up opening a bay in the back wall because the stones are too thick
the bulbs she tries give a yellow cast that is worse still
she puts a broad tilted mirror on the opposite wall
the outside light thrown back by that mirror reaches the easel without hardness
she now begins her drawing as soon as the studio opens
her colours hold good once the picture hangs elsewhere
text: Under its grimy glass roof, the studio lay in a dull grey light that took the life out of every tone she laid down. The painter complained of it each winter: her blues turned to ash, her reds lost their warmth, and she found her mistakes out only by carrying the canvas outdoors. She thought of cutting an opening in the back wall, but the stonework proved far too thick for that. She tried harsh bulbs, whose yellow cast looked worse still. The answer came to her from a mirror. She fixed a broad panel of it against the opposite wall, tilted towards the floor, and the daylight it threw back spread over the easel at last with no hardness in it. Since then she starts drawing as soon as the shutters are open, and her colours hold to their promise when the canvas hangs somewhere else.

units: the writer holds it wrong to treat an image file as the work itself
this confusion weighs on the budgets of collections
a photograph gives the outlines and the values if the lighting is set
it does not give back the thickness or the relief of the painted matter
the look of a protective layer changes with where the viewer stands
a file depends on a format, on a support and on a reading program
each of those parts ends up unusable
a print kept in a folder can be looked at with no device
the writer grants that the digital copy protects the original and carries it far
the writer concludes that the copy documents the work without replacing it
text: To set an image file beside the work it records is to muddle two objects of a different nature, and collections pay dearly for the muddle. A photograph gives back the outlines, the values, often the hue, provided the lighting has been calibrated. What escapes it is the thickness of the matter: the ridge of a loaded brushstroke, the grain of the paper, the depth of a varnish that answers the eye afresh with every step the viewer takes. The file ages worse than people suppose; it hangs on a format, on a magnetic support, on a program able to read it, and every one of those links falls out of use. A print forgotten in a folder can be read again with no device at all. Should the digital copy be refused, then? No: it spares the original from handling and carries the image where nobody will travel. But it documents a work, it does not replace it.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: a woman describes the path that led her to restoring paintings
her interest began while she was cleaning the workshop of a relative
at first she watched the yellowed layers being cleaned away
little by little she was allowed to work on parts of the painting
she set up her own premises in a courtyard once her training ended
her equipment includes a magnifying instrument and colours kept in jars
she has treated a family painting with a hole in it and a wall painting faded by water
she can spend several weeks on a very small surface
she says she finds it hard to consider a treatment finished
she teaches two beginners that the work must go unnoticed
text: It started with a broom. She was sweeping out an uncle's workshop, where damaged canvases came to be put right, and she stayed on to watch. The yellowed varnish lifted away under a damp swab of cotton, and to a child that looked like a conjuring trick. By her teens she was asking for a brush of her own. They handed her frames first, then a corner of sky, then a face. Once her training was over she rented a tiny place at the back of a courtyard, with a hinged magnifier and pigments kept in jars. Work came in slowly: a family portrait with a hole through it, a stairway mural that damp had turned grey. One painted palm, she admits, can keep her busy for weeks, and the hard part is knowing when to stop. She now has two apprentices, and tells them over and over that a good repair is one nobody notices.

units: the performance ends with a lukewarm response from the audience
the staging amounts to a dark rug and two seats
nothing painted appears on the stage
the lack of scenery leaves the audience without any clue about where the action happens
the script does not make up for this missing information
the musical accompaniment is played on the spot, hidden behind a hanging cloth
the sound covers the lines that are spoken quietly
one sequence carried by an actress is judged successful
the reviewer puts the failure down to excessive austerity
text: The audience filed out without much applause, and the chill in the room is easy enough to account for. Everything here rests on a bare stage: a dark rug, two stools, not a scrap of painted canvas. That could have thrown the whole weight onto the performers. It does the opposite, because the staging no longer tells us where we are. So we hunt the script for clues, the script gives up very few, and the story slips out of reach. Live music, played behind a hanging cloth, deepens the muddle: it swallows the quieter lines, and whole sentences go missing. One passage deserves rescuing, the second scene, where an actress plays a spell of mourning almost without moving; there, at last, the emptiness earns its keep. An evening undone by too much restraint rather than too little ambition.

units: the writer is writing from a workshop where wood is worked
a piano had been damaged by water
the keys were sticking and the sound was spoilt
a specialist had judged tuning impossible in that condition
the writer thought about getting rid of the instrument
a neighbour who works in wood offers to take it apart and dry it
the padding ruined by damp is replaced
the repair took up the two people through a cold season
the instrument now holds its tuning
the writer invites the reader to come and play it
text: I am writing from the joiner's workshop, among off-cuts, wood shavings and the smell of warm glue. You remember that old piano, the one the rain got into? I had given it up for lost. The keys stuck, the strings gave back a cracked sort of note, and the tuner I called said there was nothing to be done with it in that state. I nearly let it go for firewood. Then a neighbour who works in wood put another way to me: lift out the soundboard, dry the pieces flat under clamps, replace the felts that the damp had eaten. The two of us spent the whole winter on it, with no plan worth the name. Since the day before yesterday it holds its tuning. In the evenings I sit down and improvise clumsy things that nobody else will ever hear. Come and try it whenever you like; it is waiting for you.

units: the text sets sculpture made by taking material away against sculpture made by casting
carving does not let what has been removed be put back
the casting process starts from a model in clay
a hollow impression is taken from that model
metal or plaster is then poured into it
a cast piece can be made again for as long as the model survives
the carver must study the structure and the flaws of the block before starting
the caster must watch the tightness of the mould and the speed of setting
a carved surface keeps the mark of the tools
a cast piece shows lines where the parts of the mould met
text: What sets a carved sculpture apart from a cast one? Carving takes material away, and nothing puts it back; every stroke of the chisel is final. Casting runs the other way round: the maker shapes a model in clay, draws a hollow mould from it, then pours in metal or plaster, so the form can be had again for as long as the model lasts. Do the two ask for the same preparation? They do not. Carving means reading the block first, its grain and its hidden cracks, or the thing will split. Casting shifts the difficulty onto a tight mould and a rate of cooling held under control. And does the result look different? It does. Cut stone keeps the bite of the tool, while a cast piece carries thin ridges along the seams where the parts of the mould came together. The choice follows the effect you are after.

units: a museum official explains to visitors how a collection is built up
purchases follow a logic of completing a group already held
gifts raise the difficulty of the conditions set by the donor
some works are lent by another institution for a limited period
a visitor asks what becomes of the pieces that are never shown
objects not on display are kept in crates where the air is controlled
those pieces remain available for research work
a student asks what share of the collection can be seen
the official admits that the part on show is small
text: Standing by the central case, the keeper set out for his listeners, at some length, the way a collection comes together. He began with purchases: a museum rarely buys at random, and each fresh arrival has to round out a group already held. He turned next to gifts, which raise a delicate matter, since a donor commonly wants the bequest kept on permanent display. He mentioned loans as well, entrusted by another institution for a fixed term. A visitor then asked what became of the pieces that are never brought out at all. They sleep in store, he replied, in crates where the air is held steady, and scholars are free to work on them. A student wanted to know how much of the whole is on view. He granted that the share is small, and that no room, however grand, could reveal it all at once.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: the first tapestries answered practical needs of insulation and division
they also served to signal rank
the earliest patterns were geometric and repetitive
specialised workshops appear near the courts of the nobility
the hangings then begin to tell stories in pictures
the figures were recognised by the objects that went with them
dyeing improves and offers brighter colours
trade in these fabrics enriches merchant towns
a model painted by an artist was reproduced by unnamed workers
mechanisation reduced this craft to a narrow luxury trade
text: The earliest picture weaving grew out of plain need: to keep a cold wall at bay, to divide one room from the next, to mark rank. The patterns of that time were geometric, easy to repeat and easy to hold in the head. Then specialised workshops gathered around the courts of the nobility, and the hanging turned into a tale, whole scenes read from left to right, each figure known by the object it carried. Demand pushed the dyers to widen their range, and the glowing threads drawn from insects and from roots made the fortune of several trading towns. Later came the painted cartoon, laid down by an artist and then followed stitch by stitch by weavers who never signed their work. The arrival of the mechanical loom finally shrank this patient craft to a narrow trade in luxury goods.

units: the text explains why old paintings darken
the protective layer laid on the surface breaks down in contact with the air
that layer takes on a yellow tint which alters all the colours
how well the colouring matter lasts depends on where it comes from
colouring matter drawn from plants fades under too strong a light
the loss of one colour can change the tint of a whole area
deposits from burning form a greasy film over the work
what is seen today differs from the original appearance
these changes are what justify a careful cleaning
text: You have surely stood in front of an old painting at some point and wondered where that brownish haze comes from. Blame the varnish first of all. A coat goes on to shield the surface, but the film reacts with the air, turns yellow, and ends up tinting the whole picture like dirty glass. Then there are the pigments. Some colours hold for generations without shifting; others, drawn from plants, fade as soon as they get too much light, so a blue sky can drift towards green once the yellow that warmed it has gone. Add the soot from lamps and hearths, which settles as a fine greasy skin over the lot. The upshot is that the painting in front of you barely keeps the colour it had when it left the workshop. That is precisely why a clean carried out with caution is worth the trouble.

units: a water leak flooded the dressing room the night before the opening performance
the costumes were left soaked
the colours of a heavy cloth ran into pale garments
giving up the performance would have meant losing money
playing in rehearsal clothes was judged unacceptable
the technical manager suggests evening out the spoilt shades on purpose
every fabric is dipped again in one pale colour bath
the lighting is changed to suit these new shades
the audience knew nothing of the accident and enjoyed the result
the company has kept this version born of a mishap
text: The night before opening, a pipe gave way and the company found the dressing room under water, with the costumes lying in soaked heaps on the cold tiles. Dye from the heavy velvet cloaks had run into the pale shirts, and the stiffened collars hung limp. Calling it off would cost a great deal; going on in rehearsal clothes felt beneath them. The stage manager offered a way out that nobody expected: since the shades had bled anyway, why not let the whole stage look washed out. The team spent the night dipping every piece of cloth in one pale bath, until the range settled into an even greyish pink. The lighting crew cooled their lamps to suit. The audience, who knew nothing of the flood, praised a look that seemed coherent and bold. The company has played it that way ever since.

units: the text sets out two printmaking techniques to choose between
the first means cutting into a metal support
the metal is covered with a protective film before the drawing is made
a corrosive liquid deepens the lines opened with a point
the second technique calls for cutting away from a wood block the parts meant to stay white
this second method allows no correction
both processes involve inking the surface and then wiping it
the paper used must be dampened before it goes under the press
the hollow process gives a thick line that can be felt
the wood process gives even areas with sharp edges
text: Choose your road first, for two hands are held out to you and they ask for quite different kinds of patience. To work in hollow, take a metal plate under a thin coat of varnish, draw your lines through it with a point, then lower the plate into a biting bath: the acid eats down wherever you have opened the ground. To work in relief, take a block of soft wood and cut away everything that must come out white; here nothing at all can be taken back. Either way, ink the surface, wipe it clean, lay on damp paper and send the lot under the press. The eye tells the two apart soon enough. The hollow holds the ink and yields a dense line you can feel beneath a fingertip, while the wood gives flat areas and clean edges. Pull a first sheet, look hard at it, correct what jars, begin again.

units: a centre for preserving recordings has opened in a converted industrial building
a first station deals with magnetic tape
the tapes go through an oven before they are played
this heating stops the recording layer from clinging
a second station reads discs with an optical device that makes no contact
a third service writes the description of the sound documents
that description calls for listening to each recording right through
the security copies are spread over two sites
the manager judges the documentation more decisive than the medium itself
a recording without a description can no longer be found
text: A laboratory for sound preservation has just opened in a converted industrial hall, and the man in charge took us through the work station by station. The first station handles magnetic tape: the reels go into a drying oven before playback, so that the coating stops clinging to itself. The second deals with cut discs, whose grooves are read by an optical sensor that never touches them. The third looks after description, slow work, since every item has to be heard right through before it can be indexed. A fourth space, kept apart, holds the security copies, which are stored in two separate buildings. He comes back to one point: the medium matters less than the description file that travels with it, because an undescribed recording becomes unfindable and all but ceases to exist.

units: the smell of the damp material reaches the visitor before anything else
a fine dust covers the floor of the room
the fast spinning of the wheel is the cause of that dust
unfired vessels pile up on the shelves
their greyish tint will change once they have been through the kiln
the presence of the kiln speeds up the drying of the pieces
the craftsman therefore protects some pieces with a wet cloth
the walls have never been given any paint
every object set down in the workshop serves a practical purpose
text: Push the workshop door open and the damp clay strikes you before anything else, a persistent smell settling at the back of the throat. Fine dust lies right across the floorboards, thrown off the wheel whenever it picks up speed. The shelves sag under unfired bowls, a dull greyish colour that will warm considerably once they have come out of the kiln. That kiln stands at the far end of the room, and because it stands there the heat climbs and dries the pottery much faster than the potter would like, so he keeps a soaked cloth spread over the pieces still awaiting their turn. The walls are rough and have never seen a coat of paint. Stay an hour and the arrangement becomes obvious: nothing here is decorative. Every tool on the workbench has earned its place by performing a task.

units: the closing of a venue happens in successive stages
the usual explanation blames the public for drifting away
the crowds at neighbouring stages contradict that explanation
the level of rent swallows the margin left by the takings
a first solution is to share technical costs between venues
those venues wrongly take one another for rivals
a second solution rests on leases of long duration
that guarantee demands in return affordable prices and original work given a stage
text: A theatre does not shut its doors in one go. It fades away by stages, a season cut short, a subscription put on hold, a technical crew reduced to a handful. The usual verdict blames audiences for drifting away, yet the queues outside the stages down the road make that lazy reading rather hard to defend. The real squeeze is rent, which swallows whatever margin the box office still manages to return. Two remedies exist, and neither of them calls for a miracle. The first is to share the heavy costs, sets, lighting desks and insurance, between houses that take each other for rivals while courting one and the same public. The second is to secure long leases, granted against a plain undertaking: affordable seats, and original work given a stage. Otherwise we shall go on mourning closures that we arranged ourselves.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: a specialist repairs old paintings
her manner recalls that of a woman who repairs watches
both trades call for tiny movements repeated again and again
she lifts the darkened varnish with a swab of cotton
she halts her hand as soon as the tint underneath turns doubtful
the material of a movement answers in a predictable way
a painting instead sets against her old retouching and deposits of smoke
the aim of the woman who repairs watches is to start the object again
the aim of the specialist is to keep the painter's hand legible
text: The woman who mends old paintings leans over her canvas much the way a watch repairer leans over a movement that has stopped. Both trades live off the same small motions, made again and again, and neither of them forgives a slip. She lifts the darkened varnish a thumbnail at a time, with cotton wound round the end of a stick, and her arm halts the moment the colour underneath turns uncertain. The watch repairer straightens a wheel that a knock has bent, and the metal answers her plainly, while paint argues back with old retouching and with layers dulled by the smoke of lamps. What parts the two of them is the aim. One wants the machine running again. The other wants nothing at all to run: she asks only that some later eye should still read what a hand laid down there, one evening, on stretched cloth.

units: the exhibition shows prints
the deep inks do not fill in the dark areas
the paper used has a coarse texture
that texture softens the contrast of the light surfaces
the order of hanging follows the successive states of the plates
that arrangement makes the progress of the engraved drawing visible
the labels lack any indication of the technique used
that absence hampers the unversed visitor
text: Three things go right in this hanging of prints, and one thing goes wrong. Take the inking first: the blacks hold their depth without ever filling in the hollows, so that the finest lines keep their air and several plates take on a startling relief. Then the support, a paper of coarse grain, almost felted under the finger, which softens the whites and stops the contrast from turning harsh. Then the sequence: the plates hang by successive states, and the visitor watches the composition assemble itself, from an unfinished sketch through to the settled version. The lapse lies in the labels, silent on process, on tool, on the bite of the acid. A practised eye will rebuild the method unaided; whoever meets this field for the first time leaves with a vague admiration and nothing whatever learnt.

units: the writer thanks the woman who ran an etching course
he came to the workshop with no previous experience
the first session dealt with the preparation of the plates
he then learnt to control how long the bite lasts
one of his plates was ruined during a trial
the woman in charge offered him a fresh start straight away
the last session yielded a successful impression
the writer wishes to enrol on the following course
text: I am writing at the close of the etching course that you led, in order to thank you for it. I came to the workshop with no practice whatever, and rather uneasy about holding a needle among participants who plainly knew their trade.
