The opening session, given over to degreasing and grounding the plates, settled that worry at once: your instructions were spare and exact, and nobody in the room was left behind. We moved on to the control of the bite, and I understood that the time spent in the bath decides very nearly everything. My second plate was spoilt by an excess of acid; you invited me straight away to prepare another, without a word of reproach. The final session yielded a clean impression, of which I am proud. I should therefore like to enrol on the next course, if any places remain.

units: an engineer explains how old recordings are put back in order
the hiss comes from the wear of the original carrier
excessive filtering also wipes out useful sound
the top notes of the string instruments go first
the engineer therefore prefers a measured correction
he compares several copies of the same recording
that comparison serves to tell an isolated fault from a shared one
he always keeps an unaltered version of the file
text: People often ask the sound engineer where the veil over old recordings comes from. His answer runs to a single sentence: the carrier has worn, and the wear adds a steady hiss that no microphone ever picked up. Can it be taken out altogether? He says not, or rather that it should not be, because heavy filtering carries off the highest harmonics of the strings along with the hiss, and the sound goes flat. What does he do instead? He applies a restrained correction, and then compares several copies of the same disc: a crackle found on one copy belongs to that copy alone, and a crackle found on every one of them belongs to the cutting itself. One rule governs the whole business. The original is archived untouched, since a judgement made by ear yesterday may well look wrong tomorrow.

units: an actress reports a sound problem to a stage manager
her voice becomes inaudible at the back of the house
the stage manager first assumes a failure of the microphone
the wooden set is in fact throwing the sound back towards the stage
a thick rug is laid on the floor to soak up those reflections
the speakers are turned towards the distant seats
the actress checks the result from the last row
the difficulty disappears at the very next rehearsal
text: The actress caught the stage manager at the edge of the platform and told him that nobody past the third row could make her out any more. He said the microphone must be fading, that he would swap the battery over and they would see. She pushed back: the trouble started earlier, before the microphone came into it at all, because the boarded set threw her own voice straight back at her and made her force it. He granted that she was right, then offered a thick rug at the foot of the panel to swallow those returns. After that they tilted the speakers towards the back rows, which had been sitting in a dead patch. She went off to listen from there while an understudy read her line, and came back saying that it was clear at last. At the next run nobody craned forward to catch the words.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: two old ways of fixing images are set against each other
wall painting addresses a large public
the decorated manuscript is meant for a single reader
wall painting is carried out quickly on plaster that is still wet
the illuminator may break off and take up his work whenever he likes
wall painting has suffered from changes in the use of buildings
manuscripts have survived better because they were stored out of harm
both techniques used comparable pigments
text: Two ways of fixing an image ran side by side for a long stretch, and they differ on almost every count. Wall painting speaks to a crowd: it takes a whole face of stone, reads from a distance, and presses its figures on anyone who steps through the door. The decorated page is meant for a single reader, bent close over it, turning the leaf at his own pace. Part of the gap comes from the craft itself. Wet plaster grants the painter one sitting and no more, which rules out second thoughts and demands a sure line; the illuminator shuts his volume and takes the work up again whenever he pleases. Their fates parted too. Walls were whitewashed, cut through and put to other uses as buildings changed hands, while volumes shelved in a locked press came down whole. The pigments came from the same grindings.

units: the colouring matter used in painting has three distinct origins
the first origin is mineral and comes from crushed rock
those mineral powders hold their tint for a long time
the second origin is vegetable and comes from roots or berries
vegetable colours grow pale under a strong light
the third origin comes from insects or shells
these last were rare and costly
a binder turns the coloured powder into a usable paste
text: Three families of colour share the painter's palette, and each of them carries the story of where it came from. The first is quarried: a stone is crushed, the powder sifted, and out of it comes a deep blue or a warm ochre that will hold for ages without weakening, for rock keeps no memory of the light that falls on it. The second rises from plants, from roots torn up, from berries pressed, from wood left to steep; these tints are airy, almost floating, lovely at first glance, yet they grow pale under a strong light and end as shadows of themselves. The third comes from living creatures, from gathered shells and dried insects, and its scarcity kept it for lavish commissions. One gesture is common to all: powder is nothing until a binder takes it up and makes a workable paste of it.

units: a tuner works on an instrument before a concert
the hall was too warm when he arrived
the heat had slackened the strings unevenly
he first set a reference note against the fork
he then adjusted the other notes by successive fifths
a bass string gave way during the operation
he replaced that string and then stretched it by hand
he measured the temperature before checking a second time
text: The tuner walked into the hall a full hour before the concert and judged the air too warm from the doorway itself. The heat had slackened the stringing unevenly, the bass having shifted a good deal more than the middle register. He began by setting a reference note against the fork, by ear, with no device at all, then worked upward in fifths, narrowing each interval by a beat that he counted off. The going was rough: on the third pass a bass string snapped outright, and the wire coiled itself across the soundboard. He laid in a fresh one, seated it firmly on its anchor, and stretched it by hand so that it would settle before the players arrived. Then, with a thermometer to hand, he waited for the air to come down, and took the whole tuning again from the very first note.

units: a neighbourhood has two distinct ways of putting a request to a local authority
the first route rests on a document taken round for people to sign
this route calls for very little in the way of materials
the authority is obliged to keep the written request
a signed document shows neither the disagreements nor the shades of opinion
the second route means gathering people in a hall open to all
the meeting lets opposing views answer one another directly
those who cannot get out of the house are shut out of the meeting
background noise puts the quieter speakers at a disadvantage
the two routes complete each other, one measuring the discontent and the other explaining it
text: When a neighbourhood wants a local authority to consider a request, it has two quite different routes available. The first is a written request carried round from door to door for signature. It costs almost nothing, it can be prepared in a single evening, and it leaves behind a record the authority is obliged to keep. Its weakness is silence: a signed sheet reveals none of the shading, and nobody argues an objection out on paper. The second route is a meeting in a hall thrown open to anyone who cares to attend. There, opposing views answer one another immediately. But whoever cannot get out of the house is excluded altogether, and the general din drowns the quieter speakers. Neither route replaces the other. The signed sheet measures how much discontent exists; the meeting explains what lies behind it.

units: a repair van came regularly to set up on the square of a very modest village
the children arrived first, drawn by the noise and the smell of the workshop
people brought damaged things, among them a seat and a faulty lamp
a woman insisted on keeping a coffee grinder despite the state of it
every owner told how their thing had come to break
the craftsman listened without turning his eyes from his cutting bench
the square emptied little by little while the craftsman packed his crates
the narrator sees in these visits the proof that nothing was thrown out without an argument
text: Every week the repair van pulled up at the edge of the square, and the whole of that small hamlet seemed to open at once. The children came first, drawn by the smell of hot metal and by the racket of the grinder. Then came the objects: a chair whose seat had given way, a lamp with a bared wire, a coffee grinder that its owner would not be parted from. Then came the stories, for nobody went home without saying how the crack had happened in the first place. The mender listened without ever lifting his eyes from the bench, nodding in the right places. When he shut his crates the square emptied slowly, the way a hall empties after a concert. What he carried off with him was not only scrap metal. It was proof, renewed every week, that nothing here was thrown out before someone had spoken up for it.

units: preparation starts with a list of the water points and the power points available
a notice goes up by the entrance a week before the operation
this notice gives the time, the expected length and the equipment to bring
who does what is set down in writing the day before
you must check that the road running along the building is clear of bins
cleaning starts with the high parts before working down towards the ground
starting at the bottom would mean doing part of the cleaning twice
the equipment is put away before the last break, while the volunteers are still there
a written note of the damage goes to the manager at the end
text: Before you organise a clean-up in a shared yard, list the taps and the power points that you can actually make use of. A week ahead, put a notice up by the entrance giving the time, how long the work is expected to take and what equipment people should bring with them. The day before, set out who does what in writing, because a spoken instruction goes straight out of the head. On the morning itself, gather the volunteers by the gate and check that the road running along the building is clear of bins. Start high, with the gutters and the ledges, then work down towards the ground; the other way round means doing half of it twice over. Put the equipment away before the last break, while the volunteers are all still together. Finish with a written note of the damage, handed to the building manager.

units: a retaining wall collapsed in an old part of town
the collapse led to the closing of the road serving the foot of the slope
with no alternative route, traffic shifted into a narrow lane
buses cannot pass each other in that lane
people living nearby report repeated delays
a crowd formed outside a room far too small when a meeting was announced
the technical services put the damage down to an old seepage made worse by rain
the repair will take several weeks because the ground has to be surveyed first
a temporary walkway has shortened the detours without removing the congestion
text: A retaining wall gave way at the weekend in an old part of town, and the road serving the foot of the slope was shut off at once. With no alternative route on offer, the traffic shifted into a narrow lane where two buses cannot pass each other. Residents describe delays that build on one another, and a crush at the single stop still in use. When a public meeting was announced, a crowd formed outside a community room far too small to hold everyone who had come along to it. The technical services put the collapse down to a long-standing seepage, made a good deal worse by weeks of steady rain. Repairs will take several weeks, since the ground has to be surveyed before a fresh footing can be poured. A temporary walkway has been laid, which has shortened the detours without easing the congestion.

units: the reception hall sits on the lower floor of a low building
the light comes from a grimy skylight
a single counter works behind a glass panel with an opening cut into it
the queue stretches as far as the entrance door
people coming and going in search of a form break the queue
the waiting sets off arguments about whose turn it is
coloured tokens are now handed out on arrival
a board shows the colour being called and seats have been put in
the counter works at the same rate but the quarrels have almost stopped
text: The reception hall takes up the lower floor of a squat building, lit from above by a skylight thick with grime. A single counter works there, behind a glass panel with a round opening cut into it. In front of it the queue stretches all the way to the door, broken again and again by people wandering off in search of a form. Waiting breeds friction: places are disputed out loud, and newcomers are accused of pushing in. Since last season the desk has handed out wooden tokens marked with a colour as people arrive. A board shows which colour is being called, and benches have been set out along the wall. People sit down, watch the board, and stop watching each other. The counter works at the rate it always did, yet the quarrels have all but gone from a hall that used to be a loud one.

units: the writer disputes the idea that help between neighbours has gone
in the block of his childhood, tools were borrowed from the door opposite
an elderly resident minded the children without being asked
where he lives now, people pass on the stairs without speaking
that same block produced volunteers to repaint a bike store
a list of people willing to put the bins out was drawn up there
the writer puts the change down to the channel used and not to selfishness
help now goes through written messages and a notice board
the writer prefers reserved but reliable neighbours to nosy ones
text: People keep telling me that neighbours no longer help one another, and I say it has only changed its shape. In the block where I grew up, you knocked on the door opposite whenever you needed to borrow a spanner, and the lady on the top floor minded the children without ever being asked. Where I live now, nothing of the sort: we pass one another on the stairs without a word. So what? That same staircase produced two volunteers last season to repaint the bike store, and a list of residents willing to put the bins out. The difference is not selfishness, it is the channel. Helping used to require closeness; nowadays it goes through a written message and a board by the letter boxes. Give me quiet neighbours who turn up when it matters over talkative ones who sit in judgement.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: the woman described keeps her paperwork in a cupboard
she pulls out a bulky folder every week
she holds the post of treasurer in a neighbourhood association
she takes in the members' payments and chases the late ones
she writes the sums down by hand before entering them on a computer
she obtains the loan of a hall and a discount from a printer
she rules between competing costs such as sewing and the repair of a machine
she turns down the chair that is regularly offered to her
a member reckons that without her the till and the plans would be empty
text: Her office fits inside a cupboard, and once a week she pulls out of it a folder as thick as a brick. As treasurer of a neighbourhood association, she takes in the subscriptions, chases the ones who forget, and writes every sum down by hand before copying it into a spreadsheet. She also bargains: the loan of a hall next door, a discount from a printer, a bill put off, the patience of a disgruntled landlord. And she rules on spending, because the demands compete for one small till: cloth for the sewing group, a repair to the copier, refreshments for the open meetings. Each time the committee is renewed she turns down the chair, saying that accounts kept properly weigh more than any title. Without her, says a member stacking chairs, the till would be empty and so would the plans.

units: the opening of the performance looked unpromising
the stage held nothing but a bare floor and mismatched seats
the amateur players seemed tense
the first scene suffered from a script too carefully written and poorly inhabited
the room went quiet when an actress picked up a dropped bunch of keys without breaking her line
the show gained in pace from that mishap onwards
short scenes followed one another and the thin set stopped mattering
the closing sequence ran without a word and showed neighbours ignoring each other
the reviewer judges that the script must be shortened
the reviewer reckons the company would deserve a bigger hall
text: Nothing at the start of the performance promised what followed: a bare stage, three mismatched chairs, amateur players visibly stiff with nerves. The opening scene suffered from a script too carefully written, recited by voices rather than carried by them. Then the room fell quiet of its own accord when an actress playing a caretaker dropped her bunch of keys and picked it up without breaking off her line. From there the evening found its pace. Short scenes followed one another, the weariness of some answering the stubbornness of others, and the thin set stopped mattering. The closing sequence, played without a word, seemed to me the truest of all: neighbours passing on a staircase without recognising each other. The script wants tightening. The company deserves a bigger hall.

units: the writer announces a water cut affecting two staircases
the cut is planned for the following afternoon
a stopcock in the basement is eaten by corrosion and stuck
that one fitting controls the whole rising main
nothing can be done on the upper floors before it is replaced
the corrosion comes from a slow leak that ran into a drain grating
people are asked to fill containers the evening before and to close their taps
the return of the pressure will bring a noisy purge that is harmless
a whistling water heater must be reported to the manager
the cost will be covered by the shared payment already made
text: Dear neighbours, the water will be off in both staircases tomorrow afternoon. The cause is a corroded stopcock in the basement whose handle will no longer turn. Since that one fitting controls the whole rising main, nothing can be done on the upper floors until it has been replaced. The corrosion comes from a slow leak that took a long while to find, because it ran straight into a drain grating. In practice: fill two containers per household the evening before, and close your own taps while the supply is off, so that nothing floods when the pressure returns. The plumber expects a noisy purge on restart, as trapped air will set the pipes shaking, which is harmless. If your water heater whistles afterwards, report it without delay. The cost is covered by the shared payment already made.

units: the question raised concerns a rise in the members' yearly payment
the present takings no longer cover the upkeep of the premises
the treasurer thinks the rise modest but fears shutting out the poorer members
the committee suggests opening the premises to outside users for a payment
the quiet spells are what this opening is aimed at
premises left empty cost as much as premises in use
the bookings would be handled by members taking turns
a single register would prevent promises that contradict each other
a review would be discussed at a general meeting if the takings still fell short
the course chosen pairs a limited rise with partial hiring
text: Should the yearly subscription go up? The question arises because the takings no longer cover the upkeep of the premises. The treasurer answers that the rise would be a modest one, yet it would shut out the members with least to spare. Is there another way? Yes, says the committee: let outside users hire the premises during the quiet spells. An empty hall costs no less to keep than a busy one. Who would handle the bookings? A desk staffed by members in turn, working from a single register so that nothing is promised twice over. And if the money still fell short? The committee undertakes to reopen the matter at a general meeting rather than settle it alone. The course chosen pairs a limited rise with partial hiring, so the effort is shared out instead of falling on a few.

units: a woman speaking for a residents' group sets out their demands
she sorts these demands into three themes
the first theme concerns street lights that stop working at night
the second theme bears on rubbish left on the ground
the third theme targets the danger of a junction that is too narrow
an occupant of a neighbouring dwelling reports a building-site hoarding that blocks the view
a public official announces that a survey has begun
a meeting open to the public is promised for soon
every household that signed will receive a letter in reply
text: Speaking for the residents' group, the woman chosen to put their case sorted the complaints under three headings. Lighting came first. Every other lamp along the lane beside the old works, she said, goes dark once night falls. Cleanliness came second: cigarette ends piling up under the benches, and bags dumped well clear of the bins meant for them. The junction came third, where bicycles and delivery vans squeeze onto a road built for far less. A tenant from the corner block added that the hoarding round the neighbouring site blocks the view from the pavement. The official handling the matter replied that a survey is already under way, and that a meeting open to everyone would be held before the season is out. Every household that signed the register, he promised, would get a written answer.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: the earliest communities gathered near a source of water
that spot gave rise to the notion of common ground
a well was first sunk and then ringed with a rim
a stone seat there took in the oldest among them
collective affairs were talked over beside the well
the spread of settlements brought arcades around the open ground
trade came to be added to public speech
a roofed building then sheltered the traders from bad weather
the place served for publishing and for contesting common decisions
text: Long before streets carried names on plates, people gathered where the water was, and out of that habit grew the idea of ground belonging to everyone. A well was sunk first; a rim of stone was raised around it, and then a low bench where the oldest of the settlement sat. It became usual to talk beside that well about whatever concerned the whole group. As the settlements spread, arcades were built along the edges of the open ground, and goods began to change hands where words had changed hands before. Later a roofed hall went up, its pillars keeping the stalls dry through wet evenings. The square ended up as the place where common decisions were read out, listened to, and shouted down when they displeased. That slow layering explains the fondness so many still feel for an empty space hemmed in by walls.

units: the tiredness caused by night-time noise depends above all on the shape of the surrounding walls
hard surfaces send sound back instead of soaking it up
a shout in an enclosed courtyard returns as an echo to whoever is asleep
an abrupt change in level interrupts deep sleep
the sleeper may wake without keeping any memory of it
exhaustion lowers the capacity to put up with noise
heightened annoyance leads on to complaints
designers use absorbent materials and planting
a soft surface takes energy out of the sound wave
text: What wears you down in night-time noise has less to do with how loud it is than with the shape of the walls around the bed. Smooth render and glass throw sound back instead of soaking it up, so a raised voice in an enclosed courtyard returns as an echo to the ear of whoever is asleep. Deep sleep breaks at the smallest jump in level, which is why a sleeper surfaces again and again with no memory of having done so. Then the effect compounds. Tiredness lowers what a person will put up with; a lowered threshold turns ordinary noise into a nuisance; the nuisance ends in a complaint. Planners answer with open-pored materials, hedges set along the fences, and surfaces that damp the rumble of wheels. Every soft face takes a share of energy out of the wave, and a weakened wave no longer crosses the walls.

units: a dispute arises from a bin left open in a shared courtyard
the residents of one block blame the others for leaving bags on the ground
the latter answer that the passage is blocked by bicycles
the written exchanges turn hostile
two households break off all contact
a woman employed in the building suggests drawing a sketch of the courtyard together
each participant was to mark their routes and their drop-off points
the sketch shows that a blocked-up doorway forced every route through the same point
reopening that doorway and a low fence put an end to the quarrel
text: The whole thing started with a complaint about a bin that had been left standing open in the shared courtyard of a housing estate. Households on the north side accused those on the south of dropping their bags on the ground; the south side answered that the north side filled the passage with bicycles. Letters grew curt, tempers followed, and two families stopped speaking altogether. The caretaker then put forward an odd suggestion: bring both sides together, not to argue, but to draw the courtyard. Everyone was to mark where they set things down and which way they walked. What the drawing showed was a blocked-up doorway that funnelled every route through a single corner. The doorway was opened again, a low fence divided the ground, and the complaint was withdrawn before anything formal came of it.

units: two methods exist for consulting the residents of a block
the first sets up a voting arrangement in the entrance for a week
a voting slip is delivered to each letterbox
the count takes an evening and two observers
the presence of observers heads off objections to the outcome
the second method uses an accessible book in which each person writes and signs
the confidential ballot keeps opinions private
the open book makes the reasoning visible and shifts positions
the secret ballot is chosen for questions that set residents against one another
text: There are two ways for a residents' committee to find out what the occupants of a block really think, and they do not serve the same ends. The first is to stand a ballot box in the entrance hall for a week, with a voting slip posted through every letterbox. Allow an evening for the count, and arrange for two witnesses, so that nobody can pick the outcome apart afterwards. The second replaces the box with an open book, left on a table by the stairs, in which each person writes an opinion and signs it. A closed vote keeps views private and suits touchy subjects; the open book puts the reasoning on show, and opinions often shift because of it. Go for the box when the question sets households against one another, and for the book when the point is to think something through together.

units: a covered market is described through its different phases
the setting up of the stalls happens very early
the sellers squabble then over the empty wooden pallets
the period of heavy footfall makes the aisles very narrow
parents with a pushchair give up the visit and leave by the back
the packing away in the evening is reckoned the hardest
it obliges them to pack up the unsold goods
the traders help one another by lending equipment
one of them keeps an eye on the stall of a colleague who is away
text: Push through the swing doors of the market hall and the first thing you hear is the clatter of trolleys. The place runs on three rhythms, and the traders will tell you so without being asked. There is the setting up, before dawn, when each of them raises a stall and squabbles over the empty pallets. There is the thick of the crowd, when the aisles close in so tightly that pushchairs give up and turn back through the rear doors. And there is the pulling down at night, the worst of the three, the one nobody cares to talk about, because the unsold boxes have to be packed away again. Between the three runs a quieter life: a set of scales lent across the aisle, an eye kept on the stall of whoever has gone off to eat. One seller sums it up, laughing: they bicker endlessly, and they never let each other down.

units: the cleaning staff take over the space at sunrise
they gather up the leaves that fell during the night
delivery people and then office staff arrive after them
those staff cross the place without paying it any attention
a noisy procession of cyclists cuts the space in two
the public seats fill up in the early afternoon
a water basin has been out of service since the cold season
its rim serves as a rest for setting bags down
late in the evening the premises put their chairs outside
text: At first light the square belongs to the sweepers, who push the night's fallen leaves ahead of them along the paving. The delivery men come a little later, and after them the staff from the offices round about, cutting across on the diagonal without once looking up. A column of cyclists splits the space down the middle, horns and whistles together, and vanishes down the lower avenue. By early afternoon the benches have filled: older people, teenagers perched on the backrests, a mother keeping an eye on a pram. The fountain in the middle has stood dry since the cold weather came, and its rim now does duty as a shelf for shopping. As the sun drops behind the roofs the square changes colour and changes company: chairs come out onto the pavement, windows light up one by one, and the stone still gives back the warmth it took in.

units: public seats have been removed in front of a building
the place is now deserted
that emptying follows directly from the removal of the seats
the removal answered late-night gatherings and litter
a lingering smell was invoked as well
the seats also benefited peaceable users
an elderly woman used to break her walk there
the lack of anything to sit on removes the usual presence of passers-by
the presence of seated people made the place safe
text: The benches were taken off the forecourt, and now we profess surprise that nobody stops there. That is not chance; it follows. The case for removing them began with a genuine nuisance: gatherings that ran late, empty bottles, a smell that clung under the arcades. Take away the seat and you take away the gathering, and so far the arithmetic held. But the seat served more than the people who caused trouble. It served the old woman who breaks her walk in two, the delivery man catching his breath, the boy waiting for a friend. With nothing to sit on, those people no longer pause, and the space empties of its ordinary witnesses. Yet it was the gaze of seated passers-by that made the forecourt safe. In driving out the use we disliked, we drove out the quiet watch that held it in check.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: a professional carries out mediation in a very crowded district
she takes on quarrels that the courts will not look into
most complaints concern noise rubbish and parking
punishment worsens tensions without changing habits
she begins by listing the complaints block by block
she spots the places where people's comings and goings disturb the rest of others
she holds short meetings given over to a single matter
the undertakings given are written down
a check takes place about six weeks later
text: Her work is mediation in a district where people live packed close, and the quarrels that reach her are the ones neither the police nor the courts will take on. The difficulty is one of numbers. Most of what gets reported comes down to noise, bins and parking, and none of the three yields to punishment, which hardens both sides while leaving the habit untouched. So she works in steps that can be measured. She lists the complaints block by block, then marks the places where one household's coming and going runs into another's rest. After that she calls short meetings, each about a single matter, and writes down whatever is undertaken. A check follows six weeks on. Of the files reopened after that check, she says, the share is a very small part of what she handles in a year.

units: two reworkings of nearby spaces are set side by side
the first concerns a school yard given a cushioned surface
that place also has planters and tiered seating
the children spread themselves unevenly across it
each installation imposes a single way of using it
the second scheme takes over derelict ground for a far smaller outlay
its look seems unfinished with low walls left unrendered
a greater variety of activities is observed there
the absence of any imposed use explains that variety
text: Two neighbouring schemes a short walk apart invite comparison, and the verdict is not the one the drawings promised. The first gave the school yard a soft surface, planters and timber tiers; the work is neat, yet the children bunch up in some corners and desert others, because each piece of kit calls for one posture and leaves little room for invention. The second, on derelict ground nearby, cost a good deal less and looks unfinished: rolled earth, low walls left rough, young trees behind a temporary fence. And there you see a range of uses the first never gets, precisely because nothing there tells you what any one surface is meant for. Designers might do well to keep the lesson in mind. The most polished piece of ground is not automatically the one that takes in the richest life.

units: workmen put up a metal structure in front of the building opposite
the noise of the assembly disturbs the flats on the landing
a sheet stretched over the frontage takes away the tenants' view
the caretaker warns residents that the entry-phone system will be cut off
three households voice their displeasure
a temporary replacement device is adopted
contact between neighbours becomes more frequent
the longest-standing resident finds the situation unheard of
text: Dear neighbour, here is the week as it looked from my window. It began with workmen raising a metal frame against the building opposite, and the clatter of the poles woke every flat on our landing. A green sheet went up over the front of it next, so the courtyard vanished from view. The following morning the caretaker went round the letterboxes, telling us all that the entry-phone would be switched off while the hall was redone. Three households complained, and an agreement followed: a temporary bell, screwed to a plank, would stand in for the handset. By the end of the week the work had already changed our habits. We pass one another on the pavement far more, we stop and chat, and the oldest woman on our stairs says she has known nothing like it since she moved in. Much love.

units: neither the designer nor the residents decide alone how a neighbourhood looks
the shape of a neighbourhood comes out of a long argument between opposing sides
an abandoned plot usually sets off that argument
the emptiness of the place brings out proposals for its use
the proposals bring shared memories back to the surface
what the various sides ask for cannot be reconciled
the local body has to rule between those demands
public conflict usually strengthens attachment to the place
text: Who settles the look of a neighbourhood? Not the architect alone, and not the people who live there either, since the answer comes out of a slow bargaining that sets them against one another as much as it draws them together. What starts that bargaining? An abandoned plot, more often than not: waste ground, thick with nettles, that nobody dares claim. Because the emptiness unsettles people, it draws proposals; and because it draws proposals, it stirs up old memories. And then? One side wants vegetable beds, the other a music room, so the local council is left to rule between wishes that cannot be reconciled. Does the quarrel damage the street? Rarely, say those who have lived through one: by contradicting each other in public they end up acquainted, and their attachment to the place comes out stronger.

units: a maintenance worker sets out a fault to a gathering of occupants
water getting in attacks the connections of the outside panel
every spell of rain cuts the link
an occupant asks whether the whole thing must be replaced
the worker reckons a cover, a new seal and a renewed conduit will do
the woman in charge of the money asks what has to be spent
the sum announced is lower than that of a complete installation
an occupant at the top of the building reports a crackle in her handset
text: The maintenance man set out the fault to the residents' committee. Damp has got into the entry panel, he said, and it is eating the contacts, so the line drops with every shower of rain. One resident asked whether the whole unit would have to go. Not at all, came the answer: a stainless cover, a fresh seal and a length of conduit renewed from the cellar upwards would be enough to dry the circuit out. The treasurer wanted to know what the work would actually cost. He named a modest sum, well under the price of a complete entry-phone, provided the plant room could be reached without clearing it first. A tenant from the top floor mentioned that her handset had been crackling since the autumn. He wrote that down, offered to look at her cable the same afternoon, and closed the panel.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: early communities organised themselves differently according to where they settled
some formed beside a spring, others at a trading crossroads
beside water, authority served to share out a scarce resource
households were counted there and turns of use written down
cheating there brought a loss of standing
at the crossroads, the assembly saw above all to making dealings safe
it standardised the measures and settled disputes
shared memories still differ according to these two origins
present institutions keep the mark of these two models
text: Early communities did not arrange their common life in the same way, and much depended on whether they settled beside a spring or where two trading roads met. In the first case authority went into sharing out what was scarce: households were counted, turns at the water were written down, and anyone who cheated lost standing among the rest. In the second, wealth came from passing traffic, so the assembly worried less about division than about making exchange safe: it fixed the weights, judged disputes and punished sharp practice. Two different sorts of shared memory grew out of that. Where water ruled, what is recalled is shortage and squabbles between neighbours; where trade ruled, the fairs, the ruined merchants and the alliances. Our own institutions still carry the mark of that twofold inheritance.

units: a neighbourhood group rests on supports that can be named
its members first draw up the list of needs and of people available
a place to meet is needed for projects to come to anything
meetings at regular intervals are worth more than occasional enthusiasm
renewing the participants keeps the active core from wearing out
openness about money keeps mistrust away
welcoming newcomers must avoid any unspoken hierarchy
a group deprived of one of these supports survives without drawing anyone new
text: A neighbourhood association rests on supports that are easy enough to pick out. The first is stocktaking: before doing anything, the members list what is needed, and note ages, languages spoken and skills available. The second is a room, because without somewhere to settle, good intentions drift away. The third is regularity, since a meeting held on a fixed date is worth more than a burst of scattered enthusiasm. The fourth is fresh hands: if the same volunteers carry everything, they wear out and the group dies away. The fifth is clarity about money, as the smallest patch of vagueness breeds suspicion. The last is harder to spot: taking newcomers in without saddling them with an unspoken pecking order. An association that neglects one support survives, but it stops drawing anyone in.

units: a musical instrument is taken out through an opening on an upper floor
it is held by a brightly coloured strap
at first the onlookers are very few
a gathering of the curious ends up filling the road
the workman handling the move does not answer the remarks
he rests the load against the frame put up to redo the frontage
a resident fears for her vehicle parked underneath
the arrival on the ground sets off applause
the owner offers a drink to those who watched the scene
she had loathed the object since her marriage
text: You will never guess: a piano came out of a third-floor window on an orange strap. Two or three of us were watching at the start, chins up. Then one passer-by stopped, then another, and in no time the crowd had spread across the road, judging the whole manoeuvre out loud as though it were street theatre. The remover himself said nothing; he hauled on his rope, rested the case against the frame put up to redo the front of the house, let it down a notch and started again. A woman from our stairs was fretting about her car, parked right underneath. When the piano touched the ground the onlookers clapped, which at last got a smile out of him. The best came afterwards: the owner, a very dignified lady, asked the whole pavement in for a drink, to celebrate losing the thing she had hated since her wedding day.

units: clearing a neglected plot calls for organisation beforehand
the landowner's permission decides whether the operation is lawful
without that agreement, nothing covers the damage
an inspection of the ground prevents injuries from buried waste
the jobs must be handed out before the participants arrive
without a share-out arranged in advance, part of the group waits about
protection for the hands and containers in quantity are needed
a heap left behind brings fresh dumping
a shared meal at the end makes participants come back
text: Clearing waste ground calls for a method worked out beforehand, or the volunteers give up after a single outing. Start by getting the landowner to agree: without that, the whole thing is unlawful, and no insurance covers what gets damaged. Then probe the ground, because an old dump can hide broken glass or leaking drums, and a session thrown together ends up at the first-aid post. Hand out the jobs before the group turns up, since if everyone finds out what to do on arrival, half the party is left standing at the gate with nothing to do. Lay in thick gloves and skips enough to take the lot, as one heap left by the roadside pulls in more rubbish. Finish with something to eat together: tiredness sits better when it ends in company, and the volunteers come back for the next outing.

units: an electrical failure leaves a residential area without light
the lifts stopping shuts elderly occupants in at home
those occupants are left without warmth or means of calling
the fault itself is put right quickly
the real obstacle was the lack of information about isolated occupants
a woman working at the library thinks up a cheap solution
an optional register of vulnerable flats is drawn up with the caretaker
two neighbours per floor are named to check the flats when the alarm goes
two later incidents passed off without panic
text: A fault on the grid put the upper part of the neighbourhood into darkness, and the news climbed the stairs, landing by landing. With the lifts at a standstill, elderly residents were held in their flats, without heating and without a charged phone. The trouble lay not in the cut, which was mended quickly enough, but in ignorance: nobody knew who lived alone behind which door. A librarian came up with an answer that was modest and lasting. Together with the caretaker she drew up a voluntary list of the flats where somebody might need help, then gave each floor a pair of neighbours whose job was to knock at the doors the next time. The list sleeps in a sealed envelope. Two alerts have been lived through since, without alarm, and the street claims to feel a good deal less anonymous than before.

units: two stairwells in one and the same block share nothing but their height
one is built on a concrete frame
its broad, straight steps throw sound back
its landings open onto corridors lit by a band of glass
the other, more worn, turns around a stone core
its steps are hollowed by use and its metal rail shifts
its light comes from a glazed opening at the top
the newer stair carries noise from one end of the building to the other
the older stair soaks up sound but holds the damp
the narrowness of the second makes its users meet
text: Two stairwells face each other inside one and the same block of flats, and nothing makes them comparable but their height. The one in the east wing stands on a concrete frame: the steps are straight, broad and loud, and every landing opens onto a corridor lit by a band of glass. The one in the west wing is older and winds round a stone core; the steps are hollowed in the middle by long use, the wrought-iron rail shifts under the hand, and the light drops from a glazed opening right at the top. The first carries sound, so a door slammed at the bottom is heard on the last floor. The second soaks sound up, but it holds the damp, which means repainting the walls rather often. Residents of the older wing see more of each other, since the narrow stair obliges the people who use it to slow down.

units: protecting shared life means naming what makes it fragile
the disappearance of places open to free use is the first threat
all that then remains are places given over to buying
this shift cuts down encounters between people unlike one another
a body that debates without concluding cheapens public speech
the walling-off of the ages separates childhood from old age
alarming stories turn the neighbour into a threat
the writer judges this decline reversible
modest acts such as backing a beginner repair the social bond
text: Standing up for shared life means naming, without any softening, what wears it down. First, the loss of places that cost nothing: as each bench goes, all that is left is space where people buy things, and we stop rubbing along with anyone unlike ourselves. Then the weight of decision, for an assembly that debates at length and never settles anything teaches its members that public speech carries no weight at all. Next comes the sorting of ages, which puts everyone in a separate pen, childhood here, old age elsewhere. To that must be added fear, kept alive by stories that make the neighbour a danger before making him a support. None of this is fated. A society mends itself through ordinary acts: opening a room, backing a beginner, giving up a whole evening to hear out a disagreement.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: the manager runs a neighbourhood drop-in centre
she grew up next door to a noisy workshop
quarrels between neighbours marked her childhood
she decided to face conflicts instead of avoiding them
she began by listing the causes of dispute
she set up a weekly drop-in session
so many people came that the room grew cramped
the local authority granted her a larger space
she puts her success down to experience, not to an inborn gift
text: From a glazed office looking onto the courtyard, the woman who runs a neighbourhood drop-in centre watches the families come and go. Her way of working grew out of her own life. As a child she lived in a flat that shared a wall with a noisy workshop, and the quarrels between neighbours left a lasting mark on her. Once grown up, she chose to take conflict head on rather than walk away from it. Knowing those everyday grudges from the inside, she began by listing every reason people fell out, then opened a drop-in session once a week. Families arrived in such numbers that the room was soon too cramped to hold them. That turnout persuaded the local authority to hand over a far larger space nearby. None of it, she insists, comes down to some gift she was born with: she simply turned an old wound into a useful skill.

units: the covered hall has recently been converted
the designers wanted an open volume with no partitions
the din of the stalls disturbs those who come to read
children moving about unsettle users looking for quiet
thick curtains hung on rails now divide the space
these dividers can be shifted as needs change
the work cost little and built nothing permanent
the writer judges this correction better than the original scheme
text: You step into the converted hall as into a sentence that runs on too long: the eye hunts for something to rest on and finds nothing. The flaw shows from the threshold, before you have even crossed the first row of stalls. The designers wanted one unbroken volume, with no partitions, where every use would mingle with the rest. Yet the din of the stalls swamps the readers settled at the far end, and children drifting between the tables unsettle anyone who came in search of quiet. The remedy brought in since autumn deserves praise. Nothing weighty has gone up: the nave is now broken by thick curtains, hung on rails and slid about as the hours require. The place breathes at last. It gains in gentleness what it loses in purity, and that owned-up flaw beats the fine idea that made the building unliveable.

units: the writer compares two systems for collecting waste
the first solution gives one bin to each home
this first solution is expensive to maintain
it makes sorting mistakes easy to trace
the second solution is a shared container sunk below ground
this container costs less and holds the smell in
its anonymity encourages illegal dumping
the writer recommends the second solution with clear signage
the decision will be taken at a coming residents' meeting
text: Here is my answer about the two waste systems our building is weighing up. The first gives every flat a bin of its own, emptied each week by the contractor. Upkeep costs a fair amount, though nobody can hide behind anyone else, since a sorting mistake can be traced back. The second comes far cheaper: everything drops into one shared container sunk below ground, on the strip of land beside the car park. It holds a great deal and the lid keeps the smell in, but anonymity invites illegal dumping. Set side by side, the two come down to this: one mends habits, the other mends clutter. Our real headache remains the bags piling up by the entrance, so I lean towards the sunken container, provided we put up signage anyone can read. Tell me what you think before the residents' meeting.

units: the head of an urban service is questioned about the public consultation
she believes the consultation brings incompatible uses to light
three subjects come back at almost every meeting
people living nearby want calmer traffic
shopkeepers fear a fall in custom
noise complaints clash with the need for places open late
outdoor tables cut into the room left for people on foot
the head denies that the consultation settles the disagreements
the final decision rests with the elected members
text: Asked what a public consultation is actually good for, the head of the urban service replies that it brings uses that clash with one another into the open. Three subjects come back, she notes, at almost every meeting. The first is traffic: people living nearby press for calmer roads, while shopkeepers dread a fall in custom. The second covers the hours after dark; against complaints about noise she sets the need for places that stay open late for the young. The third touches the pavement, where outdoor tables cut into the room left for pushchairs and wheelchairs. Does the consultation settle any of it? Not at all, she answers, and she does not dress the matter up. It gives the disagreements shape, puts them in order of weight, and leaves the elected members to carry the burden of choosing.

units: the chair of an association asks a volunteer about the state of the entrance hall
the volunteer reports overflowing letterboxes and parcels on the floor
the caretaker has been off sick for a fortnight
no stand-in has been arranged
one tenant had already given warning in writing without any reply
the treasurer suggests paying for a temporary replacement
the tenant objects that the fund is meant for something else
the chair decides to call round at the flats the next day
a general meeting will be called if nobody comes forward
text: As the meeting drew towards its close, the chair of the association asked the young volunteer what he had come across in the entrance hall. The letterboxes were overflowing, he said, and parcels had been lying on the floor since the day before. The chair wanted to know what lay behind such unusual disorder. The caretaker had been off sick for a fortnight, the volunteer explained, and nobody had been put in his place. One tenant added that she had already given warning in writing and had heard nothing back. The treasurer suggested paying for a temporary replacement as a one-off; the tenant objected that the fund was meant for something else. The chair settled the matter there and then: he would call round at the flats the next day, then summon a general meeting if nobody came forward.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: streets did not carry a displayed name from the outset
people once found their way by signs and shops
such bearings were enough while the neighbourhood stayed small
the spread of the outskirts made spoken directions useless
the authorities could no longer collect the taxes
they could no longer trace the people they were after
numbering house fronts grew out of that difficulty
the postman's round follows from it as well
residents objected to the measure at first
they saw it as an intrusion into their private life
text: Believe it or not, streets did not always carry a name on a plate for anyone to read. People once found their way by painted signs and shopfronts: you lived by the well, or across from the tanner, and that did the job well enough while the neighbourhood came down to no more than a handful of lanes. Then the outskirts spread, newcomers crowded in, and directions passed from door to door stopped working. The authorities moved for a very down-to-earth reason: they could no longer gather the taxes owed to them, nor lay hands on the people they were after. That is where numbered house fronts come from, and with them the postman's regular round. The odd part of the story is that residents kicked against the change at first: an address imposed on them felt like a trespass on their private life.

units: a rumour of a break-in goes round a residents' messaging group
the message is twisted and blown up within an evening
an alarming story travels faster than a denial
fear drives people to warn those close to them
setting the facts straight calls for patient enquiry
neighbourhood groups appoint two people to check
these checkers vet every alert before it goes out
a pause is imposed before anything is shared
the number of alerts falls and trust grows
text: A rumour swells in the residents' messaging group: intruders are said to have been through the basement. Within one evening the message is passed on, twisted and blown up. Researchers who study the way information travels know the pattern well enough. An alarming story travels faster than a denial, because it works on fear, and fear drives each of us to warn the people close to us. A single message rouses a whole building, whereas setting the facts straight calls for patient enquiry. Neighbourhood groups here and there are trying out a guard that works. They appoint two people to vet every alert before it goes out, and they impose a pause before anything is shared. The upshot of it all is striking: the alerts fall away, trust climbs back, and the exchanges take on some real use again.

units: the narrator watches two queues in a single week
the first stands at an official counter
this first queue stays silent and packed tight
everyone in it guards the place they hold
the second queue waits outside a volunteer-run canteen
people there talk loudly
they keep the place of a neighbour who has stepped away
the difference comes neither from the wait nor from the conditions outside
it rests on what each person hopes for at the head of the queue
text: I came across two crowds in the space of a single week, and nothing about them was alike. The first was waiting at an official counter: packed tight, silent, shuffling on the spot under a canopy that was far too short, each of them keeping an eye on the place they had won. Nothing passed between them but sighs and sidelong glances, as though waiting there forbade speech. The second had formed outside a volunteer-run canteen open to all. It shuffled on just as much, under the very same drizzle, yet voices carried, and people held the place of a neighbour who had gone off to fetch an umbrella. The gap had nothing to do with the length of the wait or with the weather. It rested on what each of them hoped for at the head of the queue: a refusal at one, hot soup and a familiar face at the other.

units: the procedure applies before an association's premises open to the public
the width of the entrance door must be measured
the slope of the ramp must be checked
a wheelchair must be able to turn without an awkward manoeuvre
the emergency exits must be found and kept clear
the charge in the extinguishers and the electrical inspection are to be checked
the furniture must be entered in a register with its condition
seats whose base gives way are to be taken out
a felt panel cures the echo of a bare ceiling
the compliance papers are to be asked of the owner after a refurbishment
text: Before an association's premises open to the public, work through these checks in the order given. Start with access: measure the width of the entrance door, check the slope of the ramp, make sure a wheelchair turns without an awkward manoeuvre. Move on to safety: find the emergency exits, clear them, check the charge in the extinguishers and the inspection of the electrical board. Then deal with the furniture: enter every chair and table in a register, note its condition, and take out anything whose base has given way. Finish with the acoustics, which tend to be forgotten: a bare ceiling throws voices back and makes talking a strain, whereas a felt panel is enough to cure the fault. If the building has been refurbished lately, ask the owner for the compliance papers and file them with the register.

units: a work-integration association applied to occupy an empty warehouse
the warehouse belongs to a public landlord
the application went unanswered at first
a technical meeting brought together the landlord, the safety officers and the people behind the scheme
the scheme planned a repair workshop and a shared kitchen
the experts demanded that the roof structure be strengthened
the landlord agreed to pay for that strengthening
the association undertook to handle upkeep and keep watch over the place
the agreement was signed at the end of autumn
a neighbouring building is now the subject of a similar request
text: It began when a work-integration association applied for temporary use of an empty warehouse held by a public landlord. The application went unanswered at first. A fortnight later a technical meeting brought together the landlord, the safety officers and the people behind the scheme, who hoped to put a repair workshop and a shared kitchen into the building. The experts found that the roof structure needed strengthening; without that, opening to the public was out of the question. The landlord offered a compromise: it would pay for the reinforcement, while the association would handle day-to-day upkeep and keep watch over the place. The agreement was signed at the end of autumn. The workshop has opened since, and the building next door, empty as well, is now the subject of a similar request.

units: a covered market is in poor condition
the roof lets the water through
the sellers are short of space
the aisles are clogged with shoppers
inspectors have declared the place unhealthy
a group of sellers puts forward a three-part answer
the requests concern the roof, the aisles and the drainage
a local body has approved the idea but lacks money
the works would be done in the quiet season
the sellers hope the buyers will come back
text: Nothing about the old market hall keeps the weather out any longer. Its timbers have rotted, cracked panes let the rain drip onto the stalls below, and the concrete floor turns slippery the moment the damp rises. Traders grumble about cramped pitches that press one against the next, while shoppers shuffle down an aisle packed tight. A traders' group has now put forward a plan in three parts. It asks first for the roof to be relaid, then for wider central walkways, and finally for drainage that would clean up premises the inspectors called unfit. The district council backed the idea and is hunting for the money. Work would begin out of season, so that no trader loses a day's selling. The traders will put up with the mess, sure that a repaired hall will win back the custom that had been drifting away.

units: two public spaces are set side by side
one is old and the other recent
trees surround the older one
you can stay there without spending
the new space is bright but has no shade
the noise there puts off anyone who would stay
the old one was made for the pause and the recent one for movement
the writer holds that a place is judged by those who stay in it for no reason
text: People set the old square against the recent forecourt as though one belonged to the past and the other to whatever is coming. The comparison is worth taking up again, and more slowly. Ringed by close-planted trees, the old square invites you to sit down and buy nothing at all: an idle man dozes on a bench, children tear about, a stallholder nods off behind her tray. The recent forecourt gleams with pale paving and hard-edged benches, yet it throws no shade at all, and its clatter drives off anyone minded to linger there. One was drawn for the quiet halt, the other for the crossing. We too readily judge a shared space by its polish; it is judged instead by how many people stay in it for no reason. A good place is not the one you walk through but the one you inhabit briefly, then leave with regret.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: a mediator works in one particular district
her work falls into four strands
she handles quarrels between neighbours
she receives the two sides in a neutral place
she helps people with their official paperwork
she runs meetings and trains volunteers
she records the closed files meticulously
her colleagues praise her warmth and her helpfulness
she studied social law before taking the post
text: Four strands make up the work of the mediator posted to the northern district, within limits laid down by a written protocol. The first covers quarrels between neighbours: she takes the complaint, checks whether it can be heard at all, then calls both sides to a room that belongs to neither. The second deals with entitlements; she helps fill in the forms and points people towards the right office. The third is prevention, since she runs meetings for whole blocks of flats and trains volunteers. The fourth concerns record-keeping, a task she handles fastidiously, because every closed file must be coded. Colleagues describe her as warm with the public and obliging towards junior staff. She read social law before taking up the post, and rounded that off with a course in attentive listening.

units: a development scheme is judged phase by phase
the consultation of local people was thorough
the papers and the objections were made public
an option that kept a courtyard was turned down without explanation
the building work moved quickly
the signs put up hindered the oldest residents
the finished result looks sturdy and easy to read
the final judgement is divided
the writer would like the opening method taken up elsewhere
text: Following this development scheme stage by stage is the surest way of weighing what it is worth. The opening phase, an open consultation of those living nearby, was handled with real care: minutes went out, objections were written down, deadlines held. The second stretch disappoints, for the client set aside, without adequate reason, the variant that would have kept the inner courtyard. Then came the building work, pushed through at a speed that deserves credit, though the signs put up around it confused the oldest residents. The handover, last of all, shows a plain scheme whose materials look hard-wearing and whose routes are easy to read. The verdict is therefore mixed: an exemplary method at the start, a murky ruling in the middle, a creditable end. One would want the next operation to keep the first quality without repeating the second failing.

units: the writer has just moved somewhere else
the building looked sound in the pictures
the shared parts turned out to be damaged
the lack of upkeep had discouraged the occupants
that discouragement made the decay worse
the writer called a meeting of the neighbours
few people came for want of notice
those present shared out the cleaning and wrote to the landlord
the state of the building has improved since
the writer asks for news from the person written to
text: I am writing from the flat I have just moved into, and I think you will grasp my mood soon enough. The building looked perfectly sound in the pictures I was sent; on the day I arrived I found a battered stairwell, letterboxes prised open and an entryphone that made no sound at all. Since nobody was looking after the shared parts, the tenants had long given up trying, and that giving-up had let the decay spread further still. So I called a meeting. Word went round badly and few people turned up, but there were still enough of us to settle on two things. We split the cleaning floor by floor, and we wrote jointly to the landlord. The stair light works now, the front door shuts properly, and the neighbours say hello. Tell me how your own move went, because I would like to set it beside mine.

units: vehicles take up the pavement of the street
people have to walk on the road used by cars
the writer says one can act without waiting for the authorities
the residents logged the blocked stretches for a week
they took pictures and wrote a short note
a local committee has to comment on a scheme without cars
two bollards were put in at a street corner
the roads department promised to paint lines
the writer sums up the method in three moves
text: You are asking what has gone wrong in our street, so here it is, straight out and unvarnished. The trouble is that the whole pavement gets used for parking, which means we push the prams along the road with the traffic instead. The next question answers itself: can we do anything without waiting for a ruling from above? We can, and we have started. For a week we logged every blocked stretch, we took photographs of it, we wrote a short note. Then you will say, who ever reads a note like that? The district committee does, as it happens, since it has to comment before the walking scheme goes to study. The upshot: two bollards went in on the corner, and the roads team promised paint on the ground before long. It has not worked everywhere, fair enough, but the method holds. Watch, measure, ask in writing.

units: a volunteer compares two districts outside a community centre
in the lower district people come in person
in the upper district they ring instead of travelling
the manager puts the gap down to the distance
a woman using the service describes a packed waiting room below
the same room above is almost empty
the number of staff differs between the two places
the volunteer finds the comparison incomplete without that fact
the speakers agree on the part played by available staff
text: Asked outside the door of the community centre, a volunteer weighs up the two districts that she knows well. Down here, she says, people knock on the door for a form; up on the hill they ring first and rarely make the journey. The man in charge softens that: to his mind the gap comes from the distance, not from the character of the people. An older woman using the service joins in and insists that the waiting room down here is packed from opening time, whereas the one up the hill struck her as nearly empty. He accepts the difference and puts it down to staffing: two workers below, only one above. The volunteer concludes that the comparison would be quite unfair if that detail were left out. All of them settle on one point: what gets done depends less on the district than on the number of hands.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: farming communities managed their own water
that management covered several matters
the upkeep of the water point fell to every household
the basin was cleaned and leaks were watched for
the sharing followed an order of turns that was respected
that order decided whether the crops succeeded
a gathering of elders punished those who broke the rule
the punishment took away a watering turn
these rules were passed on by word of mouth
they lasted as long as the mutual dependence did
text: Long before water ever ran from a tap, farming villages arranged it themselves, and the arrangement reached into several separate matters. There was the spring first of all, whose upkeep fell on every household alike: the basin was scoured, the stones reset, seepage watched for carefully. There was next the sharing, governed by turns that nobody dared disturb, since the order of watering decided what the harvest would come to. There was last the penalty, handed down by a gathering of the oldest men, which stripped the offending household of its coming turn at the water. None of this was written; it passed from use to use and lived in the memory of neighbours. What strikes you, looking back from a distance, is how long it held: as long, exactly, as the mutual need that had brought it into being.

units: a shared budget runs through ordered stages
the residents first hand in their proposals
every proposal follows the same form
technical officers then judge what can be built
requests that cost too much or fall outside the scope are dropped
the proposals kept are priced and then grouped by area
the vote is held at scattered reception points
the projects placed highest go into the works programme
progress is made public at regular intervals
the procedure comes round again from one year to the next
text: A shared-budget scheme runs through a fixed sequence, and it can be set out here step by step. The first stretch opens the door to ideas: every resident writes a proposal on one standard form, with a short description and a precise location. Technical officers then look at whether each submission can be built; they throw out anything that belongs to another budget or goes over the ceiling that has been agreed. Next comes the appraisal, where the surviving proposals are priced and then grouped by area. Voting follows over a short spell, at reception points spread right across the whole patch. The proposals that come out top are written into the works programme, and a progress table goes up at every stage. This calendar comes round again the following year, with nothing much altered in it.

units: a lift broke down in a block of flats
two occupants were stuck between two floors
one of them was elderly and the other very young
the repair was slow in coming
neighbours talked to them and brought them something to drink
a resident chased the firm responsible by telephone
the two occupants were freed during the night
the residents then drew up a list of contacts
they demanded stricter servicing
the manager agreed to change the worn cables
text: It took no more than a broken lift for the building to learn what it had never known about itself. The car came to a halt one evening of heavy rain, between two floors, carrying an elderly tenant and a teenage boy. Repair was slow in coming, so the wait stretched out, and word of it travelled from landing to landing. One neighbour went down to talk through the door, another brought a bottle of water down, a third rang the maintenance firm again and again. What followed was not merely the release of the two occupants, late that night, from the stalled car. Because they had at last spoken to one another, the residents drew up a list of contacts the week after, and then demanded stricter servicing. The manager, blamed in writing for the state of things, agreed to have the worn cables replaced.

units: the price of a handmade piece of furniture comes from several sources
the raw material bought from the supplier counts towards it
the joiner's tools wear down and have to be replaced
the solid wood bench used for shaping decays with use
the craftsman's skill is acquired through long practice
the beginner copies that skill imperfectly
the customer's wait matches a stretch with no money coming in
no single one of these sources justifies the sum asked
text: Walk into a joiner's workshop and ask where the price of a finished cabinet actually comes from. Several answers hold true at the same time. There is the timber, chosen, seasoned and paid for at the supplier's door. There are the planes and the clamps, which lose their edge and must be bought again. There is the bench itself, a heavy slab of wood that wears away quietly under years of shaping. There is the hand of the craftsman, slow to acquire, and the hand of the beginner still copying it badly. And there is the waiting the customer agrees to, a stretch of weeks in which no money comes in. Not one of these on its own explains the figure on the label. The buyer who calls it steep is looking at a smooth polished board; the maker sees behind it the whole run of costs that brought it there.

units: the head of the team kept a record of operations
the foundations progressed at the planned rate in the first week
a steel delivery arrived incomplete the following week
the load calculation had to be redone beam by beam
the supplier blamed a break in supply
an engineer suggested replacing the section with an equivalent one held in stock
the substitution was approved on condition that the slab be strengthened
the rate of output fell before it settled
the extra cost showed up on the final invoice
text: The foreman in charge of the site kept a logbook, and every operation went into it in the order it happened. Through the first week the foundations rose at exactly the rate planned. The week after, a steel delivery turned up short. The load calculation had to be worked through again, beam by beam, before anything else could be poured. The supplier put the blame on a break in supply. At the technical meeting an engineer suggested swapping the missing section for an equivalent one already held in the yard, and the substitution went through on one condition: the slab was to be strengthened. Once work resumed, output dropped a notch, hung there a while and then settled. The logbook holds the record of all of it, and the final invoice told the same story in the shape of an extra cost.

units: a written estimate must be asked for before a repair is started
an agreement made only in speech protects neither side
the document must set out the work, the materials and the time announced
the sum paid in advance ties the customer to the trader
the trader may not keep that advance if the job has not begun
proofs of payment form the basis of a claim
any change decided while the work runs must be notified in writing
the final bill must be compared point by point with the accepted estimate
text: Ask for a written estimate before any substantial piece of repair work begins. A promise made only in conversation protects neither of the two sides once a dispute starts. The document should set out the work to be carried out, the materials involved and the time the trader has announced. Look closely at the deposit clause: money handed over in advance binds the customer to the trader, though the trader may not keep it if the job has never begun. Keep every proof of payment you are given, since a claim will rest on those and on nothing else. If anything changes while the work is under way, put the change in writing and have it acknowledged. Then compare the closing bill with the estimate you accepted, point by point. A gap nobody can account for is fair ground to refuse to pay.

units: a storage building has been running slowly since it lost its main client
orders have fallen sharply
part of the workforce has moved onto reduced hours
seasonal recruitment has been halted
nearby haulage firms fear knock-on effects
sharing the building between several shippers is under consideration
converting the floor space calls for automated sorting equipment
the local authority would pay for half of that equipment
a first occupier is said to have signed a promise of lease
text: A storage building on the industrial estate has been running well below capacity since it lost its main client. Those in charge describe a steep fall in orders that has left the loading bays bare and the forklifts standing idle. Some of the workforce has moved onto reduced hours, and the seasonal recruitment planned for the coming months has been halted. Haulage firms nearby fear the effect will travel down the line to them as well. One idea is currently under study: share the building between several medium-sized shippers instead of depending on a single customer. Converting the floor space would call for automated sorting equipment, half of it paid for by the local authority. A first occupier is said to have signed a promise of lease, which would reopen hiring by the busy season.

units: the two aisles of the covered market do not run at the same rhythm
the fruit seller calls out to passers-by and announces his prices aloud
he drops a price as soon as goods risk spoiling
the cheese shop ages its products in a cellar
its displayed prices rarely change
perishable goods force selling in a hurry
a product that improves with age allows waiting
the first business takes on seasonal hands during the glut
the second keeps the same employee all year
text: Have a look at the two aisles of the covered market: they do not run at the same speed at all. Down the first one the fruit seller shouts at whoever walks past, calls his prices out over the crates and drops one the moment a tray looks like turning. Down the second the cheese shop keeps its stock ageing in a cellar, writes small quiet labels and hardly ever moves a price. The one of them sells freshness, so he lives in a hurry; the other sells patience, so he can afford to wait for his buyer. You will notice too that the first takes on extra hands when the harvest floods in, while the second keeps the same assistant all year round.
