genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: the woman running the works grew up beside a wetland
her father taught her to turn the peat
she had noticed the decline of the birds nesting there
she trained at university in ecology
her first team replanted bare riverbanks
the young trees set too deep in the ground died
she then chose species able to stand standing water
passing birds came back once the reed cover closed over
she passes her method on to crews arriving from elsewhere
she holds that a damaged place mends through patience and not through machine power
text: The woman who now runs the restoration works grew up on the edge of a marsh. Her father taught her to turn the peat while she was still small, and she watched the brackish water rise and fall each year. By the time she left school she had noticed how few birds still nested there. She read ecology at university, then joined a team replanting bare riverbanks. That first attempt went badly: the saplings were set too deep and rotted in the waterlogged ground. She changed tack, picking species that could stand having their roots submerged, and spacing the holes more widely. Seasons later the reedbed had closed over itself and the passing birds came back. She now trains crews who travel in from other regions, and tells them the same thing: a damaged place mends through patience and watching, never through the force of machinery.

units: the narrator finds the shared composting site worth attention
the site rules turn away thick woody stems
a shredding machine was therefore installed
waste broken into chips rots down twice as fast as before
more people now use the site
the noise of the machine disturbs the flats at the bottom of the building
the compost is not screened before it is handed out
users therefore take away woody pieces they cannot use
the quality of the product changes from one bin to the next
the writer holds that a screen would put most of the fault right
text: Honestly, the shared compost heap round the corner is worth a look, even if the running of it limps in places. Whole branches are not allowed in, so a shredder had to go in beside the bins, and that machine is what changed everything: waste chopped into chips rots down in one season rather than two. People turn up more readily now, and there is usually a small queue by the gate. The catch is the racket. The motor howls, and the flats on the ground floor keep their windows shut through it. Someone explained to me that the finished compost ought to be screened before it is handed out; without that step gardeners go home with woody lumps they cannot use. The step is missing, so the stuff varies wildly from one bin to the next. My verdict is short: fine idea, wobbly execution, and a screen would put most of it right.

units: the writer is staying at a water treatment site
the water arriving carries nitrogen compounds
the level climbs after rain falls on the neighbouring crops
the metal pipes are under chemical attack
putting them right is costly
a planted wetland was laid out upstream
the plants clean the water before it reaches the tanks
the pollutant load drops by about a third
the energy the site uses falls as well
the team mean to enlarge the filtering area
text: I am writing to you from the water treatment works where I am spending the week, and I think what goes on here will interest you. The water arriving in the top basin carries nitrogen compounds, and the readings climb as soon as rain washes across the crops in the fields next door. The operators worry, because the metal pipework is being eaten away and putting it right costs a great deal of money. What they have settled on here surprised me by how plain it is. A shallow pool planted with reeds was dug above the site, and the plants clean the water before it ever reaches the tanks. The load drops by about a third, and the electricity bill falls with it. The team already mean to widen the filtering pool towards the meadow. I will tell you the rest when I am back; keep an evening free for me.

units: the text sets a lack of water against too much water in a river
the nature of the ground settles the answer
ground rich in silt holds back the rising water then lets it go slowly
a slope without plant cover sheds the water at once
the specialists do not plainly name the worse of the two
rising water brings nourishing deposits for all the damage it does
a lack of water makes the surface hard and squeezes the roots
the specialists rule out hard structures and deep wells
they call for a landscape mixing water stores, plant barriers and soils that let water through
text: Which should we fear more, a river running dry or a river breaking its banks? The question keeps coming back, and the answer depends on the ground you put it to. Silty flat land takes in the flood like a sponge and gives the water back over weeks; a bare hillside throws it downstream in a single afternoon. Ask which wound heals better and the specialists hesitate. A flood tears things away, yet it also lays down fertile silt, while drought bakes the surface hard and closes it round the roots. So what is to be done? No walls and no deep boreholes, they answer, but a landscape able to do both things at once: ponds that hold, hedges that slow the flow, loose soil that drinks. Only then is the comparison worth making, for one is cured by a slow water table and the other by remembering where the run-off went.

units: a technical manager sets out the procedure to people in training
her second speaks after each explanation
plant remains are no longer put under a covering layer
breaking down deep below gives off a gas that warms the air
the sorting pulls metals aside by magnetic attraction
plastics are parted by a jet of air
glass goes through a moving screen
the dark liquids from the heaps have to be drawn off before they reach the groundwater
a covering that lets air through holds down the smells
protective kit and a ban on walking about alone are imposed
text: The engineer in charge of the site went through the procedure with the trainees, and her deputy filled in after each point. She began by reminding them that garden and kitchen waste is no longer buried, since fermenting deep down gives off a gas with a strong warming effect. He then described the sorting line: metals lifted off by magnet, plastics blown aside by an air jet, glass dropping through a shaking screen. She stressed that the dark liquid seeping under the windrows has to be pumped away before it reaches the water table. Her deputy mentioned smell control, handled by a cover sheet that breathes and by a fine spray. She closed on safety: helmet, heavy gloves, and no walking alone between the skips. The trainees asked what becomes of the rejects, and the team promised them a look at the furnace.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: the first settled groups opened modest cropped spaces at the edge of the woods
the plant cover took the ground back once a group had left
making metal called for enormous amounts of wood fuel
whole blocks of woodland were then taken away
the slopes left without trees began to slip under the rain
official texts required the cutting back of branches instead of full felling
the flows of earth pushed those in charge to replant the slopes
these plantings often rested on a single species
that sameness left the woods open to insects
a mixture of species is now held to be the best protection
text: The earliest settled communities cleared only the fringes of the woods, opening glades wide enough for a crop and no wider. When a hamlet moved on, the canopy grew back over the ground it had used, so the forest outlived that first taking. Everything altered once metal was smelted in quantity, for the furnaces swallowed charcoal, and whole blocks of woodland went down together. Stripped hillsides then began to slip under heavy rain. Written rules followed, ordering that branches be cut back and the stools left standing rather than the trunk taken. Later, alarm at the sliding earth pushed those in authority to replant the slopes, very often with one species alone, and such even stands proved easy prey for insects. The lesson drawn since holds in a word: mixture, for a varied hillside withstands both pests and dry spells.

units: part of the carbon dioxide in the air passes into the seas
this dissolving alters the chemical make-up of the water
the sea surface turns more acid
living things with a chalky shell are struck first
their thinnest edges are eaten into and break down
these small organisms feed fish and seabirds
the weakening carries through to the whole food web
warmed water holds less dissolved gas
a share of the carbon therefore goes back to the air
shallow coastal stretches react before the rest, owing to farming inputs and water loaded with sediment
text: As the air takes on more carbon dioxide, the sea soaks up a large share of it, and that changes the chemistry of the water. The dissolved gas forms a weak acid, so the surface layer turns steadily sharper. Creatures that build a chalky shell feel it first: the shell forms poorly, and its thinnest edges start to pit and wear away. Since those tiny animals feed fish and seabirds alike, a weakness at the bottom works its way up through the whole food web. A second effect piles on. Warmer water holds less dissolved gas, so part of the carbon already taken up leaks back into the air, and the process keeps itself going. Readings taken near the coast show that shallow stretches react soonest, because they also receive muddy run-off and the fertiliser washed off the fields behind them.

units: the shared garden was very nearly left to go to waste
water stood between the rows from the first heavy rain
the young shoots rotted before they came to anything
turning the soil over more deeply changed nothing
the layer of clay brought the water back up
an experienced gardener worked out the real cause
the run-off was coming from the sloping car park
a planted ditch was cut along the edge of the ground
trees that drink water were put in and the beds were raised
the following season brought a heavy crop
text: We nearly gave up on the neighbourhood plot, and I can tell you the disappointment stung. The first real downpour left water standing between the rows, turning the ground into a bog where every seedling rotted where it stood. Someone suggested digging deeper. That achieved nothing, since the clay underneath simply pushed the water back up. A retired gardener finally explained that the trouble started elsewhere: the sloping car park was tipping its run-off straight onto us. So we cut a planted ditch along the fence, put in willows to drink the surplus, and raised the beds with salvaged timber. The following season the squashes covered half the ground and the lettuces held at last. We laugh about it now, about the boots that stuck fast and the drowned rows we mourned that summer.

units: the text sets two ways of dealing with kitchen scraps at home against each other
the room available steers the choice
the first answer uses a container that lets air through
wet matter and dry matter are laid down in turn
the mixture has to be stirred once a week
the finished product shows up after two seasons
the second answer means covering the scraps in a cut trench
the depth of cover keeps small animals away
the second answer costs nothing but yields nothing you can take back
the reader is asked to weigh up the space and the number of meals cooked
text: Anyone wanting to deal with peelings at home, rather than putting them out for collection, has two routes open to them, and the choice turns above all on how much room there is. The first means building an airy bin: you lay down a wet layer, then a dry one, stir the heap once a week, and lift out the dark crumbly stuff at the end of two seasons. The second is simply to bury the scraps in a trench and cover them over with a good depth of soil, enough to put rodents off. Set the two side by side: the bin asks for steady attention but hands you a feed ready to spread; the trench costs nothing at all and enriches the ground where it lies, though you will never lift a spadeful back out of it. To decide, measure your balcony or your plot, then count up how many meals get cooked at home each week.

units: the coast described is falling back under the waves
the posts put in recently are already leaning
the water drawn from the wells has taken on a salty taste
salt water is pushing on under the cropped land
the growers have given up the most delicate crops
they are turning to hardier plants that ask for less water
the cellars suffer from damp and salt breaks down their walls
the yard of the school was raised after a flood
the residents argue over holding the shoreline or moving the houses to higher ground
no decision has been taken locally
text: At first light the wind drops on the sea wall, and you can hear at last what this place is going through. Here, the water gains: every storm carries off a slice of the dune, and the posts driven in last year already lean inland. There, the wells: what comes up tastes of salt, a sign that the wedge of seawater is creeping under the gardens. Further on, the fields: growers have given up the tender crops and fallen back on tough varieties that ask for less water. Behind the bank, the cellars: damp climbs the walls and salt crumbles the bottom courses. At the end of the lane, the school yard, built up higher after the last flooding. And everywhere the same low conversation: hold the shoreline, or move the houses up to the ridge? Nobody here decides, but nobody pretends any more that the question is not there.

units: a still stretch of water lies in the bottom of a hollow ringed with reeds
its surface used to be clear and is now covered with a greenish film
lasting heat speeds up the loss of water through evaporation
the dissolved minerals grow more concentrated in what water is left
the nearby ground dries out and splits into brittle pieces
vegetation rotting on the bed gives off a repellent smell
the water insects vanish from the place
the birds that fed there desert the bank
the spring lower down supplies almost no water to the crops
the growers sink deeper wells and draw down the buried reserve
text: Down in a hollow ringed with reeds lies a motionless sheet of water. It was formerly transparent; now a greenish film stretches right across it. The cause is straightforward. Persistent heat, week upon week, draws the water off into the atmosphere, and everything dissolved within it grows concentrated in whatever remains. Around the rim the ground desiccates and splits into brittle flakes underfoot. Vegetation decomposes on the bed and releases a smell repellent enough to drive you backwards. The insects that once inhabited the shallows have disappeared, and the birds that fed upon them no longer descend to the bank. Further down the slope, the spring that watered the plots barely trickles, so the growers sink deeper wells, and the water concealed underground subsides further still.

units: the streets overheat because they have been covered with tar and concrete
the air there becomes unfit to breathe as soon as the sun strikes
cases of illness brought on by heat are multiplying
air conditioning is put forward as the answer to the problem
an air conditioner throws outside the heat it takes from inside
this equipment swallows a considerable amount of energy
the writer proposes planting dense trees along the busy roads
he proposes making school yards absorbent and laying pale surfaces
he calls for water points where people are kept waiting
he holds that these measures call for no new technique but for a budget
text: Let us be blunt for a moment. Our streets overheat because we have covered them over with tar and concrete. Once the sun strikes them the air is hardly fit to breathe, and afterwards we affect surprise that people keep collapsing in the heat. Air conditioning, we are assured, will settle the matter. It settles nothing whatever: it discharges outdoors the very heat it strips from indoors, and it swallows an astonishing quantity of power. The way out is duller and older than that. Plant dense lines of trees along the busiest thoroughfares. Break up the school yards so that rainfall soaks in. Lay pale surfaces that throw the glare back upwards. Provide clean water wherever people are kept standing about. None of this awaits a technique nobody has invented; it awaits a budget.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: the woman in charge of a measuring station climbs each week to a rocky bowl
the man before her wrote down ice thicknesses by hand
she now receives readings that sensors send up on their own
the ice was once hard and faintly blue underfoot
the surface today is soft and gives way under the boot spikes
the front of the glacier was sharp and is now a thinned tongue
crumbling gravel streaks that tongue
she also watches two facing slopes of the same range
the slope open to the sun loses its ice far faster than the other
she holds that this gap teaches more than an overall average
text: Once a week the woman in charge of a measuring station climbs to a rocky mountain bowl in order to read her instruments. Her predecessor entered ice thicknesses into a notebook by hand; she opens her case and finds readings that the sensors have already transmitted of their own accord. He walked on a crust that was hard and faintly bluish underfoot. She works on something spongy that subsides whenever the spikes on her boots bite. Where his notes recorded a clean wall of ice, hers describe a thinned tongue streaked with gravel that crumbles between the fingers. She observes two facing slopes of the same range as well: the shaded one holds, while the one exposed to the full sun surrenders its ice far faster. That difference, she maintains, teaches her more than any overall average.

units: the review deals with a set of photographs given over to drought
the first part shows split soils covered with whitish deposits
the second part shows horizons veiled by the heat
a third part gathers emptied watercourses and abandoned watering gear
the last part shows the people who have stayed on
the reviewer holds this last part to be the finest
the work as a whole keeps clear of lament and of moral lessons
the pictures are ordered so that each one calls for the next
the reviewer reckons the silence of the frames carries more than a speech
text: Seldom has a photographic sequence handled drought with such considerable restraint. The opening series remains low, on the ground itself: clay split into plates, a whitish chalky crust, pale dust lifting at the slightest breath. The second rises away from the soil into the air, where heat veils every distant edge. A third gathers the water that is no longer there, with river beds paved in stones, emptied basins, watering pipes coiled and abandoned where they fell. The final series, and the finest, turns towards the people who have remained behind. Nowhere does the work slip into lamentation or into a lesson on how to live. It offers instead a measured crossing in which one picture calls for the next, and in which the silence inside the frames carries further than any speech could manage.

units: the writer sends word from a measuring post to tell of a repair
he opened the casing at the start of the week
a mineral deposit coated the temperature probe and skewed the readings
he cleaned that probe in an acid bath while watching the time
he then put the instrument back together and checked that the seal held
the curve showed a fixed offset once the thing was running again
so he calibrated the instrument afresh against a reference probe
he cleaned the fouled solar panel and the charging voltage climbed back
the readings have come in without a break ever since
he asks his correspondent to come and see the monitoring board he has set up
text: I said I would write from the measuring post once the sensor was working again, so here it is at last. At the start of the week I opened the casing and found the temperature probe furred over with a chalky deposit that skewed every reading. I soaked it in an acid bath, timing the operation closely, because the stuff attacks metal. Next day I reassembled the instrument and satisfied myself that the seal was holding. Transmission resumed, but the curve sat a fixed step away from where it belonged, so I set it against the reference probe and calibrated it afresh. Then I wiped the dust off the solar panel and the charging voltage climbed straight back. Nothing has dropped out of the record since. Come up to the post whenever you like and I will show you the monitoring board I have set up.

units: a common question concerns the damp that spreads through the walls of older housing
this damp comes from the groundwater rising beneath the footings
rain that falls harder and closer together feeds that rise
concentrated downpours soak packed soils that take in nothing any more
the water then makes for the cellars
a waterproof coating shuts the damp inside the brickwork
brickwork shut in this way crumbles away in patches
the specialists advise drainage laid round the building
they also advise renders that breathe and ground alongside that takes water in
the answer about cost is that acting late comes to more
text: One question comes up at every public meeting: where does the damp spreading through the walls of older housing come from? It comes from the water table pushing up beneath the footings, itself fed by rainfall that now arrives harder and closer together. The next question follows on: what has that to do with the climate? Downpours arrive all at once, the compacted soil absorbs nothing, and the water goes looking for cellars. Then somebody asks whether a waterproof coating will not do the job. It will not: it shuts the damp inside the brickwork, which turns soft and sheds in patches. So what is advised? Drainage laid right round the building, renders that let a wall breathe, ground alongside it that absorbs water. The last question is about cost, and the answer is blunt: leaving it late comes to more.

units: an angler tells an engineer that the water has smelled wrong since the cold season
a brown foam clings to the stones on the bed
the smell grows stronger as the level of the river drops
the engineer explains that a sewage line upstream spills over during storms
the angler objects that the trouble has gone on for too many seasons
the engineer also brings up the run-off from a stock farm on the plateau
the answer takes in a holding basin upstream
it takes in a thick belt of planting along the banks as well
regular checks on what is put into the river are planned
the engineer says the return of the insects will be the sign of improvement
text: On the bank an angler tells the engineer sent to investigate that the water has smelled wrong since the cold season. She asks whether the colour has shifted; he says a brown foam clings to the stones on the bed, and the stench rises whenever the level drops. She explains that a sewage line upstream overflows whenever a storm exceeds what the network can hold. He is unconvinced: the trouble has continued for far too many seasons to hang on storms alone. She grants him that and mentions the stock farm on the plateau, whose run-off drains towards the bed. Then she sets out the answer: a holding basin upstream, a thick belt of planting along both banks, regular checks on whatever is put into the river. Will it run clear again, he asks. The insects will tell him first, she says.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: in one valley wood was once burned for every purpose
the air there smelled of smoke and the walls darkened with soot
people took this state of affairs to be ordinary
a dark fuel was later cut out of the rock
the energy yield rose sharply
workshops sprang up and the sky over the working valleys turned hazy
the real turning point lies in the change of scale
a burnt forest can grow back over generations
the carbon drawn from a buried seam cannot be put back there
the older fires used what grew around them whereas the later ones drew on a store
text: Picture a valley where wood went into every fire, from the cooking pot to the forge. Smoke hung in the air, soot darkened the walls, and nobody considered it worth remarking upon. Set that beside what came afterwards, once a dark fuel was being cut out of the rock: the energy yield leapt, workshops multiplied one after another, and the sky above the working valleys turned hazy from dawn until dusk. The turn came with the scale, not with the flame. Burn a forest and it grows back again, given generations enough. Burn a seam that has lain buried and the carbon it releases goes nowhere back. The older fires consumed whatever grew around them; the ones that followed drew upon a store. Watch the flame and the difference hardly shows. Watch what feeds the flame and the difference shows immediately.

units: three workings account for what is happening to the seas
the first working has to do with the heat the water soaks up
warmed water takes more room and lifts the level with no ice melting
the second working is chemical and comes from dissolved carbon dioxide
water turned acid in this way eats at shells and chalky skeletons
the third working has to do with the stirring of the layers of water
the surface layer mixes less with the layers below
this blockage keeps nutrients from the depths away from the plankton
the three workings feed one another
a sea poorer in life holds back less carbon
text: Three workings, taken together, account for what is happening to the seas. The first of them is thermal. Water absorbs an enormous share of what accumulates, and warmed water occupies more room, so the level climbs before a single piece of ice has melted. The second of them is chemical. As more carbon dioxide dissolves, the water turns faintly corrosive, and it eats at the shells and the chalky skeletons that shellfish and corals build for themselves. The third is a matter of stirring, of how the layers mix. A warm skin of surface water mixes far less with the cold beneath, so the nutrients that formerly rose stay down there and leave the drifting plankton hungry. Each works on its own, yet each also feeds the others. A sea impoverished of life holds back less carbon than it formerly did.

units: the woman keeping a mountain refuge had shut her shutters before the sky changed
a warm breath came down off the pass in the middle of the afternoon
a curtain laden with sand then moved up along the path
sand settled even on the tables
the keeper grasped that the wind had carried this dust from dry country far away
rain tinged with ochre fell as night came on
that rain left hardened streaks down the window panes
the snow on the glacier nearby had turned rust-coloured by morning
that snow melted faster than the keeper had ever seen
she wrote the event into her register without foreseeing that it would come again
text: The woman who keeps a mountain refuge had already shut the shutters before the sky gave any sign of turning. By the middle of the afternoon a warm breath came down off the pass, so close that she left the door standing open. Then the slope went dim, a curtain of dust advanced along the path, and grit settled even on the tables inside. The wind, she understood, had carried that dust from arid country far beyond the ridges. Rain came on at nightfall, heavy and stained the colour of ochre, and dried into hardened streaks down the window panes. In the morning the snow on the glacier nearby was no longer white but rust-coloured, and it melted under her eyes faster than she had ever seen snow melt. She wrote the whole episode into her register, with no notion whatever that it would recur.

units: fear has an identifiable trigger
fear stops once the danger has passed
anxiety is aimed at a future and uncertain danger
anxiety shows itself through muscular tension and damp hands
fear is compared to a brief warning signal
anxiety is compared to a faulty warning signal that never stops
both emotions begin as a form of protection
telling the two states apart helps you respond in a fitting way
text: You are walking down a dim corridor and a door slams behind you. Your heart bolts, your shoulders lock, a chill runs down the back of your neck. That is fear. Something set it off, you know what, and it drains away the moment the threat has passed. Anxiety runs on a different clock. Nothing solid stands in front of it; it leans forward instead, towards whatever might come. You feel it as a clenched jaw, as damp palms that stay damp for no reason you can name. Fear is an alarm that rings and then stops. Anxiety is an alarm wired badly, humming away under everything else. Both of them began as ways of keeping you safe. What separates them is how long they last and what they point at. Once you can put a name to whichever one has hold of you, you are already picking a better answer.

units: adults gather every week in a room used for stage work
the workshop is meant for people whom speaking in public shuts down
the woman who runs it worked in care beforehand
the session is built round three families of exercises
the first set of exercises works on the breath
the second set works on the expressions of the face
the third set consists of looking at one another in silence
this wordless face-to-face often brings on a burst of laughter
the woman who runs it reads that laughter as a release
text: A handful of adults gather once a week in a rehearsal room with scuffed, splintered floorboards. The workshop is meant for people whom speaking in public shuts down completely. The woman who runs it trained in care work before she turned to directing, and she builds each session round three families of exercises. The first work on breath: draw the air in, hold it, let it go on a long sigh, until the throat loosens. The second work on the face: pull a grimace, keep it, drop it, so you feel the difference between tension that happens to you and tension you choose. The last work on the eyes: two people hold each other's gaze without speaking, and one of them nearly always ends up laughing. That laugh is no failure, she says. It marks the moment a grip of awkwardness lets go.

units: the first step is to settle somewhere nobody is asking anything of you
you put your hands on your legs and breathe without forcing
the next step asks you to find where anger shows in the body
you are advised to name that place silently
you then loosen the joints one after another
each loosening goes with a whole breath
you wait until the intensity falls back on its own
the last step is to say briefly what you were trying to protect
that need is most often the need to be heard
text: Begin by sitting where nobody is asking anything of you. Lay your palms flat on your thighs and let the air sink as far as your belly, without pushing it along. Then look for the exact spot where anger has settled: a heat climbing into the cheeks, a tightness under the ribs, a stiffness in the fists. Name that spot silently, the way you name the rooms of a house you are seeing for the first time. Now loosen one joint after another, the jaw, the neck, the fingers, giving each of them a whole breath. Wait for the wave to fall back of its own accord; it does fall back, though it takes the route it wants. Last of all, say quietly, out loud, the shortest sentence that describes what you were defending. More often than not it was no insult to avenge and no argument to win, but a need to be heard.

units: volunteers were kept awake through a whole night
the study pairs brain imaging with a measure of sweating
the brain structure that detects threat becomes more reactive
its reaction lasts longer than it ordinarily would
the cause put forward is a weakened control by the frontal region
frontal activity drops as the sleep debt builds
the participants take faces without expression for threatening ones
they react sharply to sounds of low intensity
the irritability produced spoils the following night and restarts the loop
text: A research team has just set out the measurements taken from volunteers who were kept awake for a whole night without a break. The protocol pairs brain imaging with readings of the sweat carried on the skin. What the loss of sleep reaches first is the deep structure that weighs up threat: it fires harder, and above all for far longer, in front of images that are perfectly ordinary. Behind that lies a slackening of the control the frontal region exerts, an activity that falls away steadily as the sleep debt builds. The behaviour then shows it plainly enough. Volunteers take blank faces for hostile ones, they flinch at faint sounds, and they report a damp grip in the hands that outlasts the session. The authors close on a loop that feeds itself: the irritability piled up spoils the night that follows, and round it goes again.

units: the waiting area was set in a cramped passage
the seats stood facing one another in two rows
a swing door made unpredictable bangs
the ceiling light was dull
people left the place more tense than they came in
the seats were regrouped into clusters turned towards the windows
a soft floor covering was laid to soak up the noise
a fitting was added to the door to stop the banging
the expected wait is now shown on display
signs of irritation have fallen since then
text: The waiting area of the department occupied a narrow passage, furnished with seats set out in two rows that faced one another. There was no escaping another person's gaze; a swing door banged at moments nobody could predict; the fitting overhead shed a dull, colourless light. People came in tense and walked out tighter still. The nursing team therefore reworked the whole layout. The rows were broken up into clusters angled towards the windows, a soft covering was laid over the floor to soak up the sound of footsteps, and the door was given a damper. A panel on the wall now shows how long the wait is expected to be, which takes away the least bearable part of it, the not knowing. Since then the staff report a clear drop in gestures of annoyance, and a calmer response whenever an appointment runs late.

units: the text sets a digital tracking tool against an exchange with a professional
the human exchange rests on a living relationship
the professional picks up signs the patient does not put into words
the digital tool catches neither the wavering of a voice nor the silences
the tool stores ratings in the form of data
the strength of the tool is the reliability of what it keeps
human memory warps memories and smooths them flat
the tool can bring out a pattern that went unnoticed
the writer holds that the two approaches fill separate roles
text: Should you hand your moods over to a logging app? The question deserves better than the flat answers it tends to attract. A session with a practitioner rests on a living relationship: the voice falters, a sigh slips out, and the person opposite picks up what the account leaves unsaid. Automated tracking hears none of that, neither the wobble in a voice nor the awkward pause; it stores ticked boxes and curves. Its strength sits elsewhere. It keeps a faithful record, where remembering warps things and smooths them flat. Someone certain of having felt low for weeks opens the log and finds a pattern he had never noticed. So the two do not stand in the same place. The log measures and reminds; the session interprets and walks alongside. To set them against each other is to choose between a scale and a gaze.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: she takes calls on a night-time telephone line
her post sits in a room with no window
she has held the job for a great many seasons
she names three qualities the role calls for
the first is to bear the silences of the callers
the second is to catch the audible signs of distress
the third is to let go once the shift is over
she walks home to shed what she has heard
a caller apologised for ringing about something small
she told him that something small deserved the same attention
text: She takes the calls that come in on a helpline late into the night, in a room with no window at all, and she has been doing it for a great many seasons now. Three things make the job, she says, laughing. Patience first of all: she lets a silence run on and on, because a caller in tears needs someone who will not rush in to fill the gap for them. Then the ear: she catches a tremor in the voice, a breath held back, a sentence that keeps breaking off at the very same word. Last, distance: once the shift ends she walks the whole way home and leaves behind her what she has heard, or she would never last out the week. The other night, she says, a caller apologised for having bothered anyone over so little. She told him that on this line the little things had the same right to be heard as the worst of them.

units: the film opens on a long still shot of an empty seat
that opening deliberately puts the audience ill at ease
the first part follows a family through the weeks after a death
that part carries no narration and no added soundtrack
specialists on grief speak in the middle part
the reviewer judges that those contributions weaken the film
the closing part goes back to the silence of the opening
the scene judged the best shows two relatives holding each other without speaking
the reviewer praises the absence of sentimentality
text: The film opens on a static shot of an empty chair, held long enough to leave the audience distinctly uneasy. That choice announces everything that follows it. The first part goes with a family through the weeks after a death, with no voice-over and no music laid over the images; all you hear are the sounds of the household and, now and then, a stifled sob. The middle part shifts gear. Specialists on grief step in, and the film loses ground here, since their explanations cover over what the faces on screen had already said. The closing part picks the silence back up and delivers the truest scene of the lot: an awkward embrace between two relatives who cannot find the words. You leave the cinema flattened, and yet with the rare sense of having watched sorrow handled without a trace of indulgence.

units: the writer explains to her reader the reason for her long silence
she stopped answering after bad news
her withdrawal did not come from any lack of affection
every conversation made her go back over her pain
keeping to herself weighed on her more than the sadness did
she has taken up walking in the evening again
the questions of neighbours still make her flush
she answers all the same and it is getting easier
she asks the person she writes to to be in touch again
text: I am writing to you because my silence over these past weeks must have hurt you, and you deserve to know where it came from. After the news you know about, I stopped answering messages. It was not that I had stopped caring. Every call asked me to tell the story again, and telling it opened the same wound, so I said nothing, and keeping to myself cut me off far more surely than the grief ever did. That is what I see now: the distance, and not the sorrow, is what made me so heavy to carry. I have started going out for a walk in the evenings again. My face still burns when a neighbour asks how I am getting on, and yet I answer, and each answer costs me a little less than the one before it. Write to me whenever you feel like it. I cannot promise to be cheerful. I promise to pick up.

units: a common question asks whether slowed breathing really works
the explanation rests on a nerve linking the brain to the inner organs
lengthening the out-breath rouses that nerve
this rousing brings the heart rate down
the protocols advise a cycle longer than ordinary breathing
the out-breath must last at least as long as the in-breath
many patients give up after a first attempt that went badly
that early failure comes from breathing too deeply
the volume drawn in must be cut while the cycle is stretched
practice is advised away from moments of strain
text: One question comes up again and again in consultations: does slowing the breath truly settle anything, or is it a comforting belief? The mechanism is well established. A drawn-out out-breath rouses the nerve that runs from the brain stem to the organs of the trunk, and that rousing brings the heart rate down. Second question: what pace? The accepted protocols stretch the cycle well past its spontaneous rate, giving the out-breath a length at least equal to the in-breath. Third question: what about failure? Plenty of patients give up because the first attempt sharpens the alarm instead of quieting it. The trouble is unintended over-breathing, brought on by drawing in far too much air. The answer is to make each breath smaller while making it longer, and to rehearse in calm conditions before calling on it under strain.

units: an acquaintance of the narrator sets down her inner states in a notebook
she records the moral exhaustion that arrives at the end of the week with no clear cause
she spots her irritation in the way she slams the cupboards shut
she also notes the worry that comes before a dreaded exchange
she marks down feeling relieved, because that state fades from memory too quickly
she records the embarrassment that reddens her cheeks after an unfortunate remark
the narrator asks her what this record is good for
the woman answers that she wants to recognise herself, not reform herself
she claims that naming an inner state by its name already settles it
text: A friend explained to me the other evening that she keeps a notebook of her moods, and she described exactly what goes into it. Weariness comes first, the flat heavy sort that settles on her towards the end of the week for no reason she can identify. Then irritation, which she recognises by the way she slams the cupboards shut. Apprehension gets an entry too, on the evenings when a difficult conversation is waiting for her. She writes down relief as well, she said, because it slips out of memory almost immediately once the worry has lifted. Last comes awkwardness, that prickle in her cheeks after she believes she has said the wrong thing. I asked her what purpose the whole inventory served. She is not attempting to mend herself, she said, only to recognise herself, and putting a name to a feeling usually settles it.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: the way melancholy is accounted for has changed over the generations
the earliest healers put low spirits down to an imbalance of the blood
they treated those low spirits by drawing blood off
a further stage consisted in shutting the sick away from public view
that confinement was not aimed at curing them
doctors then began to gather and write down the accounts of their patients
the houses that took people in were fitted with green spaces, paths and workshops
it was assumed at the time that steady activity quietened the mind
conversation became in its turn a means of care
the listening places of today carry the mark of these successive stages
text: The way low spirits get described has shifted from one generation to the next, and the shifts read like a sequence. The earliest healers filed gloom among the disorders of the blood, and their remedy was to draw the blood off. What followed was a stretch of confinement: the afflicted were shut away, not to be cured but to be kept out of common sight. Later, doctors began to listen to what their patients told them and to copy their complaints down into ledgers. The houses that took them in acquired gardens, walking paths and workshops, on the assumption that steady occupation quietened the mind. Nearer our own time, talk itself turned into a treatment, and listening into a craft that had to be taught. Every one of those stages has left its mark on the rooms where people go to be heard today.

units: an annoyance that recurs and is never put into words leaves a lasting print on the memory
silence becomes a store where whatever was left unsaid piles up
that accumulation breeds a stubborn resentment
resentment makes old memories sharper than they really were
the person replays the scene in her mind through the night
this brooding uses up the energy meant for those close to her
a quiet withdrawal from social ties then sets in
being alone allows no contradiction and so strengthens the grievance
getting out of this circle means saying the thing out loud, however clumsily
text: An annoyance that keeps returning and is never spoken wears a groove in the memory. Silence, comfortable at first, turns into a store where everything unsaid is piled up. Out of that pile comes resentment, which gives old memories a sharpness the events themselves never had. At night the sleeper goes back to the scene, plays it again, invents the lines he ought to have delivered. The brooding drains him, because the mind spends on an absent opponent the energy it owes to the people close at hand. Withdrawal follows, quietly: an invitation declined, a call cut short, an evening alone excused as tiredness. And since being alone leaves nothing to contradict the grievance, it hardens it instead of wearing it away. Breaking the circle takes one sentence said out loud, however clumsy.

units: a trainer in charge of a night team described this case in a report
the verbal clashes happened mostly at the end of the shift
examination of the data ruled out output load as the main cause
the peaks of activity fell earlier in the shift
the tensions broke out after the second scheduled break
alertness and resistance to frustration drop at that point
the handover meeting was moved forward to the start of the shift
its length was cut and an order of speaking was brought in
a form on inner state, filled in on arrival and on leaving, served as an indicator
the reported incidents fell after one whole cycle
text: A trainer responsible for a night shift set the following case down in an internal report. Verbal incidents were clustering at the end of the shift, with tempers flaring repeatedly between operators. Examination of the figures ruled out output pressure as the principal factor, since the busiest spells fell earlier in the shift. What the records did show was that exchanges soured after the second scheduled break, the point at which alertness drops and tolerance of frustration goes with it. The remedy adopted was to move the handover meeting to the start of the shift, cut its length and impose an order of speaking. A short form on how people felt, filled in on arrival and on leaving, served as the indicator. After a full cycle the reported incidents had fallen away, and the team described a lasting calm.

units: two calming procedures must be told apart before being used against a surge of anxiety
the first procedure consists in controlling the breath while seated, one hand on the stomach
the out-breath must last longer than the in-breath and the sequence is repeated
this procedure works very fast and calls for no equipment
its effect fades as soon as the annoyance shows itself again
the second procedure consists in writing the fear down then noting beside it what makes it unlikely
the page must be read again at the end of the day
this second procedure demands more effort and comforts less on the spot
its benefit, on the other hand, lasts several weeks
combining the breath for the emergency and the writing for the ground is advised
text: Two calming methods deserve to be told carefully apart before either one is applied to a surge of anxiety. The first works on the breath. Sit down, rest a hand on the stomach, draw the air in slowly, let it out for longer still, and repeat until the pulse eases. Its merit is speed: it takes effect within moments and requires no equipment whatsoever. Its limit lies in how long the effect holds, which is barely past the moment the trouble returns. The second method works on words. Write the exact fear down, set beside it whatever makes that fear unlikely, and read the page again in the evening. It asks for steadier effort and offers less comfort on the spot, yet the benefit carries over several weeks. In practice, combine the two: the breath for emergencies, the writing for the ground beneath them.

units: a place for people to talk has been set up in a former storage building
its team tells apart several functions of the site
the first function is the immediate welcome, with no appointment and no papers
group sessions bring together visitors touched by the same ordeal
these shared ordeals take in the death of someone close, a break-up or the loss of a job
a body workshop lets tension be released by walking and stretching
a fourth function consists in sending the heaviest cases on to a specialist
the manager reports that attendance has doubled since the opening
half of the visitors come again
text: A listening centre installed in a former storage warehouse has opened its doors to the public, and the team there sets out several distinct uses of the place. The first is the walk-in welcome: anyone can push the door and speak to a trained listener, with no file to open and nothing whatever to justify. The second covers the group sessions, which gather people around a shared ordeal, a death, a separation, the loss of a job. The third is a movement workshop, where tension is loosened by walking and stretching rather than by telling a story. The fourth use is quieter and amounts to referral: visitors whose distress runs deeper than a short talk can relieve are passed on to a practitioner. The manager reports that attendance has doubled since the opening and that half the visitors come back.

units: a child collapses in the middle of the room and the din fills the home
the fit starts with a stiff back, shut fists and a clamped jaw
the first gulp of crying cuts the breathing off
an odd silence follows that first gulp
the crying then carries on in successive waves
the slightest clumsy word sets the wave off again
the face reddens and the hair sticks to the temples
the calm arrives for no reason you can see and the hiccups grow further apart
the child ends up slumped against a shoulder, worn out and surprised at the quiet
he then asks for water as though nothing had happened
text: You will certainly have seen it: a child collapses in the middle of the room and the noise fills the whole flat. It starts with the back going stiff, the fists shut tight, the jaw clamped. Then comes the first sob, an enormous one that cuts the breathing off and leaves an odd silence behind it. After that the crying settles into waves, it climbs, it drops, it climbs again the moment anybody says the wrong thing. The face goes red, the hair sticks to the temples, the hands hunt for a bit of cloth to grip. Then, without anything you can point to having changed, the swell weakens. The breath breaks into hiccups that come further and further apart. In the end the child slumps against a shoulder, worn out, warm, half astonished at the quiet that has returned, and asks for water as if nothing had happened.

units: people are now required to keep a permanently steady mood
this requirement produces the opposite of its aim
a dark inner state is taken as a weakness of character
whoever feels it therefore hides it from those around him
in hiding it, he loses the sharing that would have eased it
the loneliness that results makes the burden heavier still
the inner state sets fast instead of flowing away
a shame at failing is then added, weightier than the original hurt
this chain explains the growing number of consultations begun too late
the writer judges it less costly to allow sadness to be spoken than to treat it afterwards
text: People are now expected to display an even mood in every circumstance, and the demand produces precisely the opposite of what it aims at. Because a dark feeling is read as a flaw of character, whoever happens to carry one conceals it. Concealing it, he shares it with nobody close to him, and so forfeits the one thing that would have eased it. The loneliness that follows adds further to the weight, so that the feeling hardens and settles instead of passing through. Then comes the shame of not managing, heavier by far than the hurt it started from. That chain explains the rise in consultations that are begun far too late, once the trouble has thickened beyond what ordinary talk can untie. Allowing sadness to be spoken aloud would cost a great deal less than treating it after seasons of silence.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: the woman who runs a bookbinding workshop did not take up the trade out of any liking for the material
she said little and lost her words in front of a counter clerk
she cancelled appointments for fear of being looked at
her life had shrunk to a stretch of two streets
an acquaintance offered her to come and sew folded sheets with no obligation to talk
the change came from the work of the hands itself
her speech came loose while her hands were busy
she first served customers in short sentences, then commented on her technique
she ended up taking on an apprentice in training
she says the fear is still there but no longer governs how she spends her weeks
text: The woman who runs the bookbinding workshop at the back of the courtyard did not take up the trade out of any particular love of paper. She spoke little, lost her words in front of a counter clerk, and gave up appointments rather than be looked at. Her life had shrunk until it fitted into two streets. One season an acquaintance offered her a place sewing folded sheets, with no obligation to speak to anyone. She sewed through whole evenings without lifting her head, and it suited her. The turn came from the work of the hands: with her fingers busy, her voice loosened without her noticing. She answered customers in short sentences at first, then explained what she was doing, then took on an apprentice. The fear has not gone, she says, but it no longer governs how her weeks are spent.

units: two instruments for gauging mood are in use in consulting rooms
the first instrument is a short questionnaire filled in by the patient himself
its items ask about the week that has just gone by
its internal consistency is satisfactory and it takes little attention to complete
this lightness allows repeated measurement
it is affected by a desirability bias which flatters the profile declared
the second instrument is a structured interview led by a trained professional
its scoring rests as much on observed signs as on what is said
it stands up better to the bias but costs a great deal in time and depends on the scorer's training
the writer recommends the questionnaire for close follow-up and the interview for settling a diagnosis
text: Two instruments for gauging mood are in circulation in consulting rooms, and the comparison is worth drawing on precise criteria. The first is a short self-report questionnaire whose items ask about the week just gone. Its internal consistency is sound and it demands little attention to complete, which makes repeated measurement possible. It suffers, though, from a desirability bias: the respondent presents a rosier profile than the one he lives with. The second is a structured interview conducted by a trained practitioner, scored on observed signs as much as on what is said. It stands up better to the bias, but its length makes it costly and its reliability depends on how well the scorer has been drilled. For close follow-up the questionnaire will do; for a diagnosis the interview is required.

units: the writer answers someone close who was worried about how she was
a change of home came before a stretch of bad sleep
the ringing of the phone made her body clench
an acquaintance suggested she write down her anxieties at the end of the day
she thought the advice absurd before she took it up
the writing brought out a recurring fear of being left behind
a specialist traced that anxious bond back to childhood
she now warns the people close to her instead of shutting herself away
text: Your message asked whether I was any better, so let me go back to where it started. The week we moved, sleep came apart, and every time the phone rang my shoulders locked as though someone had shouted at me. A woman I know told me to write down, each evening, whatever had tightened my throat that day. It struck me as a daft thing to do. I did it anyway. Ten evenings in, the same fear kept turning up on the page: that the people I love would quietly let me go. A psychologist put it plainly. A bond as anxious as that takes shape early, in childhood, and it loosens once you dare ask for help. So now I tell people when I am struggling, instead of disappearing without a word. It still costs me something. Last night I laughed properly, without keeping watch on myself. Write soon, and tell me about your week.

units: a mental health specialist answers questions about thoughts that keep repeating
the brain meets a threat to a relationship almost as it meets a threat to the body
the scene is replayed in the hope of finding a way out
the repeating holds the alarm open instead of settling it
the open alarm sets the repeating thoughts going again
sleep is broken because the watch kept inside does not stop at night
those close by tire of hearing the same complaint and draw away
that withdrawal deepens the loneliness of the one who ruminates
the specialist advises writing the whole episode out once
text: What becomes of a grievance you cannot put down? We put the question to a researcher in clinical psychology. Her answer came in a single word: rumination. A threat to a relationship registers in the brain much as a threat to the body does, and so the scene is replayed, again and again, in the hope that some way out will show itself. Does the replaying help? Not at all. It holds the alarm open, and the open alarm sets the thoughts running once more. Why is the sleep of such people broken? Because the watch kept inside never stands down when the light goes off. And those around them? They tire of the same complaint and drift away, which leaves the one who ruminates lonelier than before. What, then, does she advise? Writing the episode out whole, one evening, from end to end, and shutting the notebook. Thoughts given sentences stop circling.

units: a young girl admits she cannot put what she feels into words
her aunt does not press her and pours her something hot to drink
the aunt says she kept quiet at the same age out of reserve
the aunt holds that such silence shuts you in rather than shields you
the girl is afraid her words would set her mother crying
the aunt suggests placing the sensation instead of naming the sorrow
the girl points to two spots on her neck
her breathing loosens once she has described them
they settle on a hand laid on the table as an agreed signal
the mother sits down beside her without asking a thing
text: I cannot say what I feel, the girl murmured, her eyes on the rug. Her aunt did not press her. She poured out tea, and admitted that at the same age she had kept quiet too, out of a kind of reserve. You believe you are sparing everyone, she said, and all you do is shut yourself in. The girl answered that words felt too heavy, and that hers would set her mother crying. So her aunt offered a way round it: describe not the sorrow but the place where it sits. The throat first, the girl said, then the back of the neck, and her breathing loosened as she said it. They settled on a signal, hardly visible to anyone else: a hand laid flat on the table would mean it was time to talk. That evening the hand went down, and her mother came and sat beside her, asking nothing at all. The wordless thing calmed the whole house.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: having no instruments, the old practitioners went by what patients told them
their approach joined long listening to the setting side by side of similar cases
practitioners who came later took bodily measurements
among those measurements were the beat of the heart and the length of sleep
the old approach caught the fine shading but missed the regularities
the instrumented approach caught the regularities but lost the fine shading
a feeling pushed out of awareness produces no sign that can be measured
the two approaches were later joined together
each makes up for the blind spot of the other
text: Before recording instruments existed, physicians described disorders of mood from what their patients told them, and nothing else. The method rested on listening at length and on setting like cases beside one another. Clinicians trained later went about it differently: they measured the beat of the heart, the resistance of the skin, the hours of sleep. The older way caught the fine shading and missed the regularities; the instrumented one caught the regularities and let the shading escape. The difference lies in the material itself, for a feeling pushed out of awareness leaves no mark a device can pick up, whereas a bodily reaction writes itself down. In the end the two traditions met: the patient is questioned while his inner responses are followed, and the records compared afterwards. Neither replaces the other, and each corrects the blind spot of its neighbour.

units: three sorts of sign reveal that the person you are talking to is uneasy
the first sign is a matter of posture, with the shoulders drawing in
a hand travelling up towards the face goes with that posture
the second sign is in the voice, whose pace slackens
the third sign belongs to the eyes, which settle on nothing
unease has to do with the picture one gives to others
fear, on the contrary, has to do with a danger coming from outside
shame is set apart by lasting longer and cutting deeper
an alert onlooker can lower his voice and look away
text: Three sorts of sign will tell you that the person in front of you is uneasy. The first is a matter of posture: the shoulders draw in, the chin drops, and a hand travels up towards the face as though to cover it. The second lies in the voice, where the pace slackens, sentences break off, and the tone loses its footing. The third belongs to the eyes, which slide away, come back briefly, and settle on nothing. What separates these signals from those of fear is their target, since unease has to do with the picture one gives to others, while fear has to do with a danger coming from outside. They differ from shame as well, which lasts longer and cuts deeper, and drives a person to withdraw altogether. Reading them is of most use to the onlooker, who can lower his voice, look away, leave a gap in the talk. That restraint often makes the conversation bearable for the one who feels exposed.

units: a singer who is not a professional attends an audition in a borrowed hall
he had worked at his piece for several weeks
an uneasiness took hold of him the moment he stepped onto the platform
his hands went cold and his voice missed the opening
the panel granted him a second try
that second attempt turned out worse than the first
a woman musician suggested he stand with his back to the room
the performance then came out true and easy
he afterwards sang the ending again facing the room
he puts his trouble down to being looked at and not to the singing
text: A singer who does not do it for a living came to an audition in a hall lent by a group of musicians. He had worked at his piece for weeks and believed himself ready. The moment he stepped onto the platform something turned over in him: the ceiling seemed to come down, his hands went cold, and his voice missed the opening note. He asked to begin again, and the panel let him. The second attempt was worse than the first. One of the accompanists then suggested he sing with his back to the room. He laughed, and tried it. The piece came out whole, in tune, almost easy. They asked him afterwards to turn round and take the last verse facing them, and he sang it without a tremor. What frightened him, he decided, was never the singing but the being looked at, and the smallest detour had been enough to disarm it.

units: the first step is to spot the bodily signal of anxiety
naming the feeling with a word takes some of its force away
you must write down exactly the outcome you dread
you then weigh the gravity you imagine against how likely it really is
lengthening the outward breath slows the beat of the heart
arriving early spares you the strain of a room already filled
putting your feet on the floor tells the brain where the body's balance is
asking for a drink breaks the runaway feeling if panic comes
text: Start by catching the moment your stomach tightens before a meeting, because a feeling that has been named loses some of its force. Then put down in your notebook exactly what you dread: being cut off, coming across as useless, sitting through an awkward silence. Write the outcome you picture, and beside it how likely it really is, and the gap between the two will jump out at you. Breathe afterwards, drawing the outward breath long, since it is the going out and not the coming in that steadies the beat of the heart. Arrive a little early, because walking into a room already filled winds you up, whereas taking your seat before the others lets it drop. While the talk goes on, keep both feet flat on the floor, as that contact tells the brain where your balance is. And if panic climbs all the same, ask for water: the gesture gives you something to hold and breaks the loop.

units: a place offering psychological support opened in a street of shops
the men who were seen there lost their temper in the first session
those men did not turn up for the sessions that followed
the team first put those departures down to a want of willingness
the reception room could be seen from the street through a pane of glass
being open to view turned unease into aggression
the entrance was moved round to the courtyard side
a curtain was hung and the lighting brought down
the number of people breaking off their treatment fell by half
the manager advises studying the place before explaining a behaviour
text: In an old quarter, a counselling centre opened at the end of a street of small shops. The staff kept meeting the same wall: men who came to be seen lost their temper in the first session, and then never appeared again. The team put it at first down to a want of willingness. Closer observation showed something else. The reception room was glazed onto the street, so that whoever sat there sat in full view of the people going past, and the unease turned into aggression. The remedy was a matter of building work before it was a matter of therapy. The entrance was moved round to the inner courtyard, a heavy curtain was hung, the lighting was brought down. Within a season, the number of people breaking off after the first appointment had fallen by half. The manager draws a lesson from it that she repeats to her trainees: before you explain a behaviour, look hard at the place that produced it.

units: a waiting room stands apart from the other spaces in the building
its walls are a muted green against a corridor of glaring white
the seats there are turned towards one another
in the corridor the seats are ranged along the wall
a thick floor covering smothers the sound of footsteps
the hard floor of the entrance, on the contrary, throws the noise back
worn magazines lie on a low piece of furniture
those who arrive show a keen agitation in voice and gesture
they leave the room at a steadier pace
text: The waiting room at the practice is like no other space in the building. Its walls carry a muted green, where the corridor next door is a glare of white. In here the armchairs are turned slightly towards one another, as though a conversation were expected; out there the chairs are ranged along the partition. A thick carpet swallows the sound of footsteps, while the tiled floor of the entrance throws every heel back at you. On the low table lie worn magazines, shabbier than the ones at the desk, and perhaps it is that untidiness which reassures. The people who come in are keyed up, their voices pitched high, their hands quick; they go out again at a steadier pace, the jaw unclenched. The room cures nothing, of course. It only prepares, the way an airlock does, the passage from one inward state to another.

units: the writer disputes the idea that sadness is a fault to be put right
a feeling points to what has value for the one who feels it
the pace of exchanges on screens makes a mood that lasts look suspect
that pressure leads people to dread their own inward slowness
the ways of assessing things favour whatever can be counted
inward experience therefore falls outside the studies, for want of any way to code it
a feeling pushed down comes back as irritability or exhaustion
the writer grants that pain which goes on belongs to proper care
treating ordinary sorrow as an illness takes from each of us the words to speak of ourselves
text: We ought to stop treating sadness as a fault to be put right. First point: a feeling is not a defect of manufacture, it is information about what has value for the one who feels it. Second point: the pace demanded by our exchanges on screens makes any mood that lasts look suspect, so that we end by dreading our own inward slowness. Third point: the ways we have of assessing things favour whatever can be counted, and inward experience, being hard to code, drops out of the studies. Fourth point: a feeling pushed down does not go away, it comes back elsewhere, as irritability or as a tiredness that will not lift. Someone will object that pain which goes on and on belongs to proper care, and the objection holds. But to run ordinary sorrow together with illness is to take from each of us the words for saying what we are living through.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: the main figure answers calls from people in distress
early in her working life she raised the volume of her voice
that way of doing things drove callers to break off the exchange
she changed her way of speaking from top to bottom
she now leaves pauses and slows her delivery
she gives back the last word the caller has spoken
the caller's breathing ends up falling into step with hers
her colleagues have taken up the same method
she says this work has changed how she hears the people close to her
text: She speaks softly, the adviser on the helpline, and there is nothing accidental about it. When she started out, she lifted her voice to carry over the panic of the people ringing in. The effect baffled her. Callers stiffened, cut her off, put the phone down. So she turned the whole thing round. She leaves silences now, she slows down, she gives back the last word she has heard. As the breathing at the other end settles into step with her own, the strain eases without being named. She tells it plainly, with a shrug, as though anyone would have worked it out. Her colleagues took to copying her in earnest, because fewer of their calls were ending early. Then she adds something that makes her smile: the work has taught her to hear her own family, whom she thought she already knew.

units: the text passes judgement on an exhibition given over to the feelings
the first part of the route piles up video installations
that piling up wears out the attention of visitors
the feelings are handled there in a distant, teacherly way
the second part offers a space empty of any screen
there you listen to accounts of grief spoken by strangers
the public slows down there and shows feeling
the last stage invites you to set down on paper the feeling hardest to name
the critic advises walking the place in the other direction
text: You come away from this exhibition on the feelings with mixed impressions. The route through it is badly built at the start: room after room stacks screen upon screen, and the visitor, glutted, skims past everything. Anger, shame and delight get the same cool explanatory treatment, so that nothing in the visitor quickens. The designers seem to have grasped as much, since the second half puts a good deal of that right. A bare room, stripped of screens, asks you to listen to unknown voices telling of a grief; the quiet does the work on its own, and people soften, linger, double back on themselves. The last stage goes further still: you write on a card the feeling you find hardest to name, then post the card into a glass urn. The whole thing is worth the trip, so long as you walk it backwards.

units: the reader has asked a question about the kinship of two feelings
the writer describes fear as a pressure laid on the back of the neck
fear dampens the palms and cuts the breath short
sorrow is likened to a wet weight that covers you over
fear drives you to move whereas sorrow holds you still
both feelings slip away when you try to look at them head on
both grow quieter once you put them into words in front of someone
the writer explains in this way why he writes so often
the writer says he would rather have a clumsy sentence than advice
text: Your question has stayed with me since your letter came: is sorrow anything like fear? I turned it over at the window, and here is what I believe. Fear is a hand laid on the back of the neck. It grips, it presses, it wants you up and moving. It leaves the palms damp and the breath short. Sorrow presses nothing at all. It settles in, it lies on the chest like a soaked blanket, and it asks you to stop. One speeds you up, the other slows you down, and there lies the plainest difference between them. On one point, though, they are alike, and that point has occupied me since the cold months. Both slip away the moment you look straight at them, and both loosen their hold when you say them aloud to someone. That is why I write to you so often. Write back; your clumsiest sentence comforts me better than advice.

units: specialists draw a line between an emotion and a mood
three criteria hold that distinction up
an emotion is brief whereas a mood stretches much further
an emotion bears on a target you can point out
a mood has nobody it can be addressed to
the third criterion has to do with the traces left in the body
will alone does not call off the firing of an emotion
it can on the other hand shape the way that emotion shows
fear sends blood towards the muscles to make the body ready to act
text: Is an emotion, people often ask, really a different thing from a mood? Specialists say that it is, and they rest the case on three criteria. The first is duration: an emotion flares and dies away quickly, whereas a mood stretches over a far wider span. The second is the object: an emotion fastens on a target you can point to, while a mood drifts with nobody to receive it. The third is the mark left on the body, readable in the heartbeat, the sweat and the tightening of muscle. The next question is whether will alone can shut an emotion down. The answer is a qualified one: you shape the way it shows, you do not call off its firing. Last comes the use of fear. It readies the body to act by sending blood towards the muscles, which is why the hands clench and the throat closes.

units: the practitioner opens the session with a harmless question about meals
the young lad claims that he cannot remember
the young lad shuts himself off and folds his arms
the practitioner shifts the subject and speaks of the sound of the rain
the young lad owns up to dreading meals with the family
he explains that everyone at the table stares at him
the practitioner asks him which seat he would rather have
he points to the end of the table, next to the doorway
the practitioner suggests that he raise the matter at home
he agrees in the end and says that he will come back
text: The session opened on a question that seemed to lead absolutely nowhere: the psychologist asked the lad what he had eaten the evening before. He said he could not remember, then turned sullen and silent, arms folded hard across his chest. She did not press him for anything more. She talked instead about the rain hitting the glass and the colour of the sky. After a while the boy said that meals with the family unsettled him, because everyone there watched him without let-up. She asked him what he would do if the seat were his to choose. He said he would take the end of the table, right by the door. She suggested he raise it at home, in words of his own choosing. He wavered, then agreed. On his way out he called back that he would return, and he smiled without turning round.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: healers of long ago put the states of the soul down to inner liquids
that theory won people over because it offered a workable remedy
low spirits were treated by diet or by drawing off blood
failure repeated again and again weakened the belief
watching things directly took the place of the theory
healers recorded the same signs for fear and for rage
they tied those states to the nerves rather than to a fluid
suffering of the mind stopped being seen as a taint to be driven out
out of that reversal came the idea that speech listened to can cure
text: Long before measurement took hold, healers put the states of the soul down to inner liquids that had to be brought back into balance. The doctrine held because it gave people something to do: if low spirits came of an excess, diet or the opening of a vein would surely draw it off. Failure after failure ate away at that confidence, and watching took over from doctrine. Physicians noticed that fear and fury threw up the same signs in patients who had nothing else in common, and they concluded that such states belonged to the nerves and not to any liquid. The consequence of that was a considerable one. Suffering of the mind stopped being handled as a taint to be flushed out, and began instead to be questioned. Out of that turn came the notion that speech carefully received could itself cure.

units: speaking in front of an audience quickens the heart and dampens the hands
the voice starts to shake in that situation
fear itself is not to blame, since it makes the body ready to act
the difficulty comes from the thoughts added on top of the fear
you expect to be shamed and you watch out for unfriendly faces
that watching pushes the alarm higher still
the first remedy is to make the out-breath longer than the in-breath
that lengthening quietens the beat of the heart
the second remedy is to put your attention on a willing listener
carrying your attention outwards breaks the circle that feeds itself
text: It has surely happened to you at some point. Just before you speak to a roomful of attentive people, the heart thumps, the palms turn damp and cold, and the voice starts to shake. Fear is not the trouble; fear is getting you ready to move. The trouble is what you pile on top of it. You tell yourself you are about to look a fool, you scan for the one hard face in the room, and the alarm climbs a notch. The way out comes down to two very ordinary moves. First, breathe out for longer than you breathe in; a stretched out-breath settles the heart. Second, attend to someone else rather than to yourself: find the most willing face in front of you and speak to that person. Turning your attention outwards cuts the loop that keeps you trapped. You may still shake, but you will get to the end.

units: two men have been waiting since the same hour for the same medical test
the first reads a magazine and speaks of his vegetable patch
